options: A tuple whose primary-key attribute is NULL.
A tuple whose foreign key is NULL.
A tuple whose non-key attribute is NULL.
Two tuples that agree on a non-key attribute.

solution.concept: Entity integrity: no component of a primary key may be NULL, because the key is what identifies the tuple. Referential integrity, by contrast, is about foreign keys and explicitly allows NULL.
steps: A primary key identifies a tuple; a NULL is 'unknown', and an unknown value cannot identify anything — so (A) violates entity integrity.
A NULL foreign key means 'this tuple refers to nothing', which referential integrity permits — (B) is legal.
Non-key attributes may be NULL unless a NOT NULL constraint says otherwise — (C) is legal.
Only key attributes must be unique; duplicates in a non-key attribute are ordinary data — (D) is legal.
solution.trap: Confusing entity integrity with referential integrity, and so rejecting a NULL foreign key. That is exactly the case referential integrity allows.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Entity integrity: no component of a primary key may be NULL, because the key is what identifies the tuple. Referential integrity, by contrast, is about foreign keys and explicitly allows NULL.

Step by step.

  1. A primary key identifies a tuple; a NULL is 'unknown', and an unknown value cannot identify anything — so (A) violates entity integrity.
  2. A NULL foreign key means 'this tuple refers to nothing', which referential integrity permits — (B) is legal.
  3. Non-key attributes may be NULL unless a NOT NULL constraint says otherwise — (C) is legal.
  4. Only key attributes must be unique; duplicates in a non-key attribute are ordinary data — (D) is legal.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Confusing entity integrity with referential integrity, and so rejecting a NULL foreign key. That is exactly the case referential integrity allows.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Relation R has 4 tuples and 3 attributes; relation S has 5 tuples and 2 attributes. They share exactly one attribute B, which is a key of R and a foreign key in S that is never NULL. Every tuple of S matches exactly one tuple of R. The number of tuples in R ⋈ S is

solution.concept: A natural join pairs tuples that agree on the common attribute. When the common attribute is a key on one side, each tuple on the other side has at most one partner.
steps: Each of the 5 tuples of S has a B-value that is a key value of R, so it matches exactly one R-tuple.
That produces exactly one joined tuple per S-tuple: 5.
Some R-tuples may match nothing and simply do not appear — the join is not an outer join, so R's 4 tuples do not add to the count.
solution.trap: Multiplying 4 × 5 = 20, which is the size of the Cartesian product and only an upper bound for a join. Because B is a key of R, no S-tuple can have two partners.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A natural join pairs tuples that agree on the common attribute. When the common attribute is a key on one side, each tuple on the other side has at most one partner.

Step by step.

  1. Each of the 5 tuples of S has a B-value that is a key value of R, so it matches exactly one R-tuple.
  2. That produces exactly one joined tuple per S-tuple: 5.
  3. Some R-tuples may match nothing and simply do not appear — the join is not an outer join, so R's 4 tuples do not add to the count.

Answer: Option (B) — 5.

Common misconception. Multiplying 4 × 5 = 20, which is the size of the Cartesian product and only an upper bound for a join. Because B is a key of R, no S-tuple can have two partners.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: For union-compatible relations R and S, which expression is equivalent to R ∩ S?
options: R − (R − S)
(R − S) − S
(R ∪ S) − R
πall(R) − πall(S)

solution.concept: Intersection is not primitive in the core algebra; it is defined from set difference.
steps: R − S keeps the tuples of R that are not in S.
Removing those from R leaves exactly the tuples of R that are in S: R − (R − S) = R ∩ S.
(B) simplifies to R − S; (C) is S − R; (D) is just R − S again.
solution.trap: Choosing (R ∪ S) − R, which looks like it 'removes the overlap' but actually returns S − R — the opposite set.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Intersection is not primitive in the core algebra; it is defined from set difference.

Step by step.

  1. R − S keeps the tuples of R that are not in S.
  2. Removing those from R leaves exactly the tuples of R that are in S: R − (R − S) = R ∩ S.
  3. (B) simplifies to R − S; (C) is S − R; (D) is just R − S again.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Choosing (R ∪ S) − R, which looks like it 'removes the overlap' but actually returns S − R — the opposite set.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Consider Works(eid, pid) and Projects(pid). Which expressions return exactly the eids of employees who work on every project? (Select all that apply.)
options: πeid(Works) ÷ πpid(Projects)
πeid(Works) − πeid((πeid(Works) × πpid(Projects)) − Works)
πeid(Works) − πeid(πeid(Works) × πpid(Projects))
πeid(Works ⋈ Projects)

solution.concept: 'For all' is division. Equivalently, it is 'difference of difference': take everyone, subtract those who miss at least one project.
steps: (A) is the division operator applied directly: it returns the eids whose set of projects contains the whole of πpid(Projects) — true.
(B) builds the set of missing pairs — every (eid, pid) combination that is not in Works — projects it to eid, and subtracts it from all employees. What survives misses no project — true.
(C) subtracts all employees who work on anything at all, which returns only employees with no project — false.
(D) returns every employee who works on at least one project — that is 'exists', not 'for all' — false.
solution.trap: Reading (D) as the answer. A join with the projects relation answers 'works on some project'; the universal quantifier needs division or the double difference.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. 'For all' is division. Equivalently, it is 'difference of difference': take everyone, subtract those who miss at least one project.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is the division operator applied directly: it returns the eids whose set of projects contains the whole of πpid(Projects) — true.
  2. (B) builds the set of missing pairs — every (eid, pid) combination that is not in Works — projects it to eid, and subtracts it from all employees. What survives misses no project — true.
  3. (C) subtracts all employees who work on anything at all, which returns only employees with no project — false.
  4. (D) returns every employee who works on at least one project — that is 'exists', not 'for all' — false.

Answer: Options (A) and (B).

Common misconception. Reading (D) as the answer. A join with the projects relation answers 'works on some project'; the universal quantifier needs division or the double difference.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Let R(A) = {1, 2, 3} and S(A) = {2, 3, 4}. The number of tuples in R ⋈R.A < S.A S is

solution.concept: A theta join pairs every tuple of one relation with every tuple of the other that satisfies the condition — here a strict inequality, not an equality on a common attribute.
steps: List the pairs (r, s) with r ∈ R, s ∈ S and r < s.
r = 1: s = 2, 3, 4 → 3 pairs.
r = 2: s = 3, 4 → 2 pairs.
r = 3: s = 4 → 1 pair.
Total 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.
solution.trap: Joining on equality of A, which would give only the pairs (2, 2) and (3, 3). The condition is <, and both relations are kept whole — the attribute is not merged.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A theta join pairs every tuple of one relation with every tuple of the other that satisfies the condition — here a strict inequality, not an equality on a common attribute.

Step by step.

  1. List the pairs (r, s) with r ∈ R, s ∈ S and r < s.
  2. r = 1: s = 2, 3, 4 → 3 pairs.
  3. r = 2: s = 3, 4 → 2 pairs.
  4. r = 3: s = 4 → 1 pair.
  5. Total 3 + 2 + 1 = 6.

Answer: 6

Common misconception. Joining on equality of A, which would give only the pairs (2, 2) and (3, 3). The condition is <, and both relations are kept whole — the attribute is not merged.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Let S(B) be a relation with zero tuples. For a relation R(A, B), the division R ÷ S is
options: the empty relation.
πA(R).
undefined, because division needs a non-empty divisor.
R.

solution.concept: Division asks: which A-values are paired with every B-value in S? With an empty S the requirement is vacuously satisfied by every value.
steps: By definition, R ÷ S = { a | for every b ∈ S, (a, b) ∈ R }.
When S = ∅ there is no b to check, so the condition holds for every a that appears in R.
The values of a that appear in R are exactly πA(R), so R ÷ ∅ = πA(R).
Confirm with the derived formula: πA(R) − πA((πA(R) × ∅) − R) = πA(R) − πA(∅) = πA(R).
solution.trap: Answering 'the empty relation' by pattern-matching 'empty input, empty output'. Universally quantified conditions are vacuously true over an empty range, so the result is the largest possible set, not the smallest.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Division asks: which A-values are paired with every B-value in S? With an empty S the requirement is vacuously satisfied by every value.

Step by step.

  1. By definition, R ÷ S = { a | for every b ∈ S, (a, b) ∈ R }.
  2. When S = ∅ there is no b to check, so the condition holds for every a that appears in R.
  3. The values of a that appear in R are exactly πA(R), so R ÷ ∅ = πA(R).
  4. Confirm with the derived formula: πA(R) − πA((πA(R) × ∅) − R) = πA(R) − πA(∅) = πA(R).

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Answering 'the empty relation' by pattern-matching 'empty input, empty output'. Universally quantified conditions are vacuously true over an empty range, so the result is the largest possible set, not the smallest.

Takeaway. This vacuous-truth case is the same reason a universal statement over an empty domain is true, and it is a favourite GATE trap.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which of the following is not a unary relational algebra operator?
options: σ (selection)
π (projection)
⋈ (natural join)
ρ (rename)

solution.concept: Arity of an operator = number of relations it consumes. Selection, projection and rename each transform one relation; a join combines two.
steps: σcond(R) filters the tuples of a single relation — unary.
πattrs(R) keeps a subset of the attributes of a single relation — unary.
ρ renames a relation or its attributes — unary.
R ⋈ S needs both R and S — it is binary, so it is the answer.
solution.trap: Classifying the join as unary because 'it acts on the attributes in common'. It consumes two relations, which is what arity measures.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Arity of an operator = number of relations it consumes. Selection, projection and rename each transform one relation; a join combines two.

Step by step.

  1. σcond(R) filters the tuples of a single relation — unary.
  2. πattrs(R) keeps a subset of the attributes of a single relation — unary.
  3. ρ renames a relation or its attributes — unary.
  4. R ⋈ S needs both R and S — it is binary, so it is the answer.

Answer: Option (C).

Common misconception. Classifying the join as unary because 'it acts on the attributes in common'. It consumes two relations, which is what arity measures.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Let R(A, B) and S(B, C), where B is a key of R and a foreign key in S that is never NULL. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: R ⋈ S has exactly as many tuples as S.
R ⋈ S has attributes A, B and C.
R ⋈ S can contain more tuples than |R| × |S|.
The natural join is associative.

solution.concept: A natural join equates the common attributes and keeps one copy of each. When the common attribute is a key on one side, the join is a lookup, not a product.
steps: Every tuple of S has a non-NULL B-value, and referential integrity guarantees a matching R-tuple. Since B is a key of R, that partner is unique — one joined tuple per S-tuple, so the counts are equal — (A) is true.
The common attribute appears once, and the remaining attributes of both sides are retained — (B) is true.
A join can never produce more than the Cartesian product |R| × |S|; it selects a subset of those pairs — (C) is false.
(R ⋈ S) ⋈ T = R ⋈ (S ⋈ T) for natural joins, and it is commutative too — (D) is true.
solution.trap: Believing a natural join can blow up the row count. Duplication on the common attribute is what multiplies rows, and a key on one side makes that impossible.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A natural join equates the common attributes and keeps one copy of each. When the common attribute is a key on one side, the join is a lookup, not a product.

Step by step.

  1. Every tuple of S has a non-NULL B-value, and referential integrity guarantees a matching R-tuple. Since B is a key of R, that partner is unique — one joined tuple per S-tuple, so the counts are equal — (A) is true.
  2. The common attribute appears once, and the remaining attributes of both sides are retained — (B) is true.
  3. A join can never produce more than the Cartesian product |R| × |S|; it selects a subset of those pairs — (C) is false.
  4. (R ⋈ S) ⋈ T = R ⋈ (S ⋈ T) for natural joins, and it is commutative too — (D) is true.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Believing a natural join can blow up the row count. Duplication on the common attribute is what multiplies rows, and a key on one side makes that impossible.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Relations R(A, B) and S(A, B) are union-compatible, with |R| = 12, |S| = 9 and |R − S| = 5. The number of tuples in R ∩ S is

solution.concept: R splits into two disjoint parts: the tuples it shares with S, and the tuples it does not.
steps: R = (R − S) ∪ (R ∩ S), and the two parts are disjoint.
So |R| = |R − S| + |R ∩ S|.
Substituting: 12 = 5 + |R ∩ S|, hence |R ∩ S| = 7.
solution.trap: Using |R ∪ S| instead: that would give 12 + 9 − 7 = 14, a different quantity. The stated set is the difference, not the union.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. R splits into two disjoint parts: the tuples it shares with S, and the tuples it does not.

Step by step.

  1. R = (R − S) ∪ (R ∩ S), and the two parts are disjoint.
  2. So |R| = |R − S| + |R ∩ S|.
  3. Substituting: 12 = 5 + |R ∩ S|, hence |R ∩ S| = 7.

Answer: 7

Common misconception. Using |R ∪ S| instead: that would give 12 + 9 − 7 = 14, a different quantity. The stated set is the difference, not the union.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: In the tuple relational calculus formula { t | ∃s ∈ R (t[A] = s[A]) }, the variable t is
options: bound by the existential quantifier.
free.
quantified over the domain of A.
unsafe.

solution.concept: A variable is free when it is not in the scope of a quantifier. The free variables of a formula are exactly the columns of the result.
steps: s is introduced by ∃s ∈ R, so s is bound.
t is never introduced by a quantifier — it appears on the left of the bar and inside the formula as a free variable.
Free variables supply the output columns, which is why the result is a set of t tuples — so (B) is true.
Quantification over the domain of A is domain calculus syntax; here the range is a relation, so (C) is false. Nothing about safety is violated, so (D) is false.
solution.trap: Assuming the variable on the left of the bar is bound because it 'belongs to' the query. Being on the left of the bar is precisely what makes it free.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A variable is free when it is not in the scope of a quantifier. The free variables of a formula are exactly the columns of the result.

Step by step.

  1. s is introduced by ∃s ∈ R, so s is bound.
  2. t is never introduced by a quantifier — it appears on the left of the bar and inside the formula as a free variable.
  3. Free variables supply the output columns, which is why the result is a set of t tuples — so (B) is true.
  4. Quantification over the domain of A is domain calculus syntax; here the range is a relation, so (C) is false. Nothing about safety is violated, so (D) is false.

Answer: Option (B).

Common misconception. Assuming the variable on the left of the bar is bound because it 'belongs to' the query. Being on the left of the bar is precisely what makes it free.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the domain relational calculus are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: A query has the form { ⟨x₁, …, xₙ⟩ | P(x₁, …, xₙ) }.
Its variables range over domain values rather than over whole tuples.
Safety confines the result to values drawn from the active domain.
It is strictly more expressive than relational algebra.

solution.concept: Domain calculus is the value-based counterpart of tuple calculus: the variables are single values, and the result is a set of value-tuples.
steps: The result is a set of value-tuples ⟨x₁, …, xₙ⟩ satisfying P — (A) is true.
Each xᵢ ranges over the domain of an attribute, not over tuples — that is the distinction from tuple calculus — (B) is true.
Safety restricts every variable to the active domain — the set of values actually occurring in the database — which is what makes the result finite — (C) is true.
Domain calculus, tuple calculus and relational algebra are all equivalent in expressive power (Codd's theorem), so (D) is false.
solution.trap: Believing one calculus is stronger than the other. Both are exactly as strong as relational algebra — and all three fall short of transitive closure.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Domain calculus is the value-based counterpart of tuple calculus: the variables are single values, and the result is a set of value-tuples.

Step by step.

  1. The result is a set of value-tuples ⟨x₁, …, xₙ⟩ satisfying P — (A) is true.
  2. Each xᵢ ranges over the domain of an attribute, not over tuples — that is the distinction from tuple calculus — (B) is true.
  3. Safety restricts every variable to the active domain — the set of values actually occurring in the database — which is what makes the result finite — (C) is true.
  4. Domain calculus, tuple calculus and relational algebra are all equivalent in expressive power (Codd's theorem), so (D) is false.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Believing one calculus is stronger than the other. Both are exactly as strong as relational algebra — and all three fall short of transitive closure.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Let R(A, B) = {(1, 2), (2, 3), (3, 1), (4, 2), (5, 3)}. The number of tuples in { ⟨a₁, a₂⟩ | ∃b (R(a₁, b) ∧ R(a₂, b) ∧ a₁ ≠ a₂) } is

solution.concept: The shared bound variable b links two occurrences of the same relation — a self-join expressed in calculus. The condition a₁ ≠ a₂ removes the diagonal.
steps: Group the tuples by b.
b = 2: a ∈ {1, 4} → the ordered pairs (1, 4) and (4, 1) → 2.
b = 3: a ∈ {2, 5} → (2, 5) and (5, 2) → 2.
b = 1: a ∈ {3} only → no pair with a₁ ≠ a₂ → 0.
Total 2 + 2 + 0 = 4.
solution.trap: Forgetting that the answer is ordered. ⟨a₁, a₂⟩ and ⟨a₂, a₁⟩ are different tuples, so {1, 4} contributes two, not one. Dropping the a₁ ≠ a₂ condition would add the three diagonal tuples.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The shared bound variable b links two occurrences of the same relation — a self-join expressed in calculus. The condition a₁ ≠ a₂ removes the diagonal.

Step by step.

  1. Group the tuples by b.
  2. b = 2: a ∈ {1, 4} → the ordered pairs (1, 4) and (4, 1) → 2.
  3. b = 3: a ∈ {2, 5} → (2, 5) and (5, 2) → 2.
  4. b = 1: a ∈ {3} only → no pair with a₁ ≠ a₂ → 0.
  5. Total 2 + 2 + 0 = 4.

Answer: 4

Common misconception. Forgetting that the answer is ordered. ⟨a₁, a₂⟩ and ⟨a₂, a₁⟩ are different tuples, so {1, 4} contributes two, not one. Dropping the a₁ ≠ a₂ condition would add the three diagonal tuples.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: For union-compatible R(A, B) and S(A, B), which tuple calculus expression is equivalent to R − S?
options: { t | t ∈ R ∧ ¬(t ∈ S) }
{ t | ¬(t ∈ R) ∧ t ∈ S }
{ t | t ∈ R ∨ t ∈ S }
{ t | ¬(t ∈ R ∧ t ∈ S) }

solution.concept: Translation is compositional: ∧ for 'and', ∨ for 'or', ¬ for 'not', and a membership clause for each relation.
steps: 'In R and not in S' translates to t ∈ R ∧ ¬(t ∈ S) — (A).
(B) is S − R, the other difference.
(C) is R ∪ S.
(D) is the complement of the intersection — everything except the shared tuples.
solution.trap: Swapping the operands: t ∈ R ∧ ¬(t ∈ S) and ¬(t ∈ R) ∧ t ∈ S look symmetric but are different sets. Order matters in difference.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Translation is compositional: ∧ for 'and', ∨ for 'or', ¬ for 'not', and a membership clause for each relation.

Step by step.

  1. 'In R and not in S' translates to t ∈ R ∧ ¬(t ∈ S) — (A).
  2. (B) is S − R, the other difference.
  3. (C) is R ∪ S.
  4. (D) is the complement of the intersection — everything except the shared tuples.

Answer: Option (A).

Common misconception. Swapping the operands: t ∈ R ∧ ¬(t ∈ S) and ¬(t ∈ R) ∧ t ∈ S look symmetric but are different sets. Order matters in difference.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which one of the following tuple calculus expressions is safe?
options: { t | ¬(t ∈ R) }
{ t | t ∈ R ∨ t[A] > 5 }
{ t | t ∈ S ∧ ¬(t ∈ R) }
{ t | t[A] = 3 }

solution.concept: Safety is a syntactic test: every free variable must be confined by a positive membership clause in a relation, so the result is drawn from the finite active domain.
steps: (A) has a free t under a negation with no relation bounding it — it admits every tuple not in R, an infinite set. Unsafe.
(B) is a disjunction whose second branch, t[A] > 5, is unbounded — a ∨ is safe only if both branches are. Unsafe.
(C) bounds t by the positive clause t ∈ S; the negation then only filters within that finite set. Safe.
(D) constrains one attribute and leaves the rest unconstrained — infinitely many tuples satisfy it. Unsafe.
solution.trap: Assuming any formula with a negation is unsafe, or that a ∨ is safe as long as one branch is bounded. A negated or disjunctive subformula is safe only when something positive in the formula still confines the variable.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Safety is a syntactic test: every free variable must be confined by a positive membership clause in a relation, so the result is drawn from the finite active domain.

Step by step.

  1. (A) has a free t under a negation with no relation bounding it — it admits every tuple not in R, an infinite set. Unsafe.
  2. (B) is a disjunction whose second branch, t[A] > 5, is unbounded — a ∨ is safe only if both branches are. Unsafe.
  3. (C) bounds t by the positive clause t ∈ S; the negation then only filters within that finite set. Safe.
  4. (D) constrains one attribute and leaves the rest unconstrained — infinitely many tuples satisfy it. Unsafe.

Answer: Option (C).

Common misconception. Assuming any formula with a negation is unsafe, or that a ∨ is safe as long as one branch is bounded. A negated or disjunctive subformula is safe only when something positive in the formula still confines the variable.

Takeaway. The practical rule: a variable is confined if some positive membership t ∈ R appears in the same conjunction. Filtering inside a confined range is always safe.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which of the following sets contains only Data Definition Language (DDL) statements?
options: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE
CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE
GRANT, REVOKE, DENY
SELECT, COMMIT, ROLLBACK

solution.concept: SQL statements are grouped by what they act on. DDL defines and changes the schema (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME). DML changes the data inside the objects (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE). DCL controls privileges (GRANT, REVOKE). TCL controls transactions (COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT).
steps: Check each word against the four groups: definition, manipulation, control, transaction.
Option (B) lists four schema-changing statements only — all DDL.
Option (A) is the DML family; (C) is DCL; (D) mixes a DML query with two transaction-control statements.
solution.final: Option (B) — CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE are all DDL.
solution.trap: TRUNCATE looks like a row operation, so it is often filed under DML. In the SQL standard it is a DDL statement: it drops and re-creates the table's storage rather than deleting rows one at a time, which is why it is far faster than an unqualified DELETE.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. SQL statements are grouped by what they act on. DDL defines and changes the schema (CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME). DML changes the data inside the objects (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE). DCL controls privileges (GRANT, REVOKE). TCL controls transactions (COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT).

Step by step.

  1. Check each word against the four groups: definition, manipulation, control, transaction.
  2. Option (B) lists four schema-changing statements only — all DDL.
  3. Option (A) is the DML family; (C) is DCL; (D) mixes a DML query with two transaction-control statements.

Answer: Option (B) — CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE are all DDL.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and MERGE act on rows, so they are DML.
  • (C) GRANT and REVOKE hand out or take back privileges, so they are DCL (DENY is the same family).
  • (D) SELECT reads rows (DML/DQL), while COMMIT and ROLLBACK end or undo a transaction (TCL).

Common misconception. TRUNCATE looks like a row operation, so it is often filed under DML. In the SQL standard it is a DDL statement: it drops and re-creates the table's storage rather than deleting rows one at a time, which is why it is far faster than an unqualified DELETE.

Takeaway. DDL = definition, DML = data, DCL = privileges, TCL = transactions.

questions.question: Table enroll holds 8 rows. Compare DELETE FROM enroll; with DROP TABLE enroll;. Which statement is TRUE?
options: DELETE removes the table definition but leaves the rows; DROP removes the rows.
Both statements remove the rows and the table definition.
DELETE removes every row but keeps the table definition; DROP removes the rows together with the table definition.
DROP removes only the rows and leaves the definition; DELETE removes the definition.

solution.concept: The row set and the schema object are separate things. DELETE is DML: it removes rows from an existing table, and the table keeps its columns, constraints, indexes and privileges. DROP is DDL: it removes the table object itself from the catalogue, so the rows go with it and any later reference to the name fails.
steps: DELETE FROM enroll; with no WHERE deletes all 8 rows; the table still exists and accepts new inserts.
DROP TABLE enroll; deletes the definition; the 8 rows disappear because the object that held them is gone.
A re-created table has no rows and no old constraints — nothing is restored.
solution.trap: Treating DROP as "delete the rows". The distinction is testable: after DELETE, SELECT * FROM enroll returns an empty result set; after DROP, the same query raises a "no such table" error.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The row set and the schema object are separate things. DELETE is DML: it removes rows from an existing table, and the table keeps its columns, constraints, indexes and privileges. DROP is DDL: it removes the table object itself from the catalogue, so the rows go with it and any later reference to the name fails.

Step by step.

  1. DELETE FROM enroll; with no WHERE deletes all 8 rows; the table still exists and accepts new inserts.
  2. DROP TABLE enroll; deletes the definition; the 8 rows disappear because the object that held them is gone.
  3. A re-created table has no rows and no old constraints — nothing is restored.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) is wrong because DELETE never touches the definition.
  • (A) and (D) invert the two statements.

questions.question: In the schema below, enroll.roll is declared REFERENCES student(roll) ON DELETE SET NULL. Student 4 has two rows in enroll. After DELETE FROM student WHERE roll = 4; what happens to those two rows?student(roll, name, dept, cgpa) -- roll is the primary key course(cid, title, credits) -- cid is the primary key enroll(roll, cid, marks) -- marks is NULL while a course is ungraded
options: Both enroll rows are deleted with the student.
One row is deleted and the other is set to NULL.
The delete is rejected, because two rows still reference student 4.
Both enroll rows remain, with their roll value set to NULL.

solution.concept: A foreign key with a referential action decides what happens to referencing rows when the referenced row is deleted. The four standard actions are CASCADE (delete the children), SET NULL (keep the children, null out the key), SET DEFAULT, and NO ACTION/RESTRICT (reject the delete).
steps: ON DELETE SET NULL keeps every referencing row and overwrites only the foreign-key column.
Both of student 4's enrollment rows are referencing rows, so both are kept.
Their roll becomes NULL; the cid and marks values are untouched.
The student row itself is removed, so the two orphaned enrollments now have no owner.
solution.trap: Confusing "the delete is refused" with "the children are removed". A foreign key by itself does not prevent a delete; it only prevents leaving a dangling reference. SET NULL avoids the dangling reference by erasing the value, so the delete is allowed and the child rows survive. Note the column must be nullable for this action to be legal.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A foreign key with a referential action decides what happens to referencing rows when the referenced row is deleted. The four standard actions are CASCADE (delete the children), SET NULL (keep the children, null out the key), SET DEFAULT, and NO ACTION/RESTRICT (reject the delete).

Step by step.

  1. ON DELETE SET NULL keeps every referencing row and overwrites only the foreign-key column.
  2. Both of student 4's enrollment rows are referencing rows, so both are kept.
  3. Their roll becomes NULL; the cid and marks values are untouched.
  4. The student row itself is removed, so the two orphaned enrollments now have no owner.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) describes ON DELETE CASCADE.
  • (C) describes NO ACTION or RESTRICT, the default when no action is written.
  • (B) is not an action any standard system performs.

Common misconception. Confusing "the delete is refused" with "the children are removed". A foreign key by itself does not prevent a delete; it only prevents leaving a dangling reference. SET NULL avoids the dangling reference by erasing the value, so the delete is allowed and the child rows survive. Note the column must be nullable for this action to be legal.

Takeaway. Foreign key actions: CASCADE deletes children, SET NULL orphans them, RESTRICT refuses the parent delete.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about SQL constraints and privileges are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: A CHECK constraint rejects a row whose checked expression evaluates to UNKNOWN.
GRANT SELECT ON student TO analyst WITH GRANT OPTION; lets analyst pass that same privilege on to other users.
In standard SQL a UNIQUE constraint permits several rows that have NULL in the unique column.
A column declared PRIMARY KEY may contain NULL provided the table also has a UNIQUE constraint on the same column.

solution.concept: Three separate rules are being tested: how CHECK treats UNKNOWN, what WITH GRANT OPTION adds, and how the standard treats NULL inside UNIQUE and PRIMARY KEY. A constraint is violated only when its predicate is false; UNKNOWN (from a NULL operand) satisfies it. NULL is never equal to NULL, so two NULLs cannot duplicate each other in a unique column. A primary key, by definition, may not be NULL.
steps: (A) A CHECK (marks >= 0) on a NULL marks evaluates to UNKNOWN, which is accepted — so the row is inserted. The statement is false.
(B) WITH GRANT OPTION is exactly the right to re-grant. True.

(C) The unique constraint is violated only when two rows agree on every constrained column with non-NULL values; NULLs are distinct, so many NULLs may coexist. True (SQL Server is the well-known deviation, allowing only one).
(D) Entity integrity forbids NULL in any primary-key column, whatever other constraints exist. False.
solution.trap: Reading a CHECK as "must be true". SQL uses three-valued logic, so a constraint fires only on FALSE; UNKNOWN passes. This is why CHECK (marks IN (0,1)) does not stop a NULL from being inserted, and why a "not equal" check such as CHECK (a <> b) still admits rows where either side is NULL.

A constraint is violated only when its predicate is false; UNKNOWN (from a NULL operand) satisfies it. NULL is never equal to NULL, so two NULLs cannot duplicate each other in a unique column. A primary key, by definition, may not be NULL.

Step by step.

  1. (A) A CHECK (marks >= 0) on a NULL marks evaluates to UNKNOWN, which is accepted — so the row is inserted. The statement is false.
  2. (B) WITH GRANT OPTION is exactly the right to re-grant. True.
  3. (C) The unique constraint is violated only when two rows agree on every constrained column with non-NULL values; NULLs are distinct, so many NULLs may coexist. True (SQL Server is the well-known deviation, allowing only one).
  4. (D) Entity integrity forbids NULL in any primary-key column, whatever other constraints exist. False.

Answer: Options (B) and (C) are true.

Common misconception. Reading a CHECK as "must be true". SQL uses three-valued logic, so a constraint fires only on FALSE; UNKNOWN passes. This is why CHECK (marks IN (0,1)) does not stop a NULL from being inserted, and why a "not equal" check such as CHECK (a <> b) still admits rows where either side is NULL.

Takeaway. Constraints reject FALSE, not UNKNOWN; NULLs are distinct in UNIQUE; a primary key is never NULL.

questions.question: Using the schema below, which query returns exactly the students who have not enrolled in any course?student(roll, name, dept, cgpa) -- roll is the primary key course(cid, title, credits) -- cid is the primary key enroll(roll, cid, marks) -- marks is NULL while a course is ungradedstudent: (1,Aarav,CSE,9.1) (2,Bhavna,CSE,8.4) (3,Chirag,ECE,7.8) (4,Divya,CSE,8.9) (5,Esha,MECH,6.9) (6,Farhan,ECE,7.2) course: (CS101,DBMS,4) (CS102,OS,4) (EC201,Signals,3) enroll: (1,CS101,88) (1,CS102,74) (2,CS101,NULL) (2,CS102,65) (3,EC201,91) (4,CS101,95) (4,CS102,80) (5,EC201,NULL)
options: SELECT roll FROM student s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enroll e WHERE e.roll = s.roll);
SELECT roll FROM student s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enroll e WHERE e.roll = s.roll);
SELECT roll FROM student WHERE roll NOT IN (SELECT roll FROM enroll WHERE marks IS NOT NULL);
SELECT roll FROM student WHERE roll <> ALL (SELECT roll FROM enroll WHERE marks IS NULL);

solution.concept: NOT EXISTS is the standard "for no matching row" test. The inner query is correlated on s.roll, so for each student the database asks whether any enrollment row exists; NOT EXISTS keeps the student only when the answer is "no row". Unlike NOT IN it is safe in the presence of NULLs, because it never compares values — it only tests whether a row was produced.
steps: For roll 1 the inner query returns two rows, so NOT EXISTS is false and roll 1 is dropped.
For roll 6 the inner query returns no row at all, so NOT EXISTS is true and roll 6 is kept.
Applying this to every student leaves exactly roll 6.
solution.final: Option (A) — only roll 6 (Farhan) has no enrollment.
solution.trap: Assuming NOT IN and NOT EXISTS are interchangeable. They agree only when the inner column is declared NOT NULL. When a NULL can appear, NOT IN silently returns the empty set while NOT EXISTS still answers the intended question.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. NOT EXISTS is the standard "for no matching row" test. The inner query is correlated on s.roll, so for each student the database asks whether any enrollment row exists; NOT EXISTS keeps the student only when the answer is "no row". Unlike NOT IN it is safe in the presence of NULLs, because it never compares values — it only tests whether a row was produced.

Step by step.

  1. For roll 1 the inner query returns two rows, so NOT EXISTS is false and roll 1 is dropped.
  2. For roll 6 the inner query returns no row at all, so NOT EXISTS is true and roll 6 is kept.
  3. Applying this to every student leaves exactly roll 6.

Answer: Option (A) — only roll 6 (Farhan) has no enrollment.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) is the complement: it returns the five students who are enrolled.
  • (C) filters the subquery to graded rows, so the enrolled rolls it sees are {1, 2, 3, 4}. Roll 5 is absent from that set even though it is enrolled, so the query wrongly returns rolls 5 and 6.
  • (D) asks for rolls that differ from every ungraded enrollment roll ({2, 5}), which returns 1, 3, 4 and 6 — the opposite of the intended set.

Takeaway. For "has no related row", prefer NOT EXISTS: it is NULL-safe and reads as a universal test.

questions.question: A subquery refers to a column of the table named in the enclosing query. Which statement about such a subquery is TRUE?
options: It must appear in the FROM clause; a correlated reference is illegal in WHERE.
It is an independent subquery, evaluated exactly once and then reused for every outer row.
It is a correlated subquery, and conceptually it is evaluated again for each candidate row of the outer query.
It cannot contain an aggregate function.

solution.concept: A subquery that mentions an outer column is correlated. Its result depends on the current outer row, so the conceptual model is: for each candidate outer row, bind the outer columns, run the inner query, then test the predicate. An uncorrelated subquery mentions only its own tables, so it can be computed once and its result reused — which is why optimisers try to decorrelate.
steps: Spot the outer reference: here s.roll inside the inner query.
Because the inner result changes with each outer row, it is re-evaluated per row in the conceptual model.
That is the definition of a correlated subquery.
solution.trap: Believing a correlated subquery always costs one full scan per row. That is the naive plan; most engines rewrite it into a semi-join or an index lookup, so the practical cost can be close to a single join.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A subquery that mentions an outer column is correlated. Its result depends on the current outer row, so the conceptual model is: for each candidate outer row, bind the outer columns, run the inner query, then test the predicate. An uncorrelated subquery mentions only its own tables, so it can be computed once and its result reused — which is why optimisers try to decorrelate.

Step by step.

  1. Spot the outer reference: here s.roll inside the inner query.
  2. Because the inner result changes with each outer row, it is re-evaluated per row in the conceptual model.
  3. That is the definition of a correlated subquery.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) describes an uncorrelated (independent) subquery.
  • (A) is false: correlation is legal in WHERE, in the SELECT list and in HAVING.
  • (D) is false: a correlated aggregate such as (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM enroll e WHERE e.roll = s.roll) is perfectly legal.

Common misconception. Believing a correlated subquery always costs one full scan per row. That is the naive plan; most engines rewrite it into a semi-join or an index lookup, so the practical cost can be close to a single join.

Takeaway. Outer reference present = correlated = per-row semantics; absent = uncorrelated = compute once.

questions.question: Suppose the roll column of enroll is nullable and the subquery below returns at least one NULL.SELECT roll FROM student WHERE roll NOT IN (SELECT roll FROM enroll);What does the outer query return?
options: Every student roll that is absent from the non-NULL values of the subquery.
No rows at all.
Every student roll, including those present in the subquery.
A syntax error, because NULL cannot appear in an IN list.

solution.concept: x NOT IN (a, b, NULL) expands to x <> a AND x <> b AND x <> NULL. The last conjunct is UNKNOWN for every x, and TRUE AND UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN. A WHERE clause keeps a row only when the predicate is TRUE, so no row qualifies — even a roll that matches nothing in the list.
steps: Rewrite NOT IN as a chain of <> comparisons joined by AND.
One comparison is against NULL, which yields UNKNOWN.
UNKNOWN AND anything is never TRUE, so the whole predicate can never be TRUE.
The result set is therefore empty.
solution.final: Option (B) — the query returns no rows.
solution.trap: Reading NOT IN as set difference. Set difference ignores NULLs; NOT IN propagates them. The fix is either to add WHERE roll IS NOT NULL to the subquery, or to rewrite the query as NOT EXISTS, which never compares values.

  2. One comparison is against NULL, which yields UNKNOWN.
  3. UNKNOWN AND anything is never TRUE, so the whole predicate can never be TRUE.
  4. The result set is therefore empty.

Answer: Option (B) — the query returns no rows.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is what the query would return if the subquery contained no NULL; the NULL destroys it.
  • (C) is the opposite of what happens: UNKNOWN fails, it does not pass.
  • (D) is false: NULL is a legal value in a subquery result; the failure is semantic, not syntactic.

Takeaway. NOT IN + a NULL in the subquery = empty result. Use NOT EXISTS or filter the NULL.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about SQL subqueries and quantified comparisons are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: x = ANY (S) returns the same truth value as x IN (S) for every subquery S whose result is not NULL-valued.
x > ALL (S) is TRUE when the subquery S returns no rows at all.
A correlated subquery written in the SELECT list is conceptually evaluated once per row of the result.
NOT IN and NOT EXISTS always return the same rows.

solution.concept: Quantified comparisons are shorthand for a fold: = ANY is an OR over equality (that is IN), and > ALL is an AND over the comparisons. An OR over an empty set is FALSE, so = ANY on an empty subquery is false; an AND over an empty set is TRUE, so > ALL on an empty subquery is vacuously true.
steps: (A) = ANY ≡ IN, by definition of the quantifier. True.
(B) x > ALL (empty) has no counterexample, so it holds vacuously. True — this is the "every student scored more than the best student of an empty class" case.
(C) a SELECT-list subquery correlated on the outer row must be recomputed for each output row. True.
(D) false: they diverge as soon as the inner column can be NULL, where NOT IN collapses to the empty set and NOT EXISTS does not.
solution.final: Options (A), (B) and (C) are true; (D) is false.
solution.trap: Assuming > ALL needs a non-empty subquery. The empty case is exactly where GATE-style questions aim: universal quantification over an empty domain is TRUE, existential quantification over it is FALSE.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Quantified comparisons are shorthand for a fold: = ANY is an OR over equality (that is IN), and > ALL is an AND over the comparisons. An OR over an empty set is FALSE, so = ANY on an empty subquery is false; an AND over an empty set is TRUE, so > ALL on an empty subquery is vacuously true.

Step by step.

  1. (A) = ANY ≡ IN, by definition of the quantifier. True.
  2. (B) x > ALL (empty) has no counterexample, so it holds vacuously. True — this is the "every student scored more than the best student of an empty class" case.
  3. (C) a SELECT-list subquery correlated on the outer row must be recomputed for each output row. True.
  4. (D) false: they diverge as soon as the inner column can be NULL, where NOT IN collapses to the empty set and NOT EXISTS does not.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C) are true; (D) is false.

Takeaway. = ANY is IN, <> ALL is NOT IN, > ALL over an empty set is vacuously true.

questions.question: Which statement about WHERE and HAVING is TRUE?
options: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters whole groups after aggregation and may contain aggregate functions.
HAVING filters individual rows before grouping; WHERE filters groups after aggregation.
Both clauses may contain aggregate functions and are interchangeable.
WHERE may contain aggregate functions but HAVING may not.

solution.concept: SQL evaluates a grouped query in a fixed order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. Because WHERE runs before the groups exist, it cannot refer to an aggregate; because HAVING runs after grouping, it can.
steps: WHERE sees one row at a time, so its predicates use plain columns.
GROUP BY then collapses rows into groups.
HAVING tests the group, so COUNT(*), SUM(marks) and friends are legal there.
solution.trap: Trying to filter on a group with WHERE COUNT(*) > 2. The engine rejects it; the same condition belongs in HAVING. A useful memory hook: HAVING is to groups what WHERE is to rows.

Detailed solution

Concept. SQL evaluates a grouped query in a fixed order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. Because WHERE runs before the groups exist, it cannot refer to an aggregate; because HAVING runs after grouping, it can.

Step by step.

  1. WHERE sees one row at a time, so its predicates use plain columns.
  2. GROUP BY then collapses rows into groups.
  3. HAVING tests the group, so COUNT(*), SUM(marks) and friends are legal there.

Answer: Option (A).

  • (B) reverses the order of the two clauses.
  • (C) is false: an aggregate in WHERE is a syntax error in every major system.
  • (D) inverts the rule.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about grouping and aggregate functions are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: SELECT dept, name FROM student GROUP BY dept; is invalid in standard SQL, because name is neither grouped nor aggregated.
A WHERE clause may not contain an aggregate function, but a HAVING clause may.
COUNT(*) ignores rows in which some column is NULL.
An aggregate query with no GROUP BY returns exactly one row even when the table is empty.

solution.concept: After GROUP BY, the SELECT list may contain only (i) grouped columns, (ii) aggregates and (iii) expressions built from those two. Anything else has no single value per group. Separately, an aggregate query with no GROUP BY defines one implicit group covering the whole table — and a group over zero rows still exists, so one row is produced.
steps: (A) name varies inside a dept group, so the standard rejects the query. True. (MySQL with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY disabled returns an arbitrary name, which is a vendor extension, not the standard.)
(B) WHERE is evaluated before grouping, so an aggregate there is meaningless; HAVING is evaluated after grouping. True.
(C) COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of NULLs anywhere in them. False.
(D) the implicit single group exists even for an empty table: COUNT(*) = 0 and SUM/AVG return NULL, but one row is returned. True.
solution.final: Options (A), (B) and (D) are true; (C) is false.
solution.trap: Expecting an empty aggregate query to return no rows. It returns one row — the empty-group row — which is why SELECT MAX(marks) FROM enroll WHERE 1=0 yields a single NULL rather than nothing.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. After GROUP BY, the SELECT list may contain only (i) grouped columns, (ii) aggregates and (iii) expressions built from those two. Anything else has no single value per group. Separately, an aggregate query with no GROUP BY defines one implicit group covering the whole table — and a group over zero rows still exists, so one row is produced.

Step by step.

  1. (A) name varies inside a dept group, so the standard rejects the query. True. (MySQL with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY disabled returns an arbitrary name, which is a vendor extension, not the standard.)
  2. (B) WHERE is evaluated before grouping, so an aggregate there is meaningless; HAVING is evaluated after grouping. True.
  3. (C) COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of NULLs anywhere in them. False.
  4. (D) the implicit single group exists even for an empty table: COUNT(*) = 0 and SUM/AVG return NULL, but one row is returned. True.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D) are true; (C) is false.

Common misconception. Expecting an empty aggregate query to return no rows. It returns one row — the empty-group row — which is why SELECT MAX(marks) FROM enroll WHERE 1=0 yields a single NULL rather than nothing.

Takeaway. Grouped SELECT may only use grouped columns and aggregates; the no-GROUP-BY aggregate always emits one row.

questions.question: Using the data below, how many rows does the following query return?SELECT * FROM student s LEFT JOIN enroll e ON s.roll = e.roll;student: (1,Aarav,CSE,9.1) (2,Bhavna,CSE,8.4) (3,Chirag,ECE,7.8) (4,Divya,CSE,8.9) (5,Esha,MECH,6.9) (6,Farhan,ECE,7.2) course: (CS101,DBMS,4) (CS102,OS,4) (EC201,Signals,3) enroll: (1,CS101,88) (1,CS102,74) (2,CS101,NULL) (2,CS102,65) (3,EC201,91) (4,CS101,95) (4,CS102,80) (5,EC201,NULL)

solution.concept: A left outer join emits one row for every matching pair, plus one NULL-extended row for each left row that found no match. So the count is (number of matching pairs) + (number of unmatched left rows).
steps: Matching pairs: roll 1 contributes 2, roll 2 contributes 2, roll 3 contributes 1, roll 4 contributes 2, roll 5 contributes 1 — 8 pairs in total, the whole of enroll.
Unmatched left rows: roll 6 (Farhan) has no enrollment, so it contributes 1 row with cid and marks NULL.
8 + 1 = 9 rows.
solution.trap: Assuming an outer join adds one row per left row. It adds one row only for unmatched left rows; matched rows are duplicated exactly as an inner join would duplicate them.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A left outer join emits one row for every matching pair, plus one NULL-extended row for each left row that found no match. So the count is (number of matching pairs) + (number of unmatched left rows).

Step by step.

  1. Matching pairs: roll 1 contributes 2, roll 2 contributes 2, roll 3 contributes 1, roll 4 contributes 2, roll 5 contributes 1 — 8 pairs in total, the whole of enroll.
  2. Unmatched left rows: roll 6 (Farhan) has no enrollment, so it contributes 1 row with cid and marks NULL.
  3. 8 + 1 = 9 rows.

Answer: Option (C) — 9 rows.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) is the inner-join count: an inner join returns only the 8 matched pairs and silently drops roll 6.
  • (A) is the number of students, not the number of joined rows.
  • (D) would be the count if the join were many-to-many across a larger table; here the total is bounded by 8 + 6 = 14 only in the degenerate case where every enrollment failed to match.

Common misconception. Assuming an outer join adds one row per left row. It adds one row only for unmatched left rows; matched rows are duplicated exactly as an inner join would duplicate them.

Takeaway. LEFT JOIN row count = matched pairs + unmatched left rows.

solution.concept: This is the standard anti-join idiom: left-join, then keep only the NULL-extended rows. After the outer join, e.roll is NULL exactly for the left rows that found no match, so the WHERE predicate isolates the students with no enrollment.
steps: The left join produces 9 rows, of which 8 are matched and 1 is the NULL-extended row for roll 6.
e.roll IS NULL is true only on that single row.

questions.solution_html:

Concept. This is the standard anti-join idiom: left-join, then keep only the NULL-extended rows. After the outer join, e.roll is NULL exactly for the left rows that found no match, so the WHERE predicate isolates the students with no enrollment.

Step by step.

  1. The left join produces 9 rows, of which 8 are matched and 1 is the NULL-extended row for roll 6.
  2. e.roll IS NULL is true only on that single row.
  3. COUNT(*) = 1.

  • (C) counts all students, ignoring the join.
  • (A) is the size of enroll.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which of the following statements about outer joins are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: The ON condition of a left outer join also filters out left rows that fail to match.
A predicate on a right-table column placed in the WHERE clause of a left outer join can remove the NULL-extended rows and so reduce the result to that of an inner join.
A FULL OUTER JOIN returns unmatched rows from both sides, padding the other side with NULLs.
A LEFT JOIN B and B RIGHT JOIN A produce the same set of result rows (with the same column pairs) when written with the same join condition.

solution.concept: An outer join preserves one or both sides. LEFT preserves the left input, RIGHT preserves the right, FULL preserves both. Swapping the operands therefore swaps which side is preserved, and the two results describe the same pairs. The ON condition decides matching; the WHERE clause is applied after the NULL extension, so a WHERE predicate can undo the preservation.
steps: (A) false: a left row that fails the ON condition is precisely the row that is kept, padded with NULLs.

(B) if the WHERE clause requires, say, e.marks > 70, the NULL-extended rows evaluate to UNKNOWN and are discarded, leaving exactly the inner-join rows. True — this is the classic "outer join that is really an inner join" bug.
(C) is the definition of a full outer join. True.
(D) swapping the operands of a left join turns it into the mirror-image right join with identical pairs. True.
solution.final: Options (D), (B) and (C) are true; (A) is false.
solution.trap: Putting a right-table predicate in WHERE and expecting NULL-padded rows to survive. They cannot: a NULL never satisfies a comparison. To filter the matching without losing the unmatched rows, the predicate must move into the ON clause.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An outer join preserves one or both sides. LEFT preserves the left input, RIGHT preserves the right, FULL preserves both. Swapping the operands therefore swaps which side is preserved, and the two results describe the same pairs. The ON condition decides matching; the WHERE clause is applied after the NULL extension, so a WHERE predicate can undo the preservation.

Step by step.

  1. (D) swapping the operands of a left join turns it into the mirror-image right join with identical pairs. True.
  2. (B) if the WHERE clause requires, say, e.marks > 70, the NULL-extended rows evaluate to UNKNOWN and are discarded, leaving exactly the inner-join rows. True — this is the classic "outer join that is really an inner join" bug.
  3. (C) is the definition of a full outer join. True.
  4. (A) false: a left row that fails the ON condition is precisely the row that is kept, padded with NULLs.

Answer: Options (D), (B) and (C) are true; (A) is false.

Common misconception. Putting a right-table predicate in WHERE and expecting NULL-padded rows to survive. They cannot: a NULL never satisfies a comparison. To filter the matching without losing the unmatched rows, the predicate must move into the ON clause.

Takeaway. ON decides matches, WHERE prunes the final rows — and that is how a left join silently becomes an inner join.

Detailed solution

questions.question: Which statement about an SQL view is TRUE?
options: A view always stores a private copy of the rows it returns, refreshed on every insert into the base table.
A view is a named query: it stores no rows of its own (unless it is a materialised view) and its rows are recomputed from the base tables when the view is queried.
A view must be defined over exactly one base table.
Dropping a view deletes the rows of the underlying table.

solution.concept: In standard SQL a view is a derived table: the catalogue stores only the defining query. Every reference to the view expands to that query, so the view always reflects the current base tables. A materialised view is the exception — it does keep a stored copy and must be refreshed — but that is an optimisation feature, not what a plain CREATE VIEW gives you.
steps: The definition is stored as text; no tuples are copied.
Querying the view runs (or rewrites) the defining query against the base tables.
Therefore the view is always consistent with the base data, with no refresh step.
solution.trap: Believing a view is a snapshot. Because it is recomputed, a view over student immediately shows a newly inserted student — there is nothing to refresh.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. In standard SQL a view is a derived table: the catalogue stores only the defining query. Every reference to the view expands to that query, so the view always reflects the current base tables. A materialised view is the exception — it does keep a stored copy and must be refreshed — but that is an optimisation feature, not what a plain CREATE VIEW gives you.

Step by step.

  1. The definition is stored as text; no tuples are copied.
  2. Querying the view runs (or rewrites) the defining query against the base tables.
  3. Therefore the view is always consistent with the base data, with no refresh step.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) describes a materialised view, and even then the refresh is explicit or scheduled, not automatic on every insert.
  • (C) is false: a view may join any number of tables, as the aggregate view in this unit does.
  • (D) is false: DROP VIEW removes only the definition; the base tables and their rows are untouched.

Common misconception. Believing a view is a snapshot. Because it is recomputed, a view over student immediately shows a newly inserted student — there is nothing to refresh.

Takeaway. A view is stored logic, not stored data.

questions.question: Which statement about an SQL trigger is TRUE?
options: A trigger fires only for SELECT statements.
A trigger must be called explicitly, for example with EXECUTE TRIGGER, after the statement it is meant to guard.
A trigger fires automatically when its specified event (such as an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE) occurs; it cannot be invoked directly by a statement.
A table that has triggers may not also have constraints.

solution.concept: A trigger is an event–condition–action rule attached to a table or view. The database fires it as a side effect of the triggering statement; there is no SQL statement that calls a trigger by name. Triggers are declared BEFORE or AFTER the event, and FOR EACH ROW or FOR EACH STATEMENT.
steps: The event is a DML change (in standard SQL), optionally restricted with WHEN to specific columns.
The action is a block of SQL executed by the engine when the event occurs.
No user statement names the trigger, so it cannot be called directly.
solution.trap: Thinking a trigger replaces a foreign key. Triggers can enforce rules that constraints cannot express, but they are procedural, harder to reason about, and a well-modelled schema uses constraints first.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A trigger is an event–condition–action rule attached to a table or view. The database fires it as a side effect of the triggering statement; there is no SQL statement that calls a trigger by name. Triggers are declared BEFORE or AFTER the event, and FOR EACH ROW or FOR EACH STATEMENT.

Step by step.

  1. The event is a DML change (in standard SQL), optionally restricted with WHEN to specific columns.
  2. The action is a block of SQL executed by the engine when the event occurs.
  3. No user statement names the trigger, so it cannot be called directly.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) there is no such statement in standard SQL.
  • (A) triggers are defined on data-changing events; some systems add INSTEAD OF triggers on views, but a plain SELECT does not fire one.
  • (D) triggers and constraints are independent mechanisms and routinely coexist; constraints are usually preferred for declarative rules because they are cheaper.

Common misconception. Thinking a trigger replaces a foreign key. Triggers can enforce rules that constraints cannot express, but they are procedural, harder to reason about, and a well-modelled schema uses constraints first.

Takeaway. Triggers are fired by the engine, never called by the user.

questions.question: Using the schema below, which of the following views is updatable in the standard sense — that is, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE through the view can be mapped onto the single base table it reads?student(roll, name, dept, cgpa) -- roll is the primary key course(cid, title, credits) -- cid is the primary key enroll(roll, cid, marks) -- marks is NULL while a course is ungraded
options: CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT roll, name, dept FROM student WHERE dept = 'CSE';
CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS n FROM student GROUP BY dept;
CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT DISTINCT dept FROM student;
CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT s.roll, AVG(e.marks) AS avgmarks FROM student s JOIN enroll e ON e.roll = s.roll GROUP BY s.roll;

solution.concept: A view is updatable when each of its rows corresponds to exactly one row of exactly one base table. Selection and projection preserve that correspondence; aggregation, DISTINCT, GROUP BY and joins do not, because one view row can then be derived from many base rows (or from none).
steps: (A) reads one table, keeps its key column roll and only filters rows, so every view row maps back to one student row. Updatable.
(B) produces one row per department; no single student row corresponds to it. Not updatable.
(C) collapses duplicates, so a view row has no unique source row. Not updatable.
(D) aggregates over a join; again one row summarises many. Not updatable.
solution.trap: Assuming a view is read-only whenever it has a WHERE clause. A selection predicate is harmless — in fact, with WITH CHECK OPTION it becomes an enforced constraint on what may be written through the view.

Concept. A view is updatable when each of its rows corresponds to exactly one row of exactly one base table. Selection and projection preserve that correspondence; aggregation, DISTINCT, GROUP BY and joins do not, because one view row can then be derived from many base rows (or from none).

Step by step.

  1. (A) reads one table, keeps its key column roll and only filters rows, so every view row maps back to one student row. Updatable.
  2. (B) produces one row per department; no single student row corresponds to it. Not updatable.
  3. (C) collapses duplicates, so a view row has no unique source row. Not updatable.
  4. (D) aggregates over a join; again one row summarises many. Not updatable.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B), (C) and (D) are all read-only views under the standard updatability rules. A system may still let you modify them through an INSTEAD OF trigger, but that is a workaround, not updatability.

Common misconception. Assuming a view is read-only whenever it has a WHERE clause. A selection predicate is harmless — in fact, with WITH CHECK OPTION it becomes an enforced constraint on what may be written through the view.

Takeaway. One view row ↔ one base row is what makes a view updatable; aggregation and DISTINCT break it.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about views, triggers and constraints are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: With WITH CHECK OPTION on a view, an insert or update performed through the view is rejected if the new row would not satisfy the view's defining condition.
Dropping a base table that a view references is always rejected by the DBMS.
A trigger declared FOR EACH ROW fires once for every row that the triggering statement affects.
A CHECK constraint may be declared directly on a view in standard SQL.

solution.concept: Three different mechanisms are being separated. WITH CHECK OPTION makes the view's predicate a write-time constraint. Triggers are declared at row granularity or statement granularity. CHECK is a table constraint; the standard mechanism for a cross-table rule is an assertion, which no mainstream product implements.
steps: (A) is the definition of WITH CHECK OPTION: a row that would vanish from the view cannot be written through it. True.

(B) false: the standard permits the drop and leaves the view invalid ("inoperative") until it is re-created or the table returns; some systems require CASCADE, others simply fail at the next use of the view. It is not universally rejected.
(C) FOR EACH ROW means one firing per affected row; FOR EACH STATEMENT fires once for the whole statement. True.
(D) false: CHECK is declared on a table or column, not on a view.
solution.final: Options (A) and (C) are true; (B) and (D) are false.
solution.trap: Two traps. First, assuming WITH CHECK OPTION only affects SELECT — it affects writes. Second, assuming a trigger fires once per statement by default; the row granularity has to be read from the declaration, and FOR EACH ROW is the more common form.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Three different mechanisms are being separated. WITH CHECK OPTION makes the view's predicate a write-time constraint. Triggers are declared at row granularity or statement granularity. CHECK is a table constraint; the standard mechanism for a cross-table rule is an assertion, which no mainstream product implements.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is the definition of WITH CHECK OPTION: a row that would vanish from the view cannot be written through it. True.
  2. (B) false: the standard permits the drop and leaves the view invalid ("inoperative") until it is re-created or the table returns; some systems require CASCADE, others simply fail at the next use of the view. It is not universally rejected.
  3. (C) FOR EACH ROW means one firing per affected row; FOR EACH STATEMENT fires once for the whole statement. True.
  4. (D) false: CHECK is declared on a table or column, not on a view.

Answer: Options (A) and (C) are true; (B) and (D) are false.

Common misconception. Two traps. First, assuming WITH CHECK OPTION only affects SELECT — it affects writes. Second, assuming a trigger fires once per statement by default; the row granularity has to be read from the declaration, and FOR EACH ROW is the more common form.

Takeaway. CHECK OPTION guards writes through a view; FOR EACH ROW sets trigger granularity; CHECK belongs to tables.

questions.question: Table orders is declared as orders(oid INT PRIMARY KEY, qty INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 5, note VARCHAR(20)). The statement INSERT INTO orders (oid, note) VALUES (7, NULL); is then executed. Which statement is TRUE?
options: It is rejected, because qty is NOT NULL and no value was supplied for it.
It is accepted: qty receives the declared default 5, and note is stored as NULL.
It is accepted, and qty is stored as NULL because the column was left out of the column list.
It is rejected, because note may not be given a NULL.

solution.concept: A column that is omitted from an INSERT column list takes its declared DEFAULT, and a declared default satisfies NOT NULL. NOT NULL forbids only an explicit NULL or an omitted column that has no default; it never forbids a default value.
steps: The statement names two columns, oid and note; qty is not named.
An unnamed column is filled from its DEFAULT clause, here 5, so NOT NULL is satisfied.
NULL is written explicitly into note, which is nullable because no constraint forbids it.
The row (7, 5, NULL) is inserted.
solution.final: Option (B) — the row is accepted with qty = 5 and note = NULL.
solution.trap: Reading NOT NULL as "every insert must name the column". It only says the stored value may not be NULL, and the default guarantees that.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A column that is omitted from an INSERT column list takes its declared DEFAULT, and a declared default satisfies NOT NULL. NOT NULL forbids only an explicit NULL or an omitted column that has no default; it never forbids a default value.

Step by step.

  1. The statement names two columns, oid and note; qty is not named.
  2. An unnamed column is filled from its DEFAULT clause, here 5, so NOT NULL is satisfied.
  3. NULL is written explicitly into note, which is nullable because no constraint forbids it.
  4. The row (7, 5, NULL) is inserted.

Answer: Option (B) — the row is accepted with qty = 5 and note = NULL.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) confuses an omitted column with a missing value; the default supplies one.
  • (C) would hold only if qty had no DEFAULT, in which case the insert would be rejected rather than storing NULL.
  • (D) invents a constraint on note; the declaration makes it nullable.

Common misconception. Reading NOT NULL as "every insert must name the column". It only says the stored value may not be NULL, and the default guarantees that.

Takeaway. Omitted column with a DEFAULT → default value, never NULL and never an error.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Any arithmetic with NULL yields NULL, so NULL + 5 is NULL. An UPDATE writes that NULL back, which is a legal value in a nullable column. The WHERE clause tests only cid, so both C3 rows are still selected.

Step by step.

  1. Rows selected by WHERE cid = 'C3': (12,C3,68) and (16,C3,NULL).
  2. (12,C3,68) → 68 + 5 = 73.
  3. (16,C3,NULL) → NULL + 5 = NULL, so the column is set to NULL again.
  4. Two rows are updated; one value changes, the other is unchanged.

Answer: Option (C) — 73 and NULL.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) treats NULL as 0, which SQL never does for arithmetic.
  • (B) is wrong: a NULL operand is not an error, only an UNKNOWN value.
  • (D) is wrong: no statement deletes rows unless it is a DELETE.

Common misconception. Treating NULL as zero. marks + 5 on a NULL mark is NULL, not 5 — a value is only turned into 0 by an explicit COALESCE(marks,0).

Takeaway. NULL propagates through arithmetic; the row is still updated, to NULL.

questions.question: u1 holds SELECT on student WITH GRANT OPTION and has granted SELECT on it to u2. The DBA now runs REVOKE SELECT ON student FROM u1 RESTRICT;. Which statement is TRUE?
options: The statement succeeds, and u2 keeps the privilege.
The statement succeeds, and u2 loses the privilege as well.
The statement fails, but u1 still loses the privilege.
The statement fails, because u1 has passed the privilege on; REVOKE ... CASCADE would succeed and take it away from both u1 and u2.

solution.concept: A privilege that has been granted onward creates a dependency. RESTRICT refuses to revoke a privilege that others still hold through it; CASCADE revokes the privilege from the grantee and, transitively, from everyone who received it from that grantee.
steps: u1 was granted SELECT WITH GRANT OPTION, so its grant to u2 is a dependent grant.
RESTRICT is the default: it fails rather than silently changing u2's rights.
CASCADE removes the privilege from u1 and follows the dependency to u2.
Nothing is revoked when the RESTRICT form fails, so u1 keeps the privilege.
solution.final: Option (D) — RESTRICT fails; CASCADE removes it from both users.
solution.trap: Expecting RESTRICT to revoke u1 and leave u2 dangling. The statement is atomic: it either succeeds completely or not at all.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A privilege that has been granted onward creates a dependency. RESTRICT refuses to revoke a privilege that others still hold through it; CASCADE revokes the privilege from the grantee and, transitively, from everyone who received it from that grantee.

Step by step.

  1. u1 was granted SELECT WITH GRANT OPTION, so its grant to u2 is a dependent grant.
  2. RESTRICT is the default: it fails rather than silently changing u2's rights.
  3. CASCADE removes the privilege from u1 and follows the dependency to u2.
  4. Nothing is revoked when the RESTRICT form fails, so u1 keeps the privilege.

Answer: Option (D) — RESTRICT fails; CASCADE removes it from both users.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) and (B) both assume RESTRICT succeeds, which it does not when a dependent grant exists.
  • (C) invents a partial effect; a failed REVOKE changes nothing at all.

Common misconception. Expecting RESTRICT to revoke u1 and leave u2 dangling. The statement is atomic: it either succeeds completely or not at all.

Takeaway. RESTRICT protects dependent grants by failing; CASCADE is the deliberate recursive revoke.

solution.concept: A cascade chain is followed transitively. Deleting a dept row cascades to its emp rows, and deleting an emp row in turn cascades to its dependent rows.
steps: Delete dept 1 → cascade to emp rows with dno = 1: 101 and 102. That is 2 rows of emp.
Each deleted emp row cascades to its dependents: emp 101 has dependents 1 and 2; emp 102 has none. That is 2 rows of dependent.
Dept 2 and dept 3 are untouched, so emp 103, 104 and dependent 3 survive.
2 + 2 = 4 rows removed.
solution.trap: Counting only the direct children (2 emp rows) and forgetting that the cascade continues to the grandchildren.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A cascade chain is followed transitively. Deleting a dept row cascades to its emp rows, and deleting an emp row in turn cascades to its dependent rows.

Step by step.

  1. Delete dept 1 → cascade to emp rows with dno = 1: 101 and 102. That is 2 rows of emp.
  2. Each deleted emp row cascades to its dependents: emp 101 has dependents 1 and 2; emp 102 has none. That is 2 rows of dependent.
  3. Dept 2 and dept 3 are untouched, so emp 103, 104 and dependent 3 survive.
  4. 2 + 2 = 4 rows removed.

Answer: 4

Common misconception. Counting only the direct children (2 emp rows) and forgetting that the cascade continues to the grandchildren.

Takeaway. CASCADE is transitive; follow the chain until no referencing row remains.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which of the following statements about DML, DDL and privileges are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: If an UPDATE would violate a CHECK constraint for even one of the rows it touches, none of those rows is updated — the statement is atomic.
An INSERT INTO t SELECT ... that fails on the last of five rows leaves the first four rows inserted.
DELETE FROM t; with no WHERE removes every row but keeps the table definition and the privileges granted on it.
DROP TABLE t; also removes the privileges that were granted on t.

solution.concept: Two separate principles are at work. A single SQL statement is atomic: it either has its full effect or none. And privileges are attached to the object, so destroying the object destroys the privileges that depended on it.
steps: (A) True. Constraint checking is part of the statement, so a violation anywhere rolls the whole statement back.
(B) False. Statement atomicity means the four earlier rows are undone with the fifth.
(C) True. DELETE is DML: the rows go, the object and its grants stay.
(D) True. A grant is a privilege on a named object; once the object no longer exists the grant has nothing to attach to.
solution.final: Options (A), (C) and (D) are true; (B) is false.
solution.trap: Believing that a multi-row DML statement commits row by row. It does not; the whole statement succeeds or the whole statement is undone.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Two separate principles are at work. A single SQL statement is atomic: it either has its full effect or none. And privileges are attached to the object, so destroying the object destroys the privileges that depended on it.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. Constraint checking is part of the statement, so a violation anywhere rolls the whole statement back.
  2. (B) False. Statement atomicity means the four earlier rows are undone with the fifth.
  3. (C) True. DELETE is DML: the rows go, the object and its grants stay.
  4. (D) True. A grant is a privilege on a named object; once the object no longer exists the grant has nothing to attach to.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D) are true; (B) is false.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) is the classic partial-effect trap: only an explicit loop of separate statements can leave earlier rows behind.

Common misconception. Believing that a multi-row DML statement commits row by row. It does not; the whole statement succeeds or the whole statement is undone.

Takeaway. One statement = all or nothing; dropping the object drops the grants on it.

Detailed solution

Concept. An aggregate without GROUP BY always returns exactly one row, even when it sees no input rows. COUNT(*) over an empty set is 0, so the correlated subquery yields 0 rather than NULL or no row. A scalar subquery in the SELECT list is legal as long as it returns at most one row.

Step by step.

  1. For roll 14 the inner query is SELECT COUNT(*) FROM enroll e WHERE e.roll = 14, which matches nothing.
  2. An aggregate query over zero rows still produces one row: the count of an empty set is 0.
  3. The outer row for roll 14 therefore survives, with n = 0.
  4. Rolls 11, 13 and 16 get 2, 2 and 2; rolls 12 and 15 get 2 each as well — every enrolled student has exactly two rows.

Answer: Option (C) — roll 14 appears with n = 0.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) describes a join or an EXISTS filter, not a scalar subquery in the select list.
  • (B) would be right for SUM or MAX, which return NULL over no rows; COUNT does not.
  • (D) is false: correlation in the SELECT list is standard and is how per-row aggregates are written.

Common misconception. Assuming every aggregate over an empty input returns NULL. Only COUNT returns 0; SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX return NULL.

Takeaway. COUNT over nothing is 0; every other aggregate over nothing is NULL.
