questions.question: On the data below, the subquery inSELECT s.roll FROM student s WHERE s.cgpa = (SELECT e.marks FROM enroll e WHERE e.cid = 'C1');returns five rows. Which statement is TRUE?
options: The statement fails at run time, because a scalar subquery used with = must return at most one row.
The statement returns every student whose cgpa equals any of those five marks.
The statement returns no rows, because a comparison against a multi-row subquery is always UNKNOWN.
The statement is a syntax error, because a subquery may not stand on the right of = in a WHERE clause.

solution.concept: A subquery in a position that expects one value — the right operand of =, or a SELECT list item — is a scalar subquery and must produce at most one row. Producing more is a run-time cardinality error, not a silent set comparison.
steps: The right side of = expects a single value, so the subquery is scalar by position.
WHERE e.cid = 'C1' matches five rows, so the subquery returns five values.
A scalar subquery that returns more than one row raises an error when it is evaluated.
To compare against a set, the query must say so: IN or = ANY.
solution.final: Option (A) — the statement fails at run time with a cardinality error.
solution.trap: Expecting = followed by a subquery to behave like IN. It does not; = demands exactly one value, and an empty subquery would give NULL rather than an error.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A subquery in a position that expects one value — the right operand of =, or a SELECT list item — is a scalar subquery and must produce at most one row. Producing more is a run-time cardinality error, not a silent set comparison.

Step by step.

  1. The right side of = expects a single value, so the subquery is scalar by position.
  2. WHERE e.cid = 'C1' matches five rows, so the subquery returns five values.
  3. A scalar subquery that returns more than one row raises an error when it is evaluated.
  4. To compare against a set, the query must say so: IN or = ANY.

Answer: Option (A) — the statement fails at run time with a cardinality error.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) describes = ANY (equivalently IN), which is a different operator.
  • (C) confuses a cardinality error with three-valued logic; no comparison is even attempted.
  • (D) is wrong: the position is legal, only the number of rows is not.

Common misconception. Expecting = followed by a subquery to behave like IN. It does not; = demands exactly one value, and an empty subquery would give NULL rather than an error.

Takeaway. Use IN or = ANY for a set; = is for one value and fails loudly on many.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which of the following statements about subqueries are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: In the conceptual model, a correlated subquery in the SELECT list is evaluated once for each row the outer query produces.
NOT EXISTS is TRUE for an outer row whenever the inner query produces no rows, even when the inner column is nullable.
IN and EXISTS always return the same rows, so one may be substituted for the other without care.
A subquery in the FROM clause may refer to a column of another table in the same FROM clause.

solution.concept: Correlation means the inner query depends on the current outer row, so conceptually it is re-evaluated per row. EXISTS tests only whether a row was produced, which makes it immune to NULLs — unlike IN, whose comparison against a NULL yields UNKNOWN. Tables in one FROM list are combined as a set, so one cannot see the other's columns without a lateral construct, which standard SQL does not have.
steps: (A) True by the definition of correlation.
(B) True: EXISTS never compares values, only counts rows, so a NULL in the inner column cannot break it.
(C) False: they diverge as soon as the inner column can be NULL (NOT IN collapses to the empty set) and when duplicate rows matter.
(D) False: standard SQL has no LATERAL; a derived table sees only its own tables and the enclosing query.
solution.final: Options (A) and (B) are true; (C) and (D) are false.
solution.trap: Assuming IN and EXISTS are interchangeable. They agree only when the inner column is declared NOT NULL and the outer query needs no duplicate elimination.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Correlation means the inner query depends on the current outer row, so conceptually it is re-evaluated per row. EXISTS tests only whether a row was produced, which makes it immune to NULLs — unlike IN, whose comparison against a NULL yields UNKNOWN. Tables in one FROM list are combined as a set, so one cannot see the other's columns without a lateral construct, which standard SQL does not have.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True by the definition of correlation.
  2. (B) True: EXISTS never compares values, only counts rows, so a NULL in the inner column cannot break it.
  3. (C) False: they diverge as soon as the inner column can be NULL (NOT IN collapses to the empty set) and when duplicate rows matter.
  4. (D) False: standard SQL has no LATERAL; a derived table sees only its own tables and the enclosing query.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (C) fails on NULLs: x NOT IN (…, NULL) is never TRUE, while NOT EXISTS is unaffected.
  • (D) describes a lateral join, a vendor extension rather than standard SQL.

Common misconception. Assuming IN and EXISTS are interchangeable. They agree only when the inner column is declared NOT NULL and the outer query needs no duplicate elimination.

Takeaway. EXISTS counts rows, IN compares values; only one of the two survives NULLs.

HAVING is itself a condition on the group and follows the same rule. Every aggregate except COUNT(*) ignores NULL, so an all-NULL group aggregates to NULL.

(B) False: marks is neither grouped nor aggregated, so it has no value per group either — the engine rejects it.

(D) True: MAX over an empty set of non-NULL values is NULL.

  2. (B) False: marks is neither grouped nor aggregated, so it has no value per group either — the engine rejects it.

  4. (D) True: MAX over an empty set of non-NULL values is NULL.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D) are true; (B) is false.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) is the trap: HAVING may use aggregates and grouped columns, not arbitrary columns.

Detailed solution

Concept. For an inner join the two clauses are interchangeable, because both simply discard rows that fail the predicate. The distinction only becomes visible with an outer join, where ON decides which pairs match but WHERE runs after the NULL-extension and can remove the preserved rows.

Step by step.

  1. An inner join keeps exactly the pairs for which the ON predicate is TRUE.
  2. A WHERE predicate is also applied to those same pairs, before the result is produced.
  3. Conjunction is commutative, so applying either predicate first leaves the same set of pairs.
  4. Hence the two placements are equivalent for an inner join — and only for an inner join.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about joins are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: NATURAL JOIN joins on every column name the two tables share and keeps one copy of each shared column.

solution.concept: A join with no effective condition is a Cartesian product, whether it is written CROSS JOIN or INNER JOIN ... ON TRUE. An outer join guarantees the preserved side is represented: an unmatched preserved row still appears, padded with NULLs. The number of rows can therefore far exceed the sum of the inputs.
steps: (A) True — that is the definition of a natural join.
(B) True: a condition that is always TRUE restricts nothing, so the inner join degenerates to the product.
(C) True — that is exactly what the preserved side means.
(D) False: if every left row matches every right row the result has m × n rows, which exceeds m + n as soon as both sides have at least two rows.
solution.final: Options (A), (B) and (C) are true; (D) is false.
solution.trap: Assuming an outer join bounds the output by the input sizes. Only the unmatched rows are added; matched pairs are duplicated exactly as an inner join would duplicate them.

An outer join guarantees the preserved side is represented: an unmatched preserved row still appears, padded with NULLs. The number of rows can therefore far exceed the sum of the inputs.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True — that is the definition of a natural join.
  2. (B) True: a condition that is always TRUE restricts nothing, so the inner join degenerates to the product.
  3. (C) True — that is exactly what the preserved side means.
  4. (D) False: if every left row matches every right row the result has m × n rows, which exceeds m + n as soon as both sides have at least two rows.

Concept. In a LEFT JOIN the ON condition decides which pairs match; the left table is preserved regardless. The row count is (matching pairs) + (left rows with no match). Placing the right-table predicate in ON is what keeps the unmatched students in the result.

Step by step.

  1. Enrollments above 80: (11,C1,82), (11,C2,91), (13,C1,95), (13,C2,88), (16,C1,88) — 5 matching pairs.
  2. Students with at least one such enrollment: 11, 13, 16. They contribute their 5 pairs and nothing extra.
  3. Students 12, 14 and 15 have no enrollment above 80, so each contributes one NULL-extended row: 3 rows.
  4. 5 + 3 = 8 rows.

Answer: 8

Common misconception. Two traps. Putting e.marks > 80 in WHERE instead of ON, which deletes the three NULL-extended rows and leaves 5; or counting students (6) instead of joined rows.

Takeaway. LEFT JOIN row count = matching pairs + unmatched left rows, with the right-side filter kept in ON.

questions.question: CREATE VIEW high AS SELECT roll, cid, marks FROM enroll WHERE marks > 80 WITH CHECK OPTION; is created, and then INSERT INTO high VALUES (17, 'C1', 50); is executed. What happens?
options: The row is inserted into enroll and is simply invisible through high.
The row is inserted into enroll with marks raised to 81 by the check option.
The insert is rejected, because the new row would not satisfy the view's WHERE predicate.
The insert is rejected, because high is not updatable.

solution.concept: WITH CHECK OPTION turns the view's predicate into a condition on writes made through the view: a row that would fall outside the view is refused rather than inserted invisibly. Without the clause the insert would be accepted and the row would simply not appear through the view.
steps: The view is updatable: it is a selection and projection of a single base table.
The check option requires every inserted or updated row to satisfy marks > 80.
50 does not satisfy it, so the insert fails with an error.
Nothing is written to enroll.
solution.trap: Confusing WITH CHECK OPTION with WITH READ ONLY. The first permits the write if the predicate holds and rejects it otherwise; the second forbids writes altogether.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. WITH CHECK OPTION turns the view's predicate into a condition on writes made through the view: a row that would fall outside the view is refused rather than inserted invisibly. Without the clause the insert would be accepted and the row would simply not appear through the view.

Step by step.

  1. The view is updatable: it is a selection and projection of a single base table.
  2. The check option requires every inserted or updated row to satisfy marks > 80.
  3. 50 does not satisfy it, so the insert fails with an error.
  4. Nothing is written to enroll.

Answer: Option (C) — the insert is rejected.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is what happens without the check option.
  • (B) invents a coercion; SQL never adjusts data to make a constraint pass.
  • (D) is false: this view is updatable, which is why the check option is meaningful.

Common misconception. Confusing WITH CHECK OPTION with WITH READ ONLY. The first permits the write if the predicate holds and rejects it otherwise; the second forbids writes altogether.

Takeaway. WITH CHECK OPTION makes the view's predicate a write-time constraint.

questions.question: Which statement about an INSTEAD OF trigger on a view is TRUE?
options: It fires after the row has been written to the base table.
It runs in place of the triggering statement, which is how a non-updatable view is made writable.
It may be declared only for DELETE on a view.
It can be attached to a base table as well as to a view.

solution.concept: An INSTEAD OF trigger replaces the triggering DML statement on the view. Because the view has no storage of its own, the trigger body performs the real writes on the base tables — which is exactly what makes an otherwise non-updatable view writable. It is the one trigger form that is defined on views rather than on tables.
steps: The statement targets the view, and the view cannot store rows.
The trigger intercepts the statement and supplies its own actions on the base tables.
No automatic write happens, which is why the trigger body must perform it.
solution.trap: Assuming an INSTEAD OF trigger also performs the original write. It replaces it, so the base-table write must be written by hand.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An INSTEAD OF trigger replaces the triggering DML statement on the view. Because the view has no storage of its own, the trigger body performs the real writes on the base tables — which is exactly what makes an otherwise non-updatable view writable. It is the one trigger form that is defined on views rather than on tables.

Step by step.

  1. The statement targets the view, and the view cannot store rows.
  2. The trigger intercepts the statement and supplies its own actions on the base tables.
  3. No automatic write happens, which is why the trigger body must perform it.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) describes a normal AFTER trigger, which assumes the write already happened.
  • (C) is false: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE are all allowed.
  • (D) is false: INSTEAD OF is defined on views; base tables use BEFORE and AFTER.

Common misconception. Assuming an INSTEAD OF trigger also performs the original write. It replaces it, so the base-table write must be written by hand.

Takeaway. INSTEAD OF = on views, replaces the statement, body does the real work.

questions.question: In standard SQL, a CHECK constraint whose condition contains a subquery over another table …
options: is allowed, and is re-evaluated whenever the other table changes.
is allowed, but evaluated only on INSERT, never on UPDATE.
is not allowed: a CHECK condition may reference only columns of the row being tested.
is allowed, but silently ignored.

solution.concept: A CHECK constraint is a row-level predicate: it is tested against each candidate row and may mention only columns of that row. A subquery would make the constraint depend on other rows, which the standard excludes; cross-row conditions belong in a foreign key, an assertion or a trigger.
steps: The constraint is evaluated per row, at insert and update time, with no wider context.
A subquery would need the rest of the database, including rows being changed concurrently.
The standard therefore forbids subqueries in CHECK; most engines reject the DDL outright.
solution.trap: Believing a CHECK can compare against another table because the syntax accepts a general condition. The permitted scope is the current row only.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A CHECK constraint is a row-level predicate: it is tested against each candidate row and may mention only columns of that row. A subquery would make the constraint depend on other rows, which the standard excludes; cross-row conditions belong in a foreign key, an assertion or a trigger.

Step by step.

  1. The constraint is evaluated per row, at insert and update time, with no wider context.
  2. A subquery would need the rest of the database, including rows being changed concurrently.
  3. The standard therefore forbids subqueries in CHECK; most engines reject the DDL outright.

Answer: Option (C) — not permitted.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) would require re-checking every row of the table whenever the other table changes — not part of the model.
  • (B) invents a partial enforcement.
  • (D) is false: a rejected statement is not a silent ignore.

Common misconception. Believing a CHECK can compare against another table because the syntax accepts a general condition. The permitted scope is the current row only.

Takeaway. CHECK sees one row; anything cross-row needs a trigger, a key or an assertion.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which of the following statements about views, triggers and constraints are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: A view whose definition uses GROUP BY is not updatable in standard SQL.
WITH CHECK OPTION turns the view's predicate into a condition on every write made through the view.
An INSTEAD OF trigger fires only after the row has been written to the base table.
A view may rename base columns, so the same base column can appear under different names in different views.

solution.concept: Updatability requires a one-to-one map from view rows to base rows. Grouping destroys that map because one view row summarises many base rows, so such a view is read-only. WITH CHECK OPTION adds a write-time predicate. A view is a named query, so it may rename and reorder columns freely — the name in the view is what users see.
steps: (A) True: a grouped row is an aggregate over many base rows, so an update has no single target row.
(B) True — that is its definition.
(C) False: INSTEAD OF replaces the statement; nothing has been written when it runs.
(D) True: SELECT roll AS id, cgpa AS score FROM student is a legal view definition.
solution.final: Options (A), (B) and (D) are true; (C) is false.
solution.trap: Assuming any view can be written through. Grouping, DISTINCT and unions all break the one-to-one mapping and make the view read-only.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Updatability requires a one-to-one map from view rows to base rows. Grouping destroys that map because one view row summarises many base rows, so such a view is read-only. WITH CHECK OPTION adds a write-time predicate. A view is a named query, so it may rename and reorder columns freely — the name in the view is what users see.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: a grouped row is an aggregate over many base rows, so an update has no single target row.
  2. (B) True — that is its definition.
  3. (C) False: INSTEAD OF replaces the statement; nothing has been written when it runs.
  4. (D) True: SELECT roll AS id, cgpa AS score FROM student is a legal view definition.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D) are true; (C) is false.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (C) inverts the firing semantics: an INSTEAD OF trigger runs in place of the write, so no base-table row exists yet.

Common misconception. Assuming any view can be written through. Grouping, DISTINCT and unions all break the one-to-one mapping and make the view read-only.

Takeaway. Grouped view = read-only; WITH CHECK OPTION = write-time predicate; views may rename columns.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C) is subject to no constraint other than its schema. Which one of the following functional dependencies is trivial?
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C) is subject to no constraint other than its schema. Which one of the following functional dependencies is trivial?
options: A → B
AB → C
A → AB
ABC → A
options_html: A → B
AB → C
A → AB
ABC → A

solution.concept: A functional dependency X → Y is trivial when Y ⊆ X: the right-hand side is already part of the left-hand side, so the dependency holds in every relation with that schema, whatever the data. Triviality is a syntactic test on the two attribute sets, not a claim about what the data happens to satisfy.
steps: A → B: B ⊆ A is false (B is a different attribute), so this dependency constrains the data and is non-trivial.
AB → C: C ⊆ AB is false, so it is non-trivial.
A → AB: the right-hand side contains B, which is not in A, so it is non-trivial. It happens to be true whenever A → B holds, but being implied is not the same as being trivial.
ABC → A: A ⊆ ABC is true, so every tuple satisfies it automatically. This one is trivial.
(A) A → B forbids two tuples that agree on A and differ on B — a real constraint.
(B) AB → C is the ordinary kind of dependency a schema is built on.
(C) A → AB is valid only when A → B is, so it is not automatic.
solution.trap: Calling A → AB trivial because it looks obviously true. It is true only under an extra assumption; a trivial dependency needs no assumption at all. The other frequent slip is testing the left-hand side against the right-hand side instead of the other way round.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A functional dependency X → Y is trivial when Y ⊆ X: the right-hand side is already part of the left-hand side, so the dependency holds in every relation with that schema, whatever the data. Triviality is a syntactic test on the two attribute sets, not a claim about what the data happens to satisfy.

Step by step.

  1. A → B: B ⊆ A is false (B is a different attribute), so this dependency constrains the data and is non-trivial.
  2. AB → C: C ⊆ AB is false, so it is non-trivial.
  3. A → AB: the right-hand side contains B, which is not in A, so it is non-trivial. It happens to be true whenever A → B holds, but being implied is not the same as being trivial.
  4. ABC → A: A ⊆ ABC is true, so every tuple satisfies it automatically. This one is trivial.

Answer: Option (D) — ABC → A.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) A → B forbids two tuples that agree on A and differ on B — a real constraint.
  • (B) AB → C is the ordinary kind of dependency a schema is built on.
  • (C) A → AB is valid only when A → B is, so it is not automatic.

Common misconception. Calling A → AB trivial because it looks obviously true. It is true only under an extra assumption; a trivial dependency needs no assumption at all. The other frequent slip is testing the left-hand side against the right-hand side instead of the other way round.

Takeaway. Ask one question only: is every attribute on the right already on the left? If yes, the dependency is trivial and tells you nothing about the data.

questions.question: Which one of the following is the exact condition for a relation to be in first normal form (1NF)?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following is the exact condition for a relation to be in first normal form (1NF)?
options: Every attribute of every tuple holds a single atomic value from the attribute's domain.
No non-prime attribute is partially dependent on a candidate key.
No non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on a candidate key.
Every determinant of a non-trivial functional dependency is a superkey.
options_html: Every attribute of every tuple holds a single atomic value from the attribute's domain.
No non-prime attribute is partially dependent on a candidate key.
No non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on a candidate key.
Every determinant of a non-trivial functional dependency is a superkey.

solution.concept: 1NF is the weakest of the normal forms and the only one that talks about the shape of a value rather than about dependencies. It requires the relational model's basic assumption: every cell holds one atomic value from the column's domain, so there are no repeating groups, no sets, and no nested relations.
steps: 1NF = atomic values only. A cell such as {98111, 98122} in a phone column breaks it; the fix is one row per phone number.

Option (C) is the definition of 3NF, one step further up.
Option (D) is the definition of BCNF.
(B) is 2NF, which is a statement about non-prime attributes and keys, not about atomic values.
(C) is 3NF.
(D) is BCNF.

It requires the relational model's basic assumption: every cell holds one atomic value from the column's domain, so there are no repeating groups, no sets, and no nested relations.

Step by step.

  1. 1NF = atomic values only. A cell such as {98111, 98122} in a phone column breaks it; the fix is one row per phone number.
  2. Option (B) is the definition of 2NF, which presupposes 1NF and adds a constraint on partial dependencies.
  3. Option (C) is the definition of 3NF, one step further up.
  4. Option (D) is the definition of BCNF.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) is 2NF, which is a statement about non-prime attributes and keys, not about atomic values.
  • (C) is 3NF.
  • (D) is BCNF.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {A -> B, B -> C, C -> D}. Which one of the following sets is the only candidate key of R?
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {A → B, B → C, C → D}. Which one of the following sets is the only candidate key of R?
options: {A, B}
{A, C}
{A, B, C}
options_html: {A, B}
{A, C}
{A}
{A, B, C}

solution.concept: A candidate key is a minimal attribute set whose closure is the whole relation. Compute the closure by repeatedly applying the dependencies, then check minimality: no proper subset may close to R.
steps: A⁺ = {A}. Apply A → B to get B; then B → C gives C; then C → D gives D.
So A⁺ = {A, B, C, D}: the whole relation is determined by A alone.
{A} is therefore a superkey, and it has no non-empty proper subset, so it is minimal.
Every set containing A, such as {A, B} or {A, B, C}, is a superkey but not minimal. No set without A closes: B, C and D each determine only attributes further down the chain.
(A) and (D) contain A, so they are superkeys; they are not minimal, and a candidate key must be minimal.
(B) contains A as well, and C adds nothing: A alone already reaches every attribute.
solution.trap: Answering {A, B} because the schema "looks like" it needs two attributes, or missing the chain because only one dependency is applied per pass. Keep applying the rules until nothing new appears.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A candidate key is a minimal attribute set whose closure is the whole relation. Compute the closure by repeatedly applying the dependencies, then check minimality: no proper subset may close to R.

Step by step.

  1. A⁺ = {A}. Apply A → B to get B; then B → C gives C; then C → D gives D.
  2. So A⁺ = {A, B, C, D}: the whole relation is determined by A alone.
  3. {A} is therefore a superkey, and it has no non-empty proper subset, so it is minimal.
  4. Every set containing A, such as {A, B} or {A, B, C}, is a superkey but not minimal. No set without A closes: B, C and D each determine only attributes further down the chain.

Answer: Option (C) — {A}.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) and (D) contain A, so they are superkeys; they are not minimal, and a candidate key must be minimal.
  • (B) contains A as well, and C adds nothing: A alone already reaches every attribute.

Common misconception. Answering {A, B} because the schema "looks like" it needs two attributes, or missing the chain because only one dependency is applied per pass. Keep applying the rules until nothing new appears.

Takeaway. In a chain A → B → C → D the head of the chain is the only key. Chains always collapse to their first attribute.

questions.question: Relation R(X, Y, Z) satisfies the multivalued dependency X ->> Y. Which one of the following best states what this means?
questions.question_html: Relation R(X, Y, Z) satisfies the multivalued dependency X →→ Y. Which one of the following best states what this means?
options: Each value of X is associated with exactly one value of Y.
For each value of X, the set of Y values that occurs with it does not depend on which Z values occur with it.
Within each group of equal X values, Y functionally determines Z.
X, Y and Z must together form the primary key.
options_html: Each value of X is associated with exactly one value of Y.
For each value of X, the set of Y values that occurs with it does not depend on which Z values occur with it.
Within each group of equal X values, Y functionally determines Z.
X, Y and Z must together form the primary key.

solution.concept: A multivalued dependency X →→ Y in R(X, Y, Z) says that Y and Z are independent given X. Formally, whenever (x, y₁, z₁) and (x, y₂, z₂) are both in the relation, so are (x, y₁, z₂) and (x, y₂, z₁). The Y values repeat for every Z value and vice versa.
steps: Take one X value, say a student. The set of courses that student takes and the set of hobbies that student has are two independent facts about that student.
If the two facts are stored in one relation, every course must be paired with every hobby, or the table would wrongly suggest that a particular course goes with a particular hobby.
That forced cross-product is exactly the independence statement: given X, the Y set is the same whichever Z you look at.
So the meaning is (B); nothing here says a single Y per X, which would be the functional dependency X → Y.
(A) describes a functional dependency, a strictly stronger statement.
(C) invents a dependency inside the group that the MVD does not assert.
(D) confuses the MVD with a key constraint; keys are about uniqueness, not about independence.
solution.trap: Reading →→ as "many values, therefore many-to-many". An MVD is about two independent multi-valued facts sharing one determinant, which is why it needs a decomposition into two relations and not a junction table of pairs.

Step by step.

  1. Take one X value, say a student. The set of courses that student takes and the set of hobbies that student has are two independent facts about that student.
  2. If the two facts are stored in one relation, every course must be paired with every hobby, or the table would wrongly suggest that a particular course goes with a particular hobby.
  3. That forced cross-product is exactly the independence statement: given X, the Y set is the same whichever Z you look at.
  4. So the meaning is (B); nothing here says a single Y per X, which would be the functional dependency X → Y.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) describes a functional dependency, a strictly stronger statement.
  • (C) invents a dependency inside the group that the MVD does not assert.
  • (D) confuses the MVD with a key constraint; keys are about uniqueness, not about independence.

Common misconception. Reading →→ as "many values, therefore many-to-many". An MVD is about two independent multi-valued facts sharing one determinant, which is why it needs a decomposition into two relations and not a junction table of pairs.

Takeaway. FD = one value per determinant. MVD = a set of values per determinant, independent of the remaining attributes.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C) is decomposed into R1(A, B) and R2(B, C). The decomposition is lossless if and only if
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C) is decomposed into R₁(A, B) and R₂(B, C). The decomposition is lossless if and only if
options: A → B or C → B holds in R.
A → C or C → A holds in R.
B → A or B → C holds in R.
no dependency need hold: a binary decomposition is always lossless.
options_html: A → B or C → B holds in R.
A → C or C → A holds in R.
B → A or B → C holds in R.
no dependency need hold: a binary decomposition is always lossless.

solution.concept: For a decomposition into two relations, the lossless-join test is: the common attributes must functionally determine all of at least one part, i.e. the common set must be a superkey of R₁ or of R₂. Here the common attributes are {B}, so the condition is B → A (B is a key of R₁) or B → C (B is a key of R₂).
steps: Compute the intersection: R₁ ∩ R₂ = {B}.
Ask whether the intersection determines the whole of R₁, that is B → A.
Ask whether the intersection determines the whole of R₂, that is B → C.
If either holds, every tuple of the join is a tuple of the original relation, so the join loses nothing. If neither holds, the join can manufacture spurious tuples.
(A) puts the dependencies on the wrong side: A and C are not the common attributes, so they cannot reconstruct a tuple across the join.
(B) names attributes that do not even appear together in one part.
(D) is false: R₁(A, B) and R₂(B, C) with no dependencies at all can join into extra tuples.
solution.trap: Testing the common attribute in the wrong direction, for example accepting A → B. That dependency is about A, but A is in only one part; the join is stitched together on B.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

For a decomposition into two relations, the lossless-join test is: the common attributes must functionally determine all of at least one part, i.e. the common set must be a superkey of R₁ or of R₂. Here the common attributes are {B}, so the condition is B → A (B is a key of R₁) or B → C (B is a key of R₂).

Step by step.

  1. Compute the intersection: R₁ ∩ R₂ = {B}.
  2. Ask whether the intersection determines the whole of R₁, that is B → A.
  3. Ask whether the intersection determines the whole of R₂, that is B → C.
  4. If either holds, every tuple of the join is a tuple of the original relation, so the join loses nothing. If neither holds, the join can manufacture spurious tuples.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) puts the dependencies on the wrong side: A and C are not the common attributes, so they cannot reconstruct a tuple across the join.
  • (B) names attributes that do not even appear together in one part.
  • (D) is false: R₁(A, B) and R₂(B, C) with no dependencies at all can join into extra tuples.

Common misconception. Testing the common attribute in the wrong direction, for example accepting A → B. That dependency is about A, but A is in only one part; the join is stitched together on B.

Takeaway. Two-way rule: intersect the two schemas, then ask whether that intersection is a key of either side. One side is enough.

questions.question: Let F = {A -> B, B -> C, C -> D} be the set of dependencies of R(A, B, C, D). Which one of the following dependencies is NOT in F+?
questions.question_html: Let F = {A → B, B → C, C → D} be the set of dependencies of R(A, B, C, D). Which one of the following dependencies is NOT in F⁺?
options: D → A
A → C
B → D
A → D
options_html: D → A
A → C
B → D
A → D

solution.concept: F⁺ is the closure of F: every dependency implied by F. A dependency X → Y is implied exactly when Y ⊆ X⁺, so the whole question reduces to computing attribute closures.
steps: D⁺ = {D}: no dependency has D on its left-hand side, so nothing can be derived. D → A is therefore not implied.
A⁺ = {A, B, C, D}: A → B, then B → C, then C → D. So A → C and A → D are both implied.
B⁺ = {B, C, D}: B → C then C → D. So B → D is implied.
Only the first candidate fails, so (A) is the answer.
(B) follows by transitivity through B.
(C) follows by transitivity through C.
(D) is the transitive chain of all three dependencies.
solution.final: Answer: Option (A) — D → A is not implied.
solution.trap: Assuming dependencies run backwards as well as forwards. Transitivity is one-directional: A → D says nothing about D → A. Reversing an arrow is the single most common error in closure questions.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. F⁺ is the closure of F: every dependency implied by F. A dependency X → Y is implied exactly when Y ⊆ X⁺, so the whole question reduces to computing attribute closures.

Step by step.

  1. D⁺ = {D}: no dependency has D on its left-hand side, so nothing can be derived. D → A is therefore not implied.
  2. A⁺ = {A, B, C, D}: A → B, then B → C, then C → D. So A → C and A → D are both implied.
  3. B⁺ = {B, C, D}: B → C then C → D. So B → D is implied.
  4. Only the first candidate fails, so (A) is the answer.

Answer: Option (A) — D → A is not implied.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) follows by transitivity through B.
  • (C) follows by transitivity through C.
  • (D) is the transitive chain of all three dependencies.

Common misconception. Assuming dependencies run backwards as well as forwards. Transitivity is one-directional: A → D says nothing about D → A. Reversing an arrow is the single most common error in closure questions.

Takeaway. To test any dependency X → Y, compute X⁺ and look for Y inside it. Never reason from the right-hand side.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) has the single candidate key {A, B} and satisfies A -> C. Which one of the following correctly explains why R is not in 2NF?
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C, D) has the single candidate key {A, B} and satisfies A → C. Which one of the following correctly explains why R is not in 2NF?
options: C is a prime attribute, and prime attributes may not be functionally determined by anything.
The dependency A → C is transitive, and 2NF forbids transitive dependencies.
C is not determined by {A, B} at all, so the key cannot identify a tuple.
C is a non-prime attribute that is determined by A alone, a proper subset of the candidate key {A, B}.
options_html: C is a prime attribute, and prime attributes may not be functionally determined by anything.
The dependency A → C is transitive, and 2NF forbids transitive dependencies.
C is not determined by {A, B} at all, so the key cannot identify a tuple.
C is a non-prime attribute that is determined by A alone, a proper subset of the candidate key {A, B}.

solution.concept: 2NF forbids partial dependencies: a non-prime attribute must not depend on a proper subset of a candidate key. Here the key is {A, B}, so both A and B are prime and both C and D are non-prime.
steps: Prime attributes: A and B, because they belong to the candidate key {A, B}.
Non-prime attributes: C and D.
A → C has a left-hand side {A} that is a proper subset of the key, and its right-hand side C is non-prime.
That is precisely a partial dependency, so the relation violates 2NF. The fix is to split off R₁(A, C) and keep R₂(A, B, D).
(A) is false: a prime attribute may perfectly well be determined by something, including by a proper subset of another key.
(B) confuses 2NF with 3NF; transitivity is the 3NF concern, and it is measured against non-prime attributes determining other non-prime attributes.
(C) is false: C is determined by {A, B}, since A → C implies AB → C by augmentation.
solution.trap: Checking whether "a part of the key determines something" without checking that the something is non-prime. If the right-hand side is prime, the dependency is not a 2NF violation at all.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. 2NF forbids partial dependencies: a non-prime attribute must not depend on a proper subset of a candidate key. Here the key is {A, B}, so both A and B are prime and both C and D are non-prime.

Step by step.

  1. Prime attributes: A and B, because they belong to the candidate key {A, B}.
  2. Non-prime attributes: C and D.
  3. A → C has a left-hand side {A} that is a proper subset of the key, and its right-hand side C is non-prime.
  4. That is precisely a partial dependency, so the relation violates 2NF. The fix is to split off R₁(A, C) and keep R₂(A, B, D).

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is false: a prime attribute may perfectly well be determined by something, including by a proper subset of another key.
  • (B) confuses 2NF with 3NF; transitivity is the 3NF concern, and it is measured against non-prime attributes determining other non-prime attributes.
  • (C) is false: C is determined by {A, B}, since A → C implies AB → C by augmentation.

Common misconception. Checking whether "a part of the key determines something" without checking that the something is non-prime. If the right-hand side is prime, the dependency is not a 2NF violation at all.

Takeaway. Two conditions must both hold for a 2NF violation: the left-hand side is a proper subset of a candidate key, and the right-hand side is non-prime.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {AB -> C, C -> D, D -> A}. How many candidate keys does R have?
questions.question_html:
Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {AB → C, C → D, D → A}. How many candidate keys does R have?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: An attribute that never appears on the right-hand side of any dependency can never be derived, so it must be present in every candidate key. Here only B has that property, which narrows the search to sets containing B.
steps: Right-hand sides are C, D and A, so B never appears there: B is in every key.
B⁺ = {B}, so B alone is not a key; test the pairs that contain B.
(AB)⁺: AB → C, then C → D, then D → A gives {A, B, C, D}. AB is a candidate key.
(BC)⁺: C → D, D → A, and then AB → C is already satisfied — the closure is {A, B, C, D}. BC is a candidate key.
(BD)⁺: D → A gives A, and now AB → C gives C, so the closure is {A, B, C, D}. BD is a candidate key.
No larger set is minimal, and the three keys found are not supersets of one another. The count is 3.
solution.final: Answer: 3 — the candidate keys are AB, BC and BD.
solution.trap: Stopping at the first key found, or missing BD because it needs a two-step derivation: D → A first, and only then AB → C. Closure computation must be run to exhaustion.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An attribute that never appears on the right-hand side of any dependency can never be derived, so it must be present in every candidate key. Here only B has that property, which narrows the search to sets containing B.

Step by step.

  1. Right-hand sides are C, D and A, so B never appears there: B is in every key.
  2. B⁺ = {B}, so B alone is not a key; test the pairs that contain B.
  3. (AB)⁺: AB → C, then C → D, then D → A gives {A, B, C, D}. AB is a candidate key.
  4. (BC)⁺: C → D, D → A, and then AB → C is already satisfied — the closure is {A, B, C, D}. BC is a candidate key.
  5. (BD)⁺: D → A gives A, and now AB → C gives C, so the closure is {A, B, C, D}. BD is a candidate key.
  6. No larger set is minimal, and the three keys found are not supersets of one another. The count is 3.

Answer: 3 — the candidate keys are AB, BC and BD.

Common misconception. Stopping at the first key found, or missing BD because it needs a two-step derivation: D → A first, and only then AB → C. Closure computation must be run to exhaustion.

Takeaway. Find the attributes that appear on no right-hand side — they are in every key — then grow each of them with one more attribute at a time until the closure is the full relation.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about multivalued dependencies are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about multivalued dependencies are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Every functional dependency X → Y is also a multivalued dependency X →→ Y.
Every multivalued dependency X →→ Y is also a functional dependency X → Y.
X →→ Y is trivial exactly when Y ⊆ X or X ∪ Y = R.
A relation is in 4NF exactly when, for every non-trivial multivalued dependency X →→ Y that holds in it, X is a superkey.
options_html: Every functional dependency X → Y is also a multivalued dependency X →→ Y.
Every multivalued dependency X →→ Y is also a functional dependency X → Y.
X →→ Y is trivial exactly when Y ⊆ X or X ∪ Y = R.
A relation is in 4NF exactly when, for every non-trivial multivalued dependency X →→ Y that holds in it, X is a superkey.

solution.concept: Functional dependencies are a special case of multivalued dependencies, so the MVD class is strictly larger. Triviality and the 4NF condition are the two definitions the form is built on.
steps: (A) If every X value pairs with exactly one Y value, then certainly the Y values do not vary with Z. So X → Y implies X →→ Y — true.
(B) The converse fails: a student may take several courses and have several hobbies, which is an MVD but certainly not an FD — false.
(C) X →→ Y is trivial when Y is inside X (then it says nothing) or when X and Y together exhaust the relation (then the leftover part is empty and again nothing is constrained) — true.
(D) That is exactly the definition of 4NF: every non-trivial MVD must have a superkey on its left — true.
(B) reverses the containment: MVDs are the weaker, more general form.
solution.trap: Treating →→ as a notational variant of →. The arrow direction of the implication matters: FD implies MVD, never the other way.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Functional dependencies are a special case of multivalued dependencies, so the MVD class is strictly larger. Triviality and the 4NF condition are the two definitions the form is built on.

Step by step.

  1. (A) If every X value pairs with exactly one Y value, then certainly the Y values do not vary with Z. So X → Y implies X →→ Y — true.
  2. (B) The converse fails: a student may take several courses and have several hobbies, which is an MVD but certainly not an FD — false.
  3. (C) X →→ Y is trivial when Y is inside X (then it says nothing) or when X and Y together exhaust the relation (then the leftover part is empty and again nothing is constrained) — true.
  4. (D) That is exactly the definition of 4NF: every non-trivial MVD must have a superkey on its left — true.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) reverses the containment: MVDs are the weaker, more general form.

Common misconception. Treating →→ as a notational variant of →. The arrow direction of the implication matters: FD implies MVD, never the other way.

Takeaway. 4NF is to MVDs what BCNF is to FDs: every non-trivial dependency of the relevant kind must have a superkey on the left.

questions.question: Armstrong's axiom system for functional dependencies consists of three inference rules. Which of the following are among those three axioms? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Armstrong's axiom system for functional dependencies consists of three inference rules. Which of the following are among those three axioms? (Select all that apply.)
options: Reflexivity: if Y ⊆ X then X → Y.
Augmentation: if X → Y then XZ → YZ for every attribute set Z.
Pseudotransitivity: if X → Y and YW → Z then XW → Z.
Transitivity: if X → Y and Y → Z then X → Z.
options_html: Reflexivity: if Y ⊆ X then X → Y.
Augmentation: if X → Y then XZ → YZ for every attribute set Z.
Pseudotransitivity: if X → Y and YW → Z then XW → Z.
Transitivity: if X → Y and Y → Z then X → Z.

solution.concept: Armstrong's three axioms are reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity. They are sound (they never derive a dependency that fails in some legal instance) and complete (every implied dependency can be derived from them). Everything else in the literature is a derived rule.
steps: Reflexivity: a set determines its own subsets — an axiom.
Augmentation: adding the same attributes to both sides preserves the dependency — an axiom.
Transitivity: chaining two dependencies — the third axiom.
Pseudotransitivity is sound, and it can be proved from augmentation and transitivity, but it is not one of the three axioms. So (C) is not an axiom, while (A), (B) and (D) are.
(C) is a derived rule: it follows from (A), (B) and (D) rather than being assumed.
solution.trap: Listing pseudotransitivity, union, decomposition or additivity as axioms. They are all valid rules, but a valid rule is not necessarily an axiom — the system needs only three assumptions to generate all the rest.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Armstrong's three axioms are reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity. They are sound (they never derive a dependency that fails in some legal instance) and complete (every implied dependency can be derived from them). Everything else in the literature is a derived rule.

Step by step.

  1. Reflexivity: a set determines its own subsets — an axiom.
  2. Augmentation: adding the same attributes to both sides preserves the dependency — an axiom.
  3. Transitivity: chaining two dependencies — the third axiom.
  4. Pseudotransitivity is sound, and it can be proved from augmentation and transitivity, but it is not one of the three axioms. So (C) is not an axiom, while (A), (B) and (D) are.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (C) is a derived rule: it follows from (A), (B) and (D) rather than being assumed.

Common misconception. Listing pseudotransitivity, union, decomposition or additivity as axioms. They are all valid rules, but a valid rule is not necessarily an axiom — the system needs only three assumptions to generate all the rest.

Takeaway. Three axioms, three words: reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity. Any other named rule is derived.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {AB -> C, C -> D}. Which one of the following is the highest normal form that R satisfies?
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {AB → C, C → D}. Which one of the following is the highest normal form that R satisfies?
options: 1NF only
2NF
3NF
BCNF
options_html: 1NF only
2NF
3NF
BCNF

solution.concept: Test the forms bottom-up. Each one adds a condition, so the highest form satisfied is the last test that passes before the first that fails.
steps: Find the keys. A⁺ = {A}, B⁺ = {B}, C⁺ = {C, D}, D⁺ = {D}; (AB)⁺ = {A, B, C, D}. So AB is the only candidate key, A and B are prime, C and D are non-prime.
1NF: every value is atomic — satisfied.

2NF: is any non-prime attribute determined by a proper subset of AB? The only dependency with a smaller left-hand side is C → D, and C is not a subset of the key. So there is no partial dependency — 2NF holds.
3NF: for C → D, C is not a superkey and D is not prime, so the 3NF condition fails. The relation is not in 3NF.
BCNF fails for the same dependency, since C is not a superkey. The highest form is therefore 2NF.
(A) is too low: 2NF is satisfied, so the relation is better than 1NF only.
(C) fails because C → D is a transitive dependency on a non-prime attribute.
(D) fails for the same reason, and BCNF is stricter than 3NF anyway.
solution.trap: Declaring the relation to be in 3NF because "the key determines everything". A relation can be 2NF and still have a non-prime attribute determining another non-prime attribute, which is exactly the 3NF violation here.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Test the forms bottom-up. Each one adds a condition, so the highest form satisfied is the last test that passes before the first that fails.

Step by step.

  1. Find the keys. A⁺ = {A}, B⁺ = {B}, C⁺ = {C, D}, D⁺ = {D}; (AB)⁺ = {A, B, C, D}. So AB is the only candidate key, A and B are prime, C and D are non-prime.
  2. 1NF: every value is atomic — satisfied.
  3. 2NF: is any non-prime attribute determined by a proper subset of AB? The only dependency with a smaller left-hand side is C → D, and C is not a subset of the key. So there is no partial dependency — 2NF holds.
  4. 3NF: for C → D, C is not a superkey and D is not prime, so the 3NF condition fails. The relation is not in 3NF.
  5. BCNF fails for the same dependency, since C is not a superkey. The highest form is therefore 2NF.

Answer: Option (B) — 2NF, and not 3NF.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is too low: 2NF is satisfied, so the relation is better than 1NF only.
  • (C) fails because C → D is a transitive dependency on a non-prime attribute.
  • (D) fails for the same reason, and BCNF is stricter than 3NF anyway.

Common misconception. Declaring the relation to be in 3NF because "the key determines everything". A relation can be 2NF and still have a non-prime attribute determining another non-prime attribute, which is exactly the 3NF violation here.

Takeaway. Compute the keys first, then label every attribute prime or non-prime, then walk the ladder one form at a time. Skip no rung.

questions.question: The tableau (chase) test is applied to a decomposition of R into R1, ..., Rn. The test declares the decomposition lossless when
questions.question_html: The tableau (chase) test is applied to a decomposition of R into R₁, …, Rₙ. The test declares the decomposition lossless when
options: some row of the final tableau consists entirely of distinguished (a) symbols.
every row of the final tableau contains at least one distinguished symbol.
no row of the tableau can be changed by any further application of the dependencies.
the union of the parts is R and the intersection of all the parts is empty.
options_html: some row of the final tableau consists entirely of distinguished (a) symbols.
every row of the final tableau contains at least one distinguished symbol.
no row of the tableau can be changed by any further application of the dependencies.
the union of the parts is R and the intersection of all the parts is empty.

solution.concept: The chase builds a tableau with one row per decomposed relation. A cell holds the distinguished symbol aᵢ when the attribute Aᵢ belongs to that relation, and a subscripted b symbol otherwise. Dependencies are then applied until nothing changes. The decomposition is lossless exactly when one row becomes all-distinguished, because that row represents a tuple of the original relation that the join reproduces.
steps: Write one row per Rᵢ, marking aᵢ in the columns that Rᵢ contains.
Apply each dependency X → Y: if two rows agree on all of X, make them agree on all of Y, preferring an a symbol over a b symbol.
Repeat to a fixed point.
If some row is all a symbols, the join is lossless; otherwise it is lossy.
(B) is too weak: scattered a symbols across different rows prove nothing.
(C) merely says the chase has finished, which is the stopping rule, not the verdict.
(D) describes a union and an empty intersection, which is a property of the decomposition, not a lossless guarantee; it is in fact the classic lossy shape.
solution.final: Answer: Option (A) — one row must become entirely distinguished.
solution.trap: Assuming that a decomposition into relations whose union is R is automatically lossless. That condition is necessary for the decomposition to make sense at all; it says nothing about whether the join reconstructs the original tuples.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The chase builds a tableau with one row per decomposed relation. A cell holds the distinguished symbol aᵢ when the attribute Aᵢ belongs to that relation, and a subscripted b symbol otherwise. Dependencies are then applied until nothing changes. The decomposition is lossless exactly when one row becomes all-distinguished, because that row represents a tuple of the original relation that the join reproduces.

Step by step.

  1. Write one row per Rᵢ, marking aᵢ in the columns that Rᵢ contains.
  2. Apply each dependency X → Y: if two rows agree on all of X, make them agree on all of Y, preferring an a symbol over a b symbol.
  3. Repeat to a fixed point.
  4. If some row is all a symbols, the join is lossless; otherwise it is lossy.

Answer: Option (A) — one row must become entirely distinguished.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) is too weak: scattered a symbols across different rows prove nothing.
  • (C) merely says the chase has finished, which is the stopping rule, not the verdict.
  • (D) describes a union and an empty intersection, which is a property of the decomposition, not a lossless guarantee; it is in fact the classic lossy shape.

Common misconception. Assuming that a decomposition into relations whose union is R is automatically lossless. That condition is necessary for the decomposition to make sense at all; it says nothing about whether the join reconstructs the original tuples.

Takeaway. Chase verdict in one line: one all-a row means lossless, no such row means lossy.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {A -> B, B -> C, C -> D}. How many attributes are there in the closure A+?
questions.question_html:
Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {A → B, B → C, C → D}. How many attributes are there in the closure A⁺?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: X⁺ is the set of all attributes determined by X. It is computed by starting with X and repeatedly adding the right-hand side of every dependency whose left-hand side is already inside the set.
steps: Start with A⁺ = {A}.
A → B applies, so add B: {A, B}.
B → C applies, so add C: {A, B, C}.
C → D applies, so add D: {A, B, C, D}.
No further dependency applies, so the closure holds all 4 attributes.
solution.trap: Counting only the attributes reached in one pass, or forgetting that the starting attribute itself belongs to its closure. A⁺ always contains A.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. X⁺ is the set of all attributes determined by X. It is computed by starting with X and repeatedly adding the right-hand side of every dependency whose left-hand side is already inside the set.

Step by step.

  1. Start with A⁺ = {A}.
  2. A → B applies, so add B: {A, B}.
  3. B → C applies, so add C: {A, B, C}.
  4. C → D applies, so add D: {A, B, C, D}.
  5. No further dependency applies, so the closure holds all 4 attributes.

Answer: 4.

Common misconception. Counting only the attributes reached in one pass, or forgetting that the starting attribute itself belongs to its closure. A⁺ always contains A.

Takeaway. A chain A → B → C → D sweeps up every attribute downstream, so the closure of the head is the whole relation.

questions.question: Let F = {A -> B, B -> C, A -> C} be a set of dependencies on R(A, B, C). How many functional dependencies are there in a minimal cover of F?
questions.question_html:
Let F = {A → B, B → C, A → C} be a set of dependencies on R(A, B, C). How many functional dependencies are there in a minimal cover of F?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: A minimal (canonical) cover is an equivalent set of dependencies in which every right-hand side is a single attribute, no dependency is redundant, and no left-hand side can be shrunk. Here every right-hand side is already single, and every left-hand side is a single attribute that cannot be shrunk further.
steps: Right-hand sides are already singletons, so there is nothing to split.
Is A → B redundant? Remove it and compute A⁺ from {B → C, A → C}: the closure is {A, C}, which does not contain B. So it is needed.
Is B → C redundant? Remove it and the remaining set gives B⁺ = {B}, so it is needed.
Is A → C redundant? Remove it: from {A → B, B → C} we get A⁺ = {A, B, C}, which contains C, so it is redundant and can be dropped.
The minimal cover is {A → B, B → C}: two dependencies.
solution.trap: Reporting three because the original set had three. A minimal cover is not a subset of the original in general — it is an equivalent set with no redundancy — and here the transitive dependency must go.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A minimal (canonical) cover is an equivalent set of dependencies in which every right-hand side is a single attribute, no dependency is redundant, and no left-hand side can be shrunk. Here every right-hand side is already single, and every left-hand side is a single attribute that cannot be shrunk further.

Step by step.

  1. Right-hand sides are already singletons, so there is nothing to split.
  2. Is A → B redundant? Remove it and compute A⁺ from {B → C, A → C}: the closure is {A, C}, which does not contain B. So it is needed.
  3. Is B → C redundant? Remove it and the remaining set gives B⁺ = {B}, so it is needed.
  4. Is A → C redundant? Remove it: from {A → B, B → C} we get A⁺ = {A, B, C}, which contains C, so it is redundant and can be dropped.
  5. The minimal cover is {A → B, B → C}: two dependencies.

Answer: 2.

Common misconception. Reporting three because the original set had three. A minimal cover is not a subset of the original in general — it is an equivalent set with no redundancy — and here the transitive dependency must go.

Takeaway. To minimise: make right-hand sides single, then remove each dependency in turn and test whether the rest still derives it.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C) satisfies the two multivalued dependencies A ->> B and A ->> C, and no functional dependency. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C) satisfies the two multivalued dependencies A →→ B and A →→ C, and no functional dependency. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: R is in BCNF, and therefore also in 4NF.
R is in 4NF because A →→ B and A →→ C are its only dependencies.
R is not in 4NF, because A is not a superkey of R; the lossless 4NF decomposition is R₁(A, B) and R₂(A, C).
R cannot be decomposed into 4NF without loss of information.
options_html: R is in BCNF, and therefore also in 4NF.
R is in 4NF because A →→ B and A →→ C are its only dependencies.
R is not in 4NF, because A is not a superkey of R; the lossless 4NF decomposition is R₁(A, B) and R₂(A, C).
R cannot be decomposed into 4NF without loss of information.

solution.concept: 4NF asks that every non-trivial MVD have a superkey on its left. With no functional dependency at all, the only candidate key of R(A, B, C) is the full set ABC, so A is not a superkey and both MVDs violate 4NF.
steps: Keys: no FD holds, so no proper subset determines the relation; the candidate key is ABC.
A →→ B is non-trivial (B is not inside A, and A ∪ B = AB ≠ ABC) and A is not a superkey, so 4NF fails.
The standard 4NF decomposition of X →→ Y in R(X, Y, Z) is (X, Y) and (X, Z). Applying it gives R₁(A, B) and R₂(A, C), and the second MVD is then trivially satisfied inside those parts.

The decomposition is lossless: the common attribute A is a key of both parts (each part is a two-attribute relation in which A determines the other attribute by the MVD), so the join restores exactly the original tuples.
(A) is false: BCNF speaks only about FDs, so a relation with no FDs is trivially in BCNF — and that is exactly why BCNF alone cannot detect this redundancy. It is 4NF that fails.
(B) inverts the 4NF condition: having MVDs is precisely what must be checked, not a reason to pass.
(D) is false: the MVD-based decomposition above is lossless.
solution.trap: Concluding "in BCNF, therefore in 4NF". BCNF is defined on functional dependencies only; a relation can be in BCNF and still be in 3NF-violating shape for MVDs. Every 4NF relation is in BCNF, never the reverse.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. 4NF asks that every non-trivial MVD have a superkey on its left. With no functional dependency at all, the only candidate key of R(A, B, C) is the full set ABC, so A is not a superkey and both MVDs violate 4NF.

Step by step.

  1. Keys: no FD holds, so no proper subset determines the relation; the candidate key is ABC.
  2. A →→ B is non-trivial (B is not inside A, and A ∪ B = AB ≠ ABC) and A is not a superkey, so 4NF fails.
  3. The standard 4NF decomposition of X →→ Y in R(X, Y, Z) is (X, Y) and (X, Z). Applying it gives R₁(A, B) and R₂(A, C), and the second MVD is then trivially satisfied inside those parts.
  4. The decomposition is lossless: the common attribute A is a key of both parts (each part is a two-attribute relation in which A determines the other attribute by the MVD), so the join restores exactly the original tuples.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is false: BCNF speaks only about FDs, so a relation with no FDs is trivially in BCNF — and that is exactly why BCNF alone cannot detect this redundancy. It is 4NF that fails.
  • (B) inverts the 4NF condition: having MVDs is precisely what must be checked, not a reason to pass.
  • (D) is false: the MVD-based decomposition above is lossless.

Common misconception. Concluding "in BCNF, therefore in 4NF". BCNF is defined on functional dependencies only; a relation can be in BCNF and still be in 3NF-violating shape for MVDs. Every 4NF relation is in BCNF, never the reverse.

Takeaway. An MVD with no FD on the same determinant is invisible to BCNF and fatal to 4NF. Split X →→ Y into (X, Y) and (X, Z).

questions.question: A relation R is in Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF) exactly when
questions.question_html: A relation R is in Boyce–Codd normal form (BCNF) exactly when

no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on a candidate key.
every candidate key is a superkey.
for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y that holds in R, X is a superkey of R.

for every non-trivial functional dependency X → Y that holds in R, X is a superkey of R.

Ask whether X is a superkey — that is, whether X⁺ is the whole relation.

Step by step.

  1. Take every non-trivial FD X → Y that holds in the relation.
  2. Ask whether X is a superkey — that is, whether X⁺ is the whole relation.
  3. If the answer is yes for all of them, the relation is in BCNF; a single no means it is not.
  4. Option (D) states exactly this. (A) is 1NF, (B) is 3NF stated for non-prime attributes, and (C) is a consequence of the definition rather than the definition itself.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) describes 1NF.
  • (B) describes 3NF, which is weaker than BCNF.
  • (C) is true of every relation by definition — a candidate key is a minimal superkey — so it cannot be the BCNF test.

Common misconception. Quoting BCNF as "no transitive dependency". That is 3NF. The difference shows up precisely when a non-superkey determinant has a prime attribute on its right-hand side: 3NF permits it, BCNF does not.

Takeaway. BCNF = every determinant of a non-trivial FD is a superkey. No exceptions, no prime-attribute escape.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {A -> B, B -> C, C -> D}. Which of the following decompositions of R are lossless? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {A → B, B → C, C → D}. Which of the following decompositions of R are lossless? (Select all that apply.)
options: R₁(A, C) and R₂(B, D)
R₁(A, B) and R₂(B, C, D)
R₁(A, B) and R₂(A, C, D)
R₁(A, B, C) and R₂(C, D)
options_html: R₁(A, C) and R₂(B, D)
R₁(A, B) and R₂(B, C, D)
R₁(A, B) and R₂(A, C, D)
R₁(A, B, C) and R₂(C, D)

solution.concept: For a two-way decomposition the test is short: intersect the two schemas and check whether the intersection determines one of the parts. The chase test gives the same verdict.
steps: (A) R₁(A, C) ∩ R₂(B, D) = ∅. With no common attribute the join is a cartesian product, so the decomposition is lossy. (A) is out.
(B) common attribute B. B⁺ = {B, C, D}, so B is a key of R₂(B, C, D). Lossless.
(C) common attribute A. A⁺ = {A, B, C, D}, so A is a key of R₁(A, B). Lossless.
(D) common attribute C. C⁺ = {C, D}, so C is a key of R₂(C, D). Lossless.
Three of the four pass: (B), (C) and (D).
(A) shares no attribute between the two parts, which is the textbook lossy case.
solution.trap: Judging losslessness by "does the decomposition look natural" or by counting attributes. Only the intersection test decides, and a decomposition can look perfectly reasonable and still be lossy.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. For a two-way decomposition the test is short: intersect the two schemas and check whether the intersection determines one of the parts. The chase test gives the same verdict.

Step by step.

  1. (A) R₁(A, C) ∩ R₂(B, D) = ∅. With no common attribute the join is a cartesian product, so the decomposition is lossy. (A) is out.
  2. (B) common attribute B. B⁺ = {B, C, D}, so B is a key of R₂(B, C, D). Lossless.
  3. (C) common attribute A. A⁺ = {A, B, C, D}, so A is a key of R₁(A, B). Lossless.
  4. (D) common attribute C. C⁺ = {C, D}, so C is a key of R₂(C, D). Lossless.
  5. Three of the four pass: (B), (C) and (D).

Answer: Options (B), (C) and (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) shares no attribute between the two parts, which is the textbook lossy case.

Common misconception. Judging losslessness by "does the decomposition look natural" or by counting attributes. Only the intersection test decides, and a decomposition can look perfectly reasonable and still be lossy.

Takeaway. Intersect, then ask "is the intersection a key of either part?" For a chain A → B → C → D, any split whose two parts share a point of the chain is lossless.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D, E) satisfies F = {AB -> C, C -> D, D -> E, E -> A}. How many candidate keys does R have?
questions.question_html:
Relation R(A, B, C, D, E) satisfies F = {AB → C, C → D, D → E, E → A}. How many candidate keys does R have?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: B appears on no right-hand side, so B is in every candidate key. Every key is therefore B together with the smallest extra attribute or attributes needed to close the cycle A → C → D → E → A.
steps: B⁺ = {B}, so B alone is not a key; B needs a partner.
(AB)⁺: AB → C, C → D, D → E, E → A — the closure is all five. AB is a key.
(BC)⁺: C → D, D → E, E → A, then AB → C is already satisfied — all five. BC is a key.
(BD)⁺: D → E, E → A, then AB → C — all five. BD is a key.
(BE)⁺: E → A, then AB → C, C → D — all five. BE is a key.
None of the four contains another, so all four are minimal. The count is 4.
solution.final: Answer: 4 — the candidate keys are AB, BC, BD and BE.
solution.trap: Assuming the cycle A → C → D → E → A produces one key. A cycle lets you enter it at any point, and each entry point gives a different minimal key: that is exactly why there are four here and not one.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. B appears on no right-hand side, so B is in every candidate key. Every key is therefore B together with the smallest extra attribute or attributes needed to close the cycle A → C → D → E → A.

Step by step.

  1. B⁺ = {B}, so B alone is not a key; B needs a partner.
  2. (AB)⁺: AB → C, C → D, D → E, E → A — the closure is all five. AB is a key.
  3. (BC)⁺: C → D, D → E, E → A, then AB → C is already satisfied — all five. BC is a key.
  4. (BD)⁺: D → E, E → A, then AB → C — all five. BD is a key.
  5. (BE)⁺: E → A, then AB → C, C → D — all five. BE is a key.
  6. None of the four contains another, so all four are minimal. The count is 4.

Answer: 4 — the candidate keys are AB, BC, BD and BE.

Common misconception. Assuming the cycle A → C → D → E → A produces one key. A cycle lets you enter it at any point, and each entry point gives a different minimal key: that is exactly why there are four here and not one.

Takeaway. Locate the attributes that appear on no right-hand side, pair them with each possible entry into the cycle, and keep only the pairs whose closure is the whole relation.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C) satisfies F = {A -> B, B -> C}. Which of the following functional dependencies are in F+? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C) satisfies F = {A → B, B → C}. Which of the following functional dependencies are in F⁺? (Select all that apply.)
options: A → C
AB → C
A → BC
C → A
options_html: A → C
AB → C
A → BC
C → A

solution.concept: X → Y belongs to F⁺ exactly when Y ⊆ X⁺. Compute the closure of each left-hand side and test containment.
steps: A⁺ = {A, B, C}: A → B then B → C. So A → C holds, and A → BC holds too.
(AB)⁺ = {A, B, C}, so AB → C holds. It also follows directly by augmentation from B → C.
C⁺ = {C}: C is on the right-hand side only, so nothing can be derived from it and C → A fails.
Hence (A), (B) and (C) are in F⁺; (D) is not.
(D) reverses the direction of the chain; a dependency never implies its own converse.
solution.trap: Missing AB → C because "AB is bigger than the left-hand side of the original dependency". Augmentation makes any left-hand side bigger and keeps the dependency valid.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. X → Y belongs to F⁺ exactly when Y ⊆ X⁺. Compute the closure of each left-hand side and test containment.

Step by step.

  1. A⁺ = {A, B, C}: A → B then B → C. So A → C holds, and A → BC holds too.
  2. (AB)⁺ = {A, B, C}, so AB → C holds. It also follows directly by augmentation from B → C.
  3. C⁺ = {C}: C is on the right-hand side only, so nothing can be derived from it and C → A fails.
  4. Hence (A), (B) and (C) are in F⁺; (D) is not.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (D) reverses the direction of the chain; a dependency never implies its own converse.

Common misconception. Missing AB → C because "AB is bigger than the left-hand side of the original dependency". Augmentation makes any left-hand side bigger and keeps the dependency valid.

Takeaway. Closure test, every time: grow the left-hand side until it stops growing, then check that the right-hand side is inside.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C) satisfies A ->> B and A ->> C, with candidate key ABC. Which one of the following is a correct 4NF decomposition of R?
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C) satisfies A →→ B and A →→ C, with candidate key ABC. Which one of the following is a correct 4NF decomposition of R?
options: R₁(A, B, C) — R is already in 4NF, so no decomposition is needed.
R₁(A, B) and R₂(A, C)
R₁(A, B) and R₂(B, C)
R₁(A, C) and R₂(B, C)
options_html: R₁(A, B, C) — R is already in 4NF, so no decomposition is needed.
R₁(A, B) and R₂(A, C)
R₁(A, B) and R₂(B, C)
R₁(A, C) and R₂(B, C)

solution.concept: When X →→ Y holds in R(X, Y, Z), the 4NF decomposition is (X, Y) and (X, Z). The determinant X is kept in both parts, which is what makes the join lossless.
steps: A is not a superkey of ABC, so the relation is not in 4NF and must be decomposed.
Applying the rule to A →→ B with the leftover attribute C gives (A, B) and (A, C).
Check the parts: in (A, B) the MVD A →→ B is trivial because A ∪ B is the whole relation; the same holds for A →→ C in (A, C). Both parts are in 4NF.
Check losslessness: the common attribute is A, and each part is determined by A, so the join restores exactly the original tuples.
(A) leaves a non-trivial MVD with a non-superkey determinant in place, so 4NF is still violated.
(C) and (D) both drop A from one part. Joining on B or on C cannot reconstruct the pairing of Y values with Z values, so the decomposition loses information.
solution.trap: Decomposing like a binary many-to-many relationship, into (A, B) and (B, C). An MVD split is not a relationship split: the determinant must appear in both parts.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. When X →→ Y holds in R(X, Y, Z), the 4NF decomposition is (X, Y) and (X, Z). The determinant X is kept in both parts, which is what makes the join lossless.

Step by step.

  1. A is not a superkey of ABC, so the relation is not in 4NF and must be decomposed.
  2. Applying the rule to A →→ B with the leftover attribute C gives (A, B) and (A, C).
  3. Check the parts: in (A, B) the MVD A →→ B is trivial because A ∪ B is the whole relation; the same holds for A →→ C in (A, C). Both parts are in 4NF.
  4. Check losslessness: the common attribute is A, and each part is determined by A, so the join restores exactly the original tuples.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) leaves a non-trivial MVD with a non-superkey determinant in place, so 4NF is still violated.
  • (C) and (D) both drop A from one part. Joining on B or on C cannot reconstruct the pairing of Y values with Z values, so the decomposition loses information.

Common misconception. Decomposing like a binary many-to-many relationship, into (A, B) and (B, C). An MVD split is not a relationship split: the determinant must appear in both parts.

Takeaway. MVD split: keep X on both sides, put Y in one part and the remaining attributes in the other.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which of the following statements about 3NF and BCNF decompositions are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about 3NF and BCNF decompositions are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Every relation has a decomposition into 3NF that is both lossless and dependency preserving.
Every relation has a decomposition into BCNF that is lossless.
Every relation has a decomposition into BCNF that is both lossless and dependency preserving.
Every relation that is in BCNF is also in 3NF.
options_html: Every relation has a decomposition into 3NF that is both lossless and dependency preserving.
Every relation has a decomposition into BCNF that is lossless.
Every relation has a decomposition into BCNF that is both lossless and dependency preserving.
Every relation that is in BCNF is also in 3NF.

solution.concept: The two guarantees are not symmetric. 3NF can always deliver both properties at once, by the synthesis algorithm. BCNF can always deliver losslessness, but may be forced to give up dependency preservation.
steps: (A) 3NF synthesis from a minimal cover produces relations that are lossless and preserve every dependency, adding a relation over a candidate key if none of the synthesised relations contains one — true.
(B) The BCNF decomposition algorithm splits on any violating dependency and always yields a lossless join — true.
(C) is false. The classic counterexample is R(A, B, C) with {AB → C, C → B}: the BCNF decomposition into (A, C) and (B, C) loses AB → C.
(D) BCNF is strictly stronger than 3NF: its condition implies the 3NF condition, so every BCNF relation is in 3NF — true.
(C) overstates BCNF. When the two goals conflict, BCNF wins on redundancy and loses on dependency preservation, which is why 3NF is often the practical stopping point.
solution.trap: Believing BCNF is always preferable because it is "higher". A BCNF decomposition that drops a dependency forces every update to be checked by an expensive join, which is often worse than the redundancy 3NF leaves behind.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The two guarantees are not symmetric. 3NF can always deliver both properties at once, by the synthesis algorithm. BCNF can always deliver losslessness, but may be forced to give up dependency preservation.

Step by step.

  1. (A) 3NF synthesis from a minimal cover produces relations that are lossless and preserve every dependency, adding a relation over a candidate key if none of the synthesised relations contains one — true.
  2. (B) The BCNF decomposition algorithm splits on any violating dependency and always yields a lossless join — true.
  3. (C) is false. The classic counterexample is R(A, B, C) with {AB → C, C → B}: the BCNF decomposition into (A, C) and (B, C) loses AB → C.
  4. (D) BCNF is strictly stronger than 3NF: its condition implies the 3NF condition, so every BCNF relation is in 3NF — true.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (C) overstates BCNF. When the two goals conflict, BCNF wins on redundancy and loses on dependency preservation, which is why 3NF is often the practical stopping point.

Common misconception. Believing BCNF is always preferable because it is "higher". A BCNF decomposition that drops a dependency forces every update to be checked by an expensive join, which is often worse than the redundancy 3NF leaves behind.

Takeaway. 3NF = lossless + dependency preserving, always. BCNF = lossless, always; dependency preserving, only sometimes.
