questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {A -> B, BC -> D} and is decomposed into R1(A, B) and R2(A, C, D). Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {A → B, BC → D} and is decomposed into R₁(A, B) and R₂(A, C, D). Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: The decomposition is lossless and dependency preserving.
The decomposition is dependency preserving but lossy.
The decomposition is lossless but not dependency preserving.
The decomposition is both lossy and not dependency preserving.
options_html: The decomposition is lossless and dependency preserving.
The decomposition is dependency preserving but lossy.
The decomposition is lossless but not dependency preserving.
The decomposition is both lossy and not dependency preserving.

solution.concept: Losslessness and dependency preservation are independent properties and must be tested separately. Losslessness is about the join reconstructing the original tuples; preservation is about being able to check every original dependency inside a single decomposed relation.
steps: Losslessness: R₁ ∩ R₂ = {A}, and A → B holds, so A is a key of R₁(A, B). The join is lossless.
Dependency preservation: A → B is checkable inside R₁.
BC → D needs B and C together, but B appears only in R₁ and C only in R₂. Neither part contains both, and no part implies it: the projection of F on R₂ is empty, and on R₁ it is just A → B.
So BC → D is lost. The decomposition is lossless but not dependency preserving.
(A) fails on preservation, as shown above.
(B) fails on losslessness: the common attribute A is a key of R₁, so no spurious tuples can appear.
(D) is wrong on both counts.
solution.trap: Assuming a lossless decomposition automatically preserves dependencies. It does not, and this example is the smallest one that shows it: the two properties pull in different directions.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Losslessness and dependency preservation are independent properties and must be tested separately. Losslessness is about the join reconstructing the original tuples; preservation is about being able to check every original dependency inside a single decomposed relation.

Step by step.

  1. Losslessness: R₁ ∩ R₂ = {A}, and A → B holds, so A is a key of R₁(A, B). The join is lossless.
  2. Dependency preservation: A → B is checkable inside R₁.
  3. BC → D needs B and C together, but B appears only in R₁ and C only in R₂. Neither part contains both, and no part implies it: the projection of F on R₂ is empty, and on R₁ it is just A → B.
  4. So BC → D is lost. The decomposition is lossless but not dependency preserving.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) fails on preservation, as shown above.
  • (B) fails on losslessness: the common attribute A is a key of R₁, so no spurious tuples can appear.
  • (D) is wrong on both counts.

Common misconception. Assuming a lossless decomposition automatically preserves dependencies. It does not, and this example is the smallest one that shows it: the two properties pull in different directions.

Takeaway. Run two tests, not one. Lossless: does the intersection determine a part? Preserving: does every dependency live inside some single part?

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {A -> B, B -> C, C -> D}. How many superkeys does R have?
questions.question_html:
Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {A → B, B → C, C → D}. How many superkeys does R have?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: A superkey is any attribute set that contains a candidate key. Once the candidate keys are known, counting superkeys is a counting problem on the remaining attributes.
steps: Keys: A⁺ = {A, B, C, D}, and no attribute alone or in a pair without A closes, so the only candidate key is {A}.
Every superkey must contain A; the other three attributes B, C, D are free to be in or out.
The number of superkeys is therefore 2³ = 8.
Check by listing: {A}, {AB}, {AC}, {AD}, {ABC}, {ABD}, {ACD}, {ABCD} — eight.
solution.trap: Counting 2⁴ = 16 by letting A vary as well, or counting only the four subsets that are not supersets. A superkey must contain the whole candidate key, so A is not free.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A superkey is any attribute set that contains a candidate key. Once the candidate keys are known, counting superkeys is a counting problem on the remaining attributes.

Step by step.

  1. Keys: A⁺ = {A, B, C, D}, and no attribute alone or in a pair without A closes, so the only candidate key is {A}.
  2. Every superkey must contain A; the other three attributes B, C, D are free to be in or out.
  3. The number of superkeys is therefore 2³ = 8.
  4. Check by listing: {A}, {AB}, {AC}, {AD}, {ABC}, {ABD}, {ACD}, {ABCD} — eight.

Answer: 8.

Common misconception. Counting 2⁴ = 16 by letting A vary as well, or counting only the four subsets that are not supersets. A superkey must contain the whole candidate key, so A is not free.

Takeaway. With a single candidate key of size k in an n-attribute relation the superkey count is 2^(n − k); here 2³ = 8.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: In R(A, B, C), which one of the following multivalued dependencies is trivial?
questions.question_html: In R(A, B, C), which one of the following multivalued dependencies is trivial?
options: A →→ B
A →→ BC
B →→ C
C →→ A
options_html: A →→ B
A →→ BC
B →→ C
C →→ A

solution.concept: X →→ Y is trivial when Y ⊆ X or when X ∪ Y is the whole relation. In either case nothing is left for Y to be independent of, so the dependency imposes no condition on the data.
steps: A →→ B: B ⊆ A is false and A ∪ B = AB ≠ ABC, so it is non-trivial.
A →→ BC: BC ⊆ A is false, but the second clause holds, because A ∪ BC = ABC = R. There is no leftover attribute, so the dependency is trivial.
B →→ C: C ⊆ B is false and B ∪ C = BC ≠ ABC, so it is non-trivial.
C →→ A: A ⊆ C is false and C ∪ A = AC ≠ ABC, so it is non-trivial.
(A), (C) and (D) all leave a genuinely undetermined remainder, so each one constrains the data.
solution.trap: Using only the functional-dependency rule Y ⊆ X and forgetting the second clause X ∪ Y = R. That second clause is what makes A →→ BC trivial, and it is also why a dependency can be trivial without looking obviously so.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. X →→ Y is trivial when Y ⊆ X or when X ∪ Y is the whole relation. In either case nothing is left for Y to be independent of, so the dependency imposes no condition on the data.

Step by step.

  1. A →→ B: B ⊆ A is false and A ∪ B = AB ≠ ABC, so it is non-trivial.
  2. A →→ BC: BC ⊆ A is false, but the second clause holds, because A ∪ BC = ABC = R. There is no leftover attribute, so the dependency is trivial.
  3. B →→ C: C ⊆ B is false and B ∪ C = BC ≠ ABC, so it is non-trivial.
  4. C →→ A: A ⊆ C is false and C ∪ A = AC ≠ ABC, so it is non-trivial.

Answer: Option (B) — A →→ BC.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A), (C) and (D) all leave a genuinely undetermined remainder, so each one constrains the data.

Common misconception. Using only the functional-dependency rule Y ⊆ X and forgetting the second clause X ∪ Y = R. That second clause is what makes A →→ BC trivial, and it is also why a dependency can be trivial without looking obviously so.

Takeaway. Two triviality clauses for MVDs, one for FDs. If nothing remains outside X ∪ Y, the dependency cannot bite.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) is decomposed into R1(A, B, C) and R2(C, D). The decomposition is lossless if
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C, D) is decomposed into R₁(A, B, C) and R₂(C, D). The decomposition is lossless if
options: C → D holds in R.
A → C holds in R.
D → C holds in R.
B → C holds in R.
options_html: C → D holds in R.
A → C holds in R.
D → C holds in R.
B → C holds in R.

solution.concept: The common attribute here is C. The decomposition is lossless when C is a superkey of at least one of the two parts: of R₂(C, D), which needs C → D, or of R₁(A, B, C), which would need C to determine A and B.
steps: R₁ ∩ R₂ = {C}.
If C → D holds, C is a key of R₂, so every tuple of the join is a tuple of the original relation — lossless.
A → C constrains A and C, both of which live inside R₁; it never relates the two parts, so it cannot make the join lossless.
D → C makes D a key of R₂, not C. The common attribute must itself be the key, so this does not help.
B → C likewise lives inside R₁ and does not involve D at all.
(B) and (D) are dependencies entirely inside one part; they say nothing about how the parts join.
(C) points the arrow the wrong way: it makes D determine C, so C is not the key of R₂.
solution.trap: Accepting any dependency that mentions the common attribute. The dependency must have the common attribute on the left and must reach across the split.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The common attribute here is C. The decomposition is lossless when C is a superkey of at least one of the two parts: of R₂(C, D), which needs C → D, or of R₁(A, B, C), which would need C to determine A and B.

Step by step.

  1. R₁ ∩ R₂ = {C}.
  2. If C → D holds, C is a key of R₂, so every tuple of the join is a tuple of the original relation — lossless.
  3. A → C constrains A and C, both of which live inside R₁; it never relates the two parts, so it cannot make the join lossless.
  4. D → C makes D a key of R₂, not C. The common attribute must itself be the key, so this does not help.
  5. B → C likewise lives inside R₁ and does not involve D at all.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) and (D) are dependencies entirely inside one part; they say nothing about how the parts join.
  • (C) points the arrow the wrong way: it makes D determine C, so C is not the key of R₂.

Common misconception. Accepting any dependency that mentions the common attribute. The dependency must have the common attribute on the left and must reach across the split.

Takeaway. Common attribute C, split into R₁ and R₂: lossless if C → (R₁ − C) or C → (R₂ − C). Here C → D is the second form.

questions.question: Which one of the following is NOT a valid inference rule for functional dependencies?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following is NOT a valid inference rule for functional dependencies?
options: Union: if X → Y and X → Z then X → YZ.
Decomposition: if X → YZ then X → Y.
Converse: if X → Y then Y → X.
Pseudotransitivity: if X → Y and YW → Z then XW → Z.
options_html: Union: if X → Y and X → Z then X → YZ.
Decomposition: if X → YZ then X → Y.
Converse: if X → Y then Y → X.
Pseudotransitivity: if X → Y and YW → Z then XW → Z.

solution.concept: A functional dependency is a one-way statement about values: equal values on the left force equal values on the right. It never licenses the reverse. Reversing the arrow is the single most common invalid inference in this unit.
steps: Union and decomposition are derived rules that follow from Armstrong's augmentation and transitivity; both are sound.
Pseudotransitivity follows from augmentation and transitivity; it is also sound.
The converse claims that X → Y implies Y → X. Take R(A, B) with the single tuple (1, 1) against (2, 1): A → B holds but B → A fails, because B = 1 maps to two different A values.
So the converse is the invalid rule.
(A) Union is valid: from X → Y and X → Z, augment and combine to get X → YZ.
(B) Decomposition is valid because a set of attributes determines each of its members.
(D) Pseudotransitivity is valid: augment X → Y to XW → YW, then transitively compose with YW → Z.
solution.trap: Treating → as if it were an equation. Augmentation adds attributes on both sides, which looks like reversibility, but it is a completely different operation from swapping the two sides.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A functional dependency is a one-way statement about values: equal values on the left force equal values on the right. It never licenses the reverse. Reversing the arrow is the single most common invalid inference in this unit.

Step by step.

  1. Union and decomposition are derived rules that follow from Armstrong's augmentation and transitivity; both are sound.
  2. Pseudotransitivity follows from augmentation and transitivity; it is also sound.
  3. The converse claims that X → Y implies Y → X. Take R(A, B) with the single tuple (1, 1) against (2, 1): A → B holds but B → A fails, because B = 1 maps to two different A values.
  4. So the converse is the invalid rule.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Union is valid: from X → Y and X → Z, augment and combine to get X → YZ.
  • (B) Decomposition is valid because a set of attributes determines each of its members.
  • (D) Pseudotransitivity is valid: augment X → Y to XW → YW, then transitively compose with YW → Z.

Common misconception. Treating → as if it were an equation. Augmentation adds attributes on both sides, which looks like reversibility, but it is a completely different operation from swapping the two sides.

Takeaway. You may add attributes to both sides, or chain arrows, but you may never reverse an arrow.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements about Armstrong's three axioms is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following statements about Armstrong's three axioms is TRUE?
options: The axioms are sound but not complete, so some dependencies in F⁺ cannot be derived from them.
The axioms are both sound and complete: every dependency they derive holds in every relation satisfying F, and every dependency that holds can be derived.
The axioms generate exactly the dependencies listed in F and never anything new.
Completeness means the axioms never derive a dependency that does not actually hold.
options_html: The axioms are sound but not complete, so some dependencies in F⁺ cannot be derived from them.
The axioms are both sound and complete: every dependency they derive holds in every relation satisfying F, and every dependency that holds can be derived.
The axioms generate exactly the dependencies listed in F and never anything new.
Completeness means the axioms never derive a dependency that does not actually hold.

solution.concept: Two separate properties are at stake. Soundness means every derived dependency is genuinely implied by F. Completeness means every dependency implied by F can be derived. Armstrong's reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity are sound and complete.
steps: Soundness: each of the three axioms is easily checked against the definition of a functional dependency.
Completeness is the harder half; it is what guarantees that closure computation by repeated application of the axioms reaches all of F⁺.
Together they mean the closure F⁺ is exactly the set of derivable dependencies.
(A) Denies completeness, which Armstrong's system has.
(C) Denies that anything new is derived, which would make transitivity useless.
(D) Describes soundness, not completeness — the two words are swapped.
solution.trap: Using the two words interchangeably. Soundness is "nothing wrong gets derived"; completeness is "nothing right is left underived".

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Two separate properties are at stake. Soundness means every derived dependency is genuinely implied by F. Completeness means every dependency implied by F can be derived. Armstrong's reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity are sound and complete.

Step by step.

  1. Soundness: each of the three axioms is easily checked against the definition of a functional dependency.
  2. Completeness is the harder half; it is what guarantees that closure computation by repeated application of the axioms reaches all of F⁺.
  3. Together they mean the closure F⁺ is exactly the set of derivable dependencies.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Denies completeness, which Armstrong's system has.
  • (C) Denies that anything new is derived, which would make transitivity useless.
  • (D) Describes soundness, not completeness — the two words are swapped.

Common misconception. Using the two words interchangeably. Soundness is "nothing wrong gets derived"; completeness is "nothing right is left underived".

Takeaway. Sound + complete is what lets a closure computation stand in for reasoning about F⁺ directly.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C) satisfies F = {AB → C, C → A}. Which one of the following functional dependencies is in F⁺?
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C) satisfies F = {AB → C, C → A}. Which one of the following functional dependencies is in F⁺?
options: B → C
A → C
C → B
BC → A
options_html: B → C
A → C
C → B
BC → A

solution.concept: A dependency X → Y is in F⁺ exactly when Y ⊆ X⁺. So the whole question is four small closure computations.
steps: B⁺ = {B} — no dependency has B alone on its left, so B → C is out.
A⁺ = {A} — AB → C needs B as well, so A → C is out.
C⁺ = {C, A} — C → A applies, then AB → C needs B. So C → B is out.
(BC)⁺ = {B, C, A} — C → A gives A, and now AB → C is already satisfied. Hence BC → A holds.
(A) and (B) have left-hand sides that determine nothing beyond themselves.
(C) would need B in C⁺; the only dependency producing B is AB → C, which produces C, not B.
solution.trap: Reading AB → C backwards as "C determines A and B". The given C → A supplies only A.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A dependency X → Y is in F⁺ exactly when Y ⊆ X⁺. So the whole question is four small closure computations.

Step by step.

  1. B⁺ = {B} — no dependency has B alone on its left, so B → C is out.
  2. A⁺ = {A} — AB → C needs B as well, so A → C is out.
  3. C⁺ = {C, A} — C → A applies, then AB → C needs B. So C → B is out.
  4. (BC)⁺ = {B, C, A} — C → A gives A, and now AB → C is already satisfied. Hence BC → A holds.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) and (B) have left-hand sides that determine nothing beyond themselves.
  • (C) would need B in C⁺; the only dependency producing B is AB → C, which produces C, not B.

Common misconception. Reading AB → C backwards as "C determines A and B". The given C → A supplies only A.

Takeaway. To test membership, compute the closure of the left-hand side only — never reason about the arrow by analogy.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C) satisfies F = {A → B, B → C}. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C) satisfies F = {A → B, B → C}. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: F is a minimal cover of itself.
A → C is in F⁺.
C → A is in F⁺.
The dependency A → B is redundant in F.
options_html: F is a minimal cover of itself.
A → C is in F⁺.
C → A is in F⁺.
The dependency A → B is redundant in F.

solution.concept: A minimal cover is a set of dependencies with singleton right-hand sides, no extraneous attribute on any left-hand side, and no dependency that is implied by the rest. A dependency is redundant when it survives in the closure of the others.
steps: Both right-hand sides are already singletons, and both left-hand sides are single attributes, so no attribute can be extraneous.
Drop A → B: with only B → C left, A⁺ = {A}, so A → B is not recoverable — it is needed.
Drop B → C: with only A → B left, B⁺ = {B}, so B → C is needed too.
Hence F is already minimal, and by transitivity A⁺ = {A, B, C}, so A → C holds.
C⁺ = {C}, so C → A does not hold.
(C) inverts the chain: the arrows run A → B → C, never back.
(D) removing A → B leaves nothing that produces B, so the dependency is essential.
solution.final: Answer: Options (A) and (B) are true; (C) and (D) are false.
solution.trap: Believing a minimal cover must be unique. Several minimal covers can exist for the same F; here there happens to be only one.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A minimal cover is a set of dependencies with singleton right-hand sides, no extraneous attribute on any left-hand side, and no dependency that is implied by the rest. A dependency is redundant when it survives in the closure of the others.

Step by step.

  1. Both right-hand sides are already singletons, and both left-hand sides are single attributes, so no attribute can be extraneous.
  2. Drop A → B: with only B → C left, A⁺ = {A}, so A → B is not recoverable — it is needed.
  3. Drop B → C: with only A → B left, B⁺ = {B}, so B → C is needed too.
  4. Hence F is already minimal, and by transitivity A⁺ = {A, B, C}, so A → C holds.
  5. C⁺ = {C}, so C → A does not hold.

Answer: Options (A) and (B) are true; (C) and (D) are false.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (C) inverts the chain: the arrows run A → B → C, never back.
  • (D) removing A → B leaves nothing that produces B, so the dependency is essential.

Common misconception. Believing a minimal cover must be unique. Several minimal covers can exist for the same F; here there happens to be only one.

Takeaway. Minimal means no redundancy, not minimum cardinality over all possible equivalent sets in every case.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {A → BC, B → D, C → D}. How many functional dependencies are there in a minimal cover of F?(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {A → BC, B → D, C → D}. How many functional dependencies are there in a minimal cover of F?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Building a minimal cover has three passes: split every right-hand side into singletons, remove extraneous left-hand attributes, then remove redundant dependencies.
steps: Split: A → BC becomes A → B and A → C. The set is now {A → B, A → C, B → D, C → D}.
No left-hand side has more than one attribute, so there is no extraneous attribute to remove.
Test A → B: without it, A⁺ = {A, C, D} (via A → C and C → D), which does not contain B. Needed.
Test A → C: without it, A⁺ = {A, B, D} (via A → B and B → D), which does not contain C. Needed.
Test B → D: without it, B⁺ = {B}. Needed.
Test C → D: without it, C⁺ = {C}. Needed.
Nothing is redundant, so the minimal cover has 4 dependencies.
solution.trap: Answering 3 by counting the three original dependencies. Splitting A → BC increases the count before any redundancy removal can reduce it.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Building a minimal cover has three passes: split every right-hand side into singletons, remove extraneous left-hand attributes, then remove redundant dependencies.

Step by step.

  1. Split: A → BC becomes A → B and A → C. The set is now {A → B, A → C, B → D, C → D}.
  2. No left-hand side has more than one attribute, so there is no extraneous attribute to remove.
  3. Test A → B: without it, A⁺ = {A, C, D} (via A → C and C → D), which does not contain B. Needed.
  4. Test A → C: without it, A⁺ = {A, B, D} (via A → B and B → D), which does not contain C. Needed.
  5. Test B → D: without it, B⁺ = {B}. Needed.
  6. Test C → D: without it, C⁺ = {C}. Needed.
  7. Nothing is redundant, so the minimal cover has 4 dependencies.

Answer: 4

Common misconception. Answering 3 by counting the three original dependencies. Splitting A → BC increases the count before any redundancy removal can reduce it.

Takeaway. Split first, then prune — the two passes change the count in opposite directions, so do them in order and never skip one.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C) has exactly two candidate keys, {A} and {B, C}. Which attributes of R are prime?
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C) has exactly two candidate keys, {A} and {B, C}. Which attributes of R are prime?
options: A only
A and B
A and C
A, B and C
options_html: A only
A and B
A and C
A, B and C

solution.concept: An attribute is prime when it belongs to at least one candidate key. It need not belong to every key, and it need not be a key on its own.
steps: A is in the candidate key {A}, so A is prime.
B is in the candidate key {B, C}, so B is prime.
C is in the same candidate key, so C is prime.
All three attributes are prime.
(A) counts only the single-attribute key and forgets the composite one.
(B) and (C) each drop one member of {B, C}, but membership of a key is enough on its own.
solution.trap: Assuming a prime attribute must be able to identify a tuple by itself. Prime means "part of some key", nothing more; B alone determines nothing.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An attribute is prime when it belongs to at least one candidate key. It need not belong to every key, and it need not be a key on its own.

Step by step.

  1. A is in the candidate key {A}, so A is prime.
  2. B is in the candidate key {B, C}, so B is prime.
  3. C is in the same candidate key, so C is prime.
  4. All three attributes are prime.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) counts only the single-attribute key and forgets the composite one.
  • (B) and (C) each drop one member of {B, C}, but membership of a key is enough on its own.

Common misconception. Assuming a prime attribute must be able to identify a tuple by itself. Prime means "part of some key", nothing more; B alone determines nothing.

Takeaway. Collect every candidate key first, then take their union — that union is exactly the set of prime attributes.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {AB → C, C → D, D → B}. Which one of the following is a candidate key of R?
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {AB → C, C → D, D → B}. Which one of the following is a candidate key of R?
options: {A, B, C}
{A, C}
{B, D}
{C, D}
options_html: {A, B, C}
{A, C}
{B, D}
{C, D}

solution.concept: A candidate key is a minimal superkey. First find the attributes that can never be produced by any dependency — they must appear in every key — then close each smallest candidate.
steps: A appears on no right-hand side, so every key must contain A. A⁺ = {A}, so A alone is not a key.
(AB)⁺ = {A, B, C, D}: AB → C, then C → D. So {A, B} is a key.
(AC)⁺ = {A, C, D, B}: C → D, then D → B. So {A, C} is a key.
(AD)⁺ = {A, D, B, C}: D → B, then AB → C. So {A, D} is a key.
The candidate keys are therefore {A, B}, {A, C} and {A, D}; {A, C} is the only option among them.
(A) {A, B, C} is a superkey but not minimal — C is unnecessary because {A, B} already determines everything.
(C) (BD)⁺ = {B, D}: nothing determines A or C from B and D.
(D) (CD)⁺ = {C, D, B}: A is still missing.
solution.trap: Stopping at the first superkey found. {A, B, C} closes to everything but fails minimality, which is the whole difference between a superkey and a key.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A candidate key is a minimal superkey. First find the attributes that can never be produced by any dependency — they must appear in every key — then close each smallest candidate.

Step by step.

  1. A appears on no right-hand side, so every key must contain A. A⁺ = {A}, so A alone is not a key.
  2. (AB)⁺ = {A, B, C, D}: AB → C, then C → D. So {A, B} is a key.
  3. (AC)⁺ = {A, C, D, B}: C → D, then D → B. So {A, C} is a key.
  4. (AD)⁺ = {A, D, B, C}: D → B, then AB → C. So {A, D} is a key.
  5. The candidate keys are therefore {A, B}, {A, C} and {A, D}; {A, C} is the only option among them.

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) {A, B, C} is a superkey but not minimal — C is unnecessary because {A, B} already determines everything.
  • (C) (BD)⁺ = {B, D}: nothing determines A or C from B and D.
  • (D) (CD)⁺ = {C, D, B}: A is still missing.

Common misconception. Stopping at the first superkey found. {A, B, C} closes to everything but fails minimality, which is the whole difference between a superkey and a key.

Takeaway. Start from the attributes that appear in no right-hand side; they are forced into every key and cut the search down immediately.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {A → B, B → C, C → D, D → A}. How many superkeys does R have?(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {A → B, B → C, C → D, D → A}. How many superkeys does R have?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: A superkey is any attribute set whose closure is the whole relation. Count keys by finding the minimal ones first, then count every set that contains at least one of them.
steps: The dependencies form a single cycle A → B → C → D → A, so from any one attribute the closure grows to all four.
Every single attribute is therefore a candidate key, and no proper subset of a singleton exists.
A superkey is any non-empty set containing at least one attribute — which is every non-empty subset of a four-attribute relation.
Count: 2⁴ − 1 = 15.
solution.trap: Answering 4 by counting only the candidate keys. The question asks for superkeys, and every set that contains a key is one.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A superkey is any attribute set whose closure is the whole relation. Count keys by finding the minimal ones first, then count every set that contains at least one of them.

Step by step.

  1. The dependencies form a single cycle A → B → C → D → A, so from any one attribute the closure grows to all four.
  2. A⁺ = {A, B, C, D}, B⁺ = {B, C, D, A}, C⁺ = {C, D, A, B}, D⁺ = {D, A, B, C}.
  3. Every single attribute is therefore a candidate key, and no proper subset of a singleton exists.
  4. A superkey is any non-empty set containing at least one attribute — which is every non-empty subset of a four-attribute relation.
  5. Count: 2⁴ − 1 = 15.

Answer: 15

Common misconception. Answering 4 by counting only the candidate keys. The question asks for superkeys, and every set that contains a key is one.

Takeaway. When every attribute is a key, every non-empty subset is a superkey — the count is 2ⁿ − 1.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {AB → C, C → D, D → A}. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {AB → C, C → D, D → A}. Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)

solution.trap: Concluding that D is non-prime because it sits on the right-hand side of C → D. Being determined by something says nothing about prime status; only key membership does.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Candidate keys here are all pairs containing B, because B appears on no right-hand side and so must be in every key. Prime attributes are the union of all candidate keys.

Step by step.

  1. B is never determined, so every key contains B. B⁺ = {B}, so {B} is not a key.
  2. (AB)⁺ = {A, B, C, D} — a candidate key.
  3. (BC)⁺ = {B, C, D, A} — a candidate key.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D) are true; (C) is false.

Why the other option is wrong.

  • (C) A determines nothing at all: the only dependency with A on the left is AB → C, which needs B.

Common misconception. Concluding that D is non-prime because it sits on the right-hand side of C → D. Being determined by something says nothing about prime status; only key membership does.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D, E) satisfies F = {AB → C, BC → D, CD → E, DE → A}. How many superkeys does R have?
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C, D, E) satisfies F = {AB → C, BC → D, CD → E, DE → A}. How many superkeys does R have?

solution.concept: Count candidate keys first, then count the attribute sets that contain at least one of them. Where keys overlap, inclusion–exclusion removes the double counts.
steps: No single attribute determines all five: A⁺ = {A}, B⁺ = {B}, C⁺ = {C}, D⁺ = {D}, E⁺ = {E}.
(AB)⁺ = {A, B, C, D, E}: AB → C, BC → D, CD → E. So {A, B} is a key.
(BC)⁺ = {B, C, D, E, A}: BC → D, CD → E, DE → A. So {B, C} is a key.
(BDE)⁺ = {B, D, E, A, C}: DE → A, then AB → C. So {B, D, E} is a third key — easy to miss.
No other set closes to all five: (CD)⁺ = {C, D, E, A} is missing B, and (AC)⁺ = {A, C}.
Count the supersets of each key: {A, B} gives 2³ = 8, {B, C} gives 8, {B, D, E} gives 2² = 4.

Remove the double counts: sets containing both {A, B} and {B, C} number 4, both {A, B} and {B, D, E} number 2, both {B, C} and {B, D, E} number 2, and the set containing all three is counted back once.
(A) 10 ignores the third key {B, D, E} altogether.
(B) 12 is what you get if the two overlapping keys are treated as disjoint and the triple overlap is dropped.
(D) 16 is every non-empty subset of the five attributes, which would need every attribute to be a key.
solution.trap: Stopping after the first two keys found. {B, D, E} only closes to everything through the chain DE → A → C, and missing it changes the answer.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Count candidate keys first, then count the attribute sets that contain at least one of them. Where keys overlap, inclusion–exclusion removes the double counts.

Step by step.

  1. No single attribute determines all five: A⁺ = {A}, B⁺ = {B}, C⁺ = {C}, D⁺ = {D}, E⁺ = {E}.
  2. (AB)⁺ = {A, B, C, D, E}: AB → C, BC → D, CD → E. So {A, B} is a key.
  3. (BC)⁺ = {B, C, D, E, A}: BC → D, CD → E, DE → A. So {B, C} is a key.
  4. (BDE)⁺ = {B, D, E, A, C}: DE → A, then AB → C. So {B, D, E} is a third key — easy to miss.
  5. No other set closes to all five: (CD)⁺ = {C, D, E, A} is missing B, and (AC)⁺ = {A, C}.
  6. Count the supersets of each key: {A, B} gives 2³ = 8, {B, C} gives 8, {B, D, E} gives 2² = 4.
  7. Remove the double counts: sets containing both {A, B} and {B, C} number 4, both {A, B} and {B, D, E} number 2, both {B, C} and {B, D, E} number 2, and the set containing all three is counted back once.
  8. 8 + 8 + 4 − 4 − 2 − 2 + 1 = 13.

Answer: Option (C) — 13 superkeys.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) 10 ignores the third key {B, D, E} altogether.
  • (B) 12 is what you get if the two overlapping keys are treated as disjoint and the triple overlap is dropped.
  • (D) 16 is every non-empty subset of the five attributes, which would need every attribute to be a key.

Common misconception. Stopping after the first two keys found. {B, D, E} only closes to everything through the chain DE → A → C, and missing it changes the answer.

Takeaway. Superkey counts need the complete key list plus inclusion–exclusion; never count from the number of dependencies.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: A relation R is in third normal form (3NF) exactly when, for every non-trivial functional dependency X → A that holds in R,
questions.question_html: A relation R is in third normal form (3NF) exactly when, for every non-trivial functional dependency X → A that holds in R,
options: X is a superkey of R.
A is a prime attribute of R.
X is a superkey of R, or A is a prime attribute of R.
X contains no prime attribute of R.
options_html: X is a superkey of R.
A is a prime attribute of R.
X is a superkey of R, or A is a prime attribute of R.
X contains no prime attribute of R.

solution.concept: 3NF relaxes BCNF with one escape clause. BCNF demands that every non-trivial determinant be a superkey; 3NF allows a determinant that is not a superkey provided the determined attribute is prime.
steps: The strict condition alone is the BCNF definition, so option (A) describes BCNF, not 3NF.
The prime-attribute condition alone is too weak on its own and does not state 3NF either.
The correct statement is the disjunction: for each non-trivial X → A, either X is a superkey or A is prime.
Because a superkey condition implies the prime condition is irrelevant once satisfied, 3NF is a strict weakening of BCNF.
(A) is exactly BCNF and is therefore too strong.
(B) ignores the superkey route entirely and would wrongly reject relations whose determinants are keys.
(D) is not part of any normal-form definition.
solution.trap: Reciting 3NF as "no transitive dependency" and then applying it literally. The usable test is the disjunction above; the transitive-dependency phrasing is only an informal description.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. 3NF relaxes BCNF with one escape clause. BCNF demands that every non-trivial determinant be a superkey; 3NF allows a determinant that is not a superkey provided the determined attribute is prime.

Step by step.

  1. The strict condition alone is the BCNF definition, so option (A) describes BCNF, not 3NF.
  2. The prime-attribute condition alone is too weak on its own and does not state 3NF either.
  3. The correct statement is the disjunction: for each non-trivial X → A, either X is a superkey or A is prime.
  4. Because a superkey condition implies the prime condition is irrelevant once satisfied, 3NF is a strict weakening of BCNF.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is exactly BCNF and is therefore too strong.
  • (B) ignores the superkey route entirely and would wrongly reject relations whose determinants are keys.
  • (D) is not part of any normal-form definition.

Common misconception. Reciting 3NF as "no transitive dependency" and then applying it literally. The usable test is the disjunction above; the transitive-dependency phrasing is only an informal description.

Takeaway. 3NF = BCNF + the prime-attribute escape. Remember the escape, because every 3NF-but-not-BCNF question turns on it.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: A relation R is in 2NF but not in 3NF. Which one of the following must be TRUE?
questions.question_html: A relation R is in 2NF but not in 3NF. Which one of the following must be TRUE?
options: Some non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on a candidate key.
Some non-prime attribute is partially dependent on a candidate key.
Some determinant of a non-trivial dependency is not a superkey, and its right-hand side is a prime attribute.
R has at least two candidate keys.
options_html: Some non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on a candidate key.
Some non-prime attribute is partially dependent on a candidate key.
Some determinant of a non-trivial dependency is not a superkey, and its right-hand side is a prime attribute.
R has at least two candidate keys.

solution.concept: 2NF removes partial dependencies of non-prime attributes on part of a key. 3NF additionally removes transitive dependencies of non-prime attributes on a key. Being in 2NF but not 3NF therefore means the remaining defect is transitive, not partial.
steps: Since R is in 2NF, no non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset of a candidate key.
Since R is not in 3NF, some non-trivial X → A has X not a superkey and A non-prime.
Because A is non-prime and determined by a non-superkey, it reaches A only through another attribute set — that is precisely a transitive dependency on a candidate key.
Hence option (A) must hold.
(B) describes a violation of 2NF, which contradicts the premise.
(C) describes 3NF-but-not-BCNF: there the right-hand side is prime, so 3NF still holds.
(D) is not forced; a relation with a single candidate key can be in 2NF and not 3NF.
solution.trap: Reading "not in 3NF" as "not in 2NF". The forms are nested — every 3NF relation is in 2NF — so a 3NF failure leaves the 2NF guarantee intact.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. 2NF removes partial dependencies of non-prime attributes on part of a key. 3NF additionally removes transitive dependencies of non-prime attributes on a key. Being in 2NF but not 3NF therefore means the remaining defect is transitive, not partial.

Step by step.

  1. Since R is in 2NF, no non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset of a candidate key.
  2. Since R is not in 3NF, some non-trivial X → A has X not a superkey and A non-prime.
  3. Because A is non-prime and determined by a non-superkey, it reaches A only through another attribute set — that is precisely a transitive dependency on a candidate key.
  4. Hence option (A) must hold.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) describes a violation of 2NF, which contradicts the premise.
  • (C) describes 3NF-but-not-BCNF: there the right-hand side is prime, so 3NF still holds.
  • (D) is not forced; a relation with a single candidate key can be in 2NF and not 3NF.

Common misconception. Reading "not in 3NF" as "not in 2NF". The forms are nested — every 3NF relation is in 2NF — so a 3NF failure leaves the 2NF guarantee intact.

Takeaway. Read a normal-form gap as a diagnosis: 2NF fixes partial dependencies, 3NF fixes transitive ones, BCNF fixes everything else.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D, E) satisfies F = {A → BC, CD → E, B → D, E → A}. How many of the five attributes of R are non-prime?(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Relation R(A, B, C, D, E) satisfies F = {A → BC, CD → E, B → D, E → A}. How many of the five attributes of R are non-prime?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: An attribute is prime when it belongs to at least one candidate key. So the only way to count non-prime attributes is to enumerate candidate keys and take the complement of their union.
steps: A⁺ = {A, B, C, D, E}: A → BC, B → D, CD → E. So {A} is a candidate key.
E⁺ = {E, A, B, C, D}: E → A, then A → BC, B → D. So {E} is a candidate key.
(BC)⁺ = {B, C, D, E, A}: B → D, CD → E, E → A. So {B, C} is a candidate key.
(CD)⁺ = {C, D, E, A, B}, so {C, D} is a candidate key.
(CE)⁺ = {C, E, A, B, D}, so {C, E} is a candidate key.
(BE)⁺ = {B, E, A, C, D}, so {B, E} is a candidate key.
Union of all candidate keys = {A, B, C, D, E}. Every attribute is prime, so 0 attributes are non-prime.
solution.trap: Assuming every relation has some non-prime attribute, so answering 1 or more without checking. Here the dependency structure is so tightly connected that each attribute sits inside some key.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An attribute is prime when it belongs to at least one candidate key. So the only way to count non-prime attributes is to enumerate candidate keys and take the complement of their union.

Step by step.

  1. A⁺ = {A, B, C, D, E}: A → BC, B → D, CD → E. So {A} is a candidate key.
  2. E⁺ = {E, A, B, C, D}: E → A, then A → BC, B → D. So {E} is a candidate key.
  3. (BC)⁺ = {B, C, D, E, A}: B → D, CD → E, E → A. So {B, C} is a candidate key.
  4. (CD)⁺ = {C, D, E, A, B}, so {C, D} is a candidate key.
  5. (CE)⁺ = {C, E, A, B, D}, so {C, E} is a candidate key.
  6. (BE)⁺ = {B, E, A, C, D}, so {B, E} is a candidate key.
  7. Union of all candidate keys = {A, B, C, D, E}. Every attribute is prime, so 0 attributes are non-prime.

Answer: 0

Common misconception. Assuming every relation has some non-prime attribute, so answering 1 or more without checking. Here the dependency structure is so tightly connected that each attribute sits inside some key.

Takeaway. When every attribute is prime, the 3NF prime-attribute escape applies to every dependency, so the relation is automatically in 3NF — a useful shortcut worth checking before a long normal-form analysis.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which of the following statements about second normal form are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about second normal form are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: 2NF forbids a non-prime attribute from depending on a proper subset of any candidate key.
A relation in 1NF whose only candidate key is a single attribute is automatically in 2NF.
Every relation in BCNF is also in 2NF.
Every relation in 2NF is also in 3NF.
options_html: 2NF forbids a non-prime attribute from depending on a proper subset of any candidate key.
A relation in 1NF whose only candidate key is a single attribute is automatically in 2NF.
Every relation in BCNF is also in 2NF.
Every relation in 2NF is also in 3NF.

solution.concept: 2NF is about partial dependencies: a non-prime attribute must depend on a whole candidate key, never on part of one. Partial dependency can only arise when a candidate key has at least two attributes.
steps: (A) is the definition of 2NF, stated for every candidate key rather than just the primary key.
(B) follows because a single-attribute key has no non-empty proper subset, so no partial dependency is possible.
(C) follows because BCNF forbids every non-superkey determinant, which includes the partial ones; BCNF is the strongest of the three forms and implies the weaker two.
(D) is false: a relation can be in 2NF and still carry a transitive dependency, which is exactly what 3NF removes.
(D) reverses the containment: 3NF ⊂ 2NF ⊂ 1NF, so 3NF implies 2NF and never the other way round.
solution.final: Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C) are true; (D) is false.
solution.trap: Checking partial dependency against the primary key only. 2NF is defined against every candidate key, and a relation can be clean on one key and dirty on another.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. 2NF is about partial dependencies: a non-prime attribute must depend on a whole candidate key, never on part of one. Partial dependency can only arise when a candidate key has at least two attributes.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is the definition of 2NF, stated for every candidate key rather than just the primary key.
  2. (B) follows because a single-attribute key has no non-empty proper subset, so no partial dependency is possible.
  3. (C) follows because BCNF forbids every non-superkey determinant, which includes the partial ones; BCNF is the strongest of the three forms and implies the weaker two.
  4. (D) is false: a relation can be in 2NF and still carry a transitive dependency, which is exactly what 3NF removes.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C) are true; (D) is false.

Why the other option is wrong.

  • (D) reverses the containment: 3NF ⊂ 2NF ⊂ 1NF, so 3NF implies 2NF and never the other way round.

Common misconception. Checking partial dependency against the primary key only. 2NF is defined against every candidate key, and a relation can be clean on one key and dirty on another.

Takeaway. Nested order 1NF ⊂ 2NF ⊂ 3NF ⊂ BCNF; each step removes one specific defect.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D, E) satisfies F = {A → B, BC → D, D → E, E → C}. Which one of the following is the highest normal form that R satisfies?
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C, D, E) satisfies F = {A → B, BC → D, D → E, E → C}. Which one of the following is the highest normal form that R satisfies?
options: 1NF only
2NF
3NF
BCNF
options_html: 1NF only
2NF
3NF
BCNF

solution.concept: Test the forms from the strongest down, but you need the candidate keys first: whether a dependency is partial depends on which attributes form a key.
steps: A appears on no right-hand side, so A is in every key. A⁺ = {A, B}, so {A} is not a key.
(AC)⁺ = {A, B, C, D, E}: A → B, BC → D, D → E. So {A, C} is a key.
(AD)⁺ = {A, B, D, E, C}: D → E, E → C, then BC → D. So {A, D} is a key. Likewise {A, E} is a key.
Candidate keys are {A, C}, {A, D} and {A, E}; the non-prime attribute is B alone.
2NF: A → B determines the non-prime B from A, a proper subset of the key {A, C}. That is a partial dependency, so 2NF fails.
Since 2NF fails, 3NF and BCNF fail too, and the highest form satisfied is 1NF.
(B) would require B to depend on the whole of every key, but A → B gives it from A alone.
(C) and (D) cannot hold once 2NF has failed, because the forms are nested.
solution.trap: Spotting that all three keys contain A and concluding the relation is fine. A shared attribute in every key makes partial dependencies more likely, not less.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Test the forms from the strongest down, but you need the candidate keys first: whether a dependency is partial depends on which attributes form a key.

Step by step.

  1. A appears on no right-hand side, so A is in every key. A⁺ = {A, B}, so {A} is not a key.
  2. (AC)⁺ = {A, B, C, D, E}: A → B, BC → D, D → E. So {A, C} is a key.
  3. (AD)⁺ = {A, B, D, E, C}: D → E, E → C, then BC → D. So {A, D} is a key. Likewise {A, E} is a key.
  4. Candidate keys are {A, C}, {A, D} and {A, E}; the non-prime attribute is B alone.
  5. 2NF: A → B determines the non-prime B from A, a proper subset of the key {A, C}. That is a partial dependency, so 2NF fails.
  6. Since 2NF fails, 3NF and BCNF fail too, and the highest form satisfied is 1NF.

Answer: Option (A) — 1NF only.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) would require B to depend on the whole of every key, but A → B gives it from A alone.
  • (C) and (D) cannot hold once 2NF has failed, because the forms are nested.

Common misconception. Spotting that all three keys contain A and concluding the relation is fine. A shared attribute in every key makes partial dependencies more likely, not less.

Takeaway. Find the candidate keys first; without them "partial dependency" is not even a well-defined test.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: A decomposition of R into R₁, …, Rₙ is dependency preserving when
questions.question_html: A decomposition of R into R₁, …, Rₙ is dependency preserving when
options: the union of the projections of F onto the parts is equivalent to F.
every pair of parts shares at least one attribute.
the union of the parts is R, so no attribute is lost.
every part is in BCNF.
options_html: the union of the projections of F onto the parts is equivalent to F.
every pair of parts shares at least one attribute.
the union of the parts is R, so no attribute is lost.
every part is in BCNF.

solution.concept: Dependency preservation is about whether the constraints can still be enforced without joining the parts back together. Each part Rᵢ can only enforce the dependencies whose attributes all lie inside it — its projection Fᵢ of F⁺.
steps: Project F onto each part: Fᵢ contains every dependency of F⁺ whose attributes are all in Rᵢ.
Take the union G = F₁ ∪ … ∪ Fₙ.
The decomposition preserves dependencies exactly when G⁺ = F⁺, i.e. when G is equivalent to F.
(B) describes a condition sometimes used for losslessness, not for dependency preservation; two parts can share an attribute and still lose a dependency.
(C) is the basic sanity condition for any decomposition at all, and is satisfied by decompositions that lose dependencies.
(D) is a normal-form property and is unrelated to whether dependencies survive.
solution.trap: Confusing dependency preservation with losslessness. They are independent: a decomposition can be lossless and not preserve dependencies, or preserve them and be lossy.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Dependency preservation is about whether the constraints can still be enforced without joining the parts back together. Each part Rᵢ can only enforce the dependencies whose attributes all lie inside it — its projection Fᵢ of F⁺.

Step by step.

  1. Project F onto each part: Fᵢ contains every dependency of F⁺ whose attributes are all in Rᵢ.
  2. Take the union G = F₁ ∪ … ∪ Fₙ.
  3. The decomposition preserves dependencies exactly when G⁺ = F⁺, i.e. when G is equivalent to F.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) describes a condition sometimes used for losslessness, not for dependency preservation; two parts can share an attribute and still lose a dependency.
  • (C) is the basic sanity condition for any decomposition at all, and is satisfied by decompositions that lose dependencies.
  • (D) is a normal-form property and is unrelated to whether dependencies survive.

Common misconception. Confusing dependency preservation with losslessness. They are independent: a decomposition can be lossless and not preserve dependencies, or preserve them and be lossy.

Takeaway. Lossless = no spurious tuples on join; dependency preserving = constraints still enforceable part by part.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {A → B, C → D} and is decomposed into R₁(A, B) and R₂(C, D). Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {A → B, C → D} and is decomposed into R₁(A, B) and R₂(C, D). Which one of the following statements is TRUE?
options: The decomposition is lossless and dependency preserving.
The decomposition is lossless but not dependency preserving.
The decomposition is lossy but dependency preserving.
The decomposition is both lossy and not dependency preserving.
options_html: The decomposition is lossless and dependency preserving.
The decomposition is lossless but not dependency preserving.
The decomposition is lossy but dependency preserving.
The decomposition is both lossy and not dependency preserving.

solution.concept: Two independent tests. Losslessness for a binary decomposition: the common attributes must be a superkey of at least one part. Dependency preservation: the union of the projected dependencies must cover F.
steps: R₁ ∩ R₂ = ∅. An empty intersection is never a superkey of either part, so the join test fails and the decomposition is lossy.
Concretely, the join of the two parts produces every combination of the A, B pairs with the C, D pairs, including tuples that were never in R.
Projection onto R₁(A, B) gives A → B; projection onto R₂(C, D) gives C → D.
Their union is exactly F, so both dependencies survive: the decomposition is dependency preserving.
(A) and (B) both claim losslessness, which an empty intersection rules out.
(D) claims the dependencies are lost, but each dependency lies entirely inside one part.
solution.trap: Assuming a decomposition that keeps every attribute and every dependency must be lossless. Losing no attribute is not the same as losing no information.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Two independent tests. Losslessness for a binary decomposition: the common attributes must be a superkey of at least one part. Dependency preservation: the union of the projected dependencies must cover F.

Step by step.

  1. R₁ ∩ R₂ = ∅. An empty intersection is never a superkey of either part, so the join test fails and the decomposition is lossy.
  2. Concretely, the join of the two parts produces every combination of the A, B pairs with the C, D pairs, including tuples that were never in R.
  3. Projection onto R₁(A, B) gives A → B; projection onto R₂(C, D) gives C → D.
  4. Their union is exactly F, so both dependencies survive: the decomposition is dependency preserving.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) and (B) both claim losslessness, which an empty intersection rules out.
  • (D) claims the dependencies are lost, but each dependency lies entirely inside one part.

Common misconception. Assuming a decomposition that keeps every attribute and every dependency must be lossless. Losing no attribute is not the same as losing no information.

Takeaway. Check the intersection first — if R₁ ∩ R₂ is empty, the binary decomposition is lossy no matter how the dependencies fall.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {A → B, B → C, C → D}. Which of the following decompositions of R are dependency preserving? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {A → B, B → C, C → D}. Which of the following decompositions of R are dependency preserving? (Select all that apply.)
options: R₁(A, B), R₂(B, C), R₃(C, D)
R₁(A, B), R₂(B, D)
R₁(A, B), R₂(A, C, D)
R₁(A, B, C), R₂(C, D)
options_html: R₁(A, B), R₂(B, C), R₃(C, D)
R₁(A, B), R₂(B, D)
R₁(A, B), R₂(A, C, D)
R₁(A, B, C), R₂(C, D)

solution.concept: For each dependency of F, compute the closure of its left-hand side under the union of the projected dependencies. The decomposition preserves dependencies only if every dependency passes.
steps: (A) Projections give A → B, B → C and C → D — exactly F. Preserved.
(B) Projections give A → B and B → D (valid since B⁺ = {B, C, D}). Under these, B⁺ = {B, D}, so B → C is lost.
(C) Projections give A → B and, on A, C, D, A → C, A → D, C → D. Under these, B⁺ = {B}, so B → C is lost.
(D) Projections give A → B, B → C, A → C and C → D. All three dependencies of F are recovered. Preserved.
(B) and (C) both split B away from C, so nothing inside either part can express B → C.
solution.final: Answer: Options (A) and (D) are dependency preserving; (B) and (C) are not.
solution.trap: Judging preservation by whether the original dependencies "appear" in the parts. A dependency can be implied by the projections even when it is not written down, as A → C in part (D) shows.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. For each dependency of F, compute the closure of its left-hand side under the union of the projected dependencies. The decomposition preserves dependencies only if every dependency passes.

Step by step.

  1. (A) Projections give A → B, B → C and C → D — exactly F. Preserved.
  2. (B) Projections give A → B and B → D (valid since B⁺ = {B, C, D}). Under these, B⁺ = {B, D}, so B → C is lost.
  3. (C) Projections give A → B and, on A, C, D, A → C, A → D, C → D. Under these, B⁺ = {B}, so B → C is lost.
  4. (D) Projections give A → B, B → C, A → C and C → D. All three dependencies of F are recovered. Preserved.

Answer: Options (A) and (D) are dependency preserving; (B) and (C) are not.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) and (C) both split B away from C, so nothing inside either part can express B → C.

Common misconception. Judging preservation by whether the original dependencies "appear" in the parts. A dependency can be implied by the projections even when it is not written down, as A → C in part (D) shows.

Takeaway. Preservation is a closure test on the union of projections, not a visual check for identical arrows.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D, E) satisfies F = {AB → C, C → D, D → E} and is decomposed into R₁(A, B, C), R₂(A, B, D) and R₃(D, E). How many of the three dependencies of F are preserved by this decomposition?(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Relation R(A, B, C, D, E) satisfies F = {AB → C, C → D, D → E} and is decomposed into R₁(A, B, C), R₂(A, B, D) and R₃(D, E). How many of the three dependencies of F are preserved by this decomposition?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Project F⁺ onto each part, union the projections into G, then test each dependency of F by computing the left-hand closure under G.
steps: Projection onto R₁(A, B, C): AB → C (attributes A, B, C all present).
Projection onto R₂(A, B, D): AB → D, which is valid because (AB)⁺ = {A, B, C, D, E} in F.
Projection onto R₃(D, E): D → E.
So G = {AB → C, AB → D, D → E}.
Test AB → C: (AB)⁺ under G = {A, B, C, D, E}. Preserved.
Test C → D: C⁺ under G = {C}, because no dependency in G has C on its left. Lost.
Test D → E: D⁺ under G = {D, E}. Preserved.
Two of the three are preserved.
solution.trap: Counting C → D as preserved because C and D both survive somewhere in the schema. They never appear together in a single part, so no part can enforce that dependency.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Project F⁺ onto each part, union the projections into G, then test each dependency of F by computing the left-hand closure under G.

Step by step.

  1. Projection onto R₁(A, B, C): AB → C (attributes A, B, C all present).
  2. Projection onto R₂(A, B, D): AB → D, which is valid because (AB)⁺ = {A, B, C, D, E} in F.
  3. Projection onto R₃(D, E): D → E.
  4. So G = {AB → C, AB → D, D → E}.
  5. Test AB → C: (AB)⁺ under G = {A, B, C, D, E}. Preserved.
  6. Test C → D: C⁺ under G = {C}, because no dependency in G has C on its left. Lost.
  7. Test D → E: D⁺ under G = {D, E}. Preserved.
  8. Two of the three are preserved.

Answer: 2

Common misconception. Counting C → D as preserved because C and D both survive somewhere in the schema. They never appear together in a single part, so no part can enforce that dependency.

Takeaway. A dependency survives only if some single part contains all its attributes and the union of projections still implies it.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {A → B, C → D}. Which one of the following decompositions of R is lossless?
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies F = {A → B, C → D}. Which one of the following decompositions of R is lossless?
options: R₁(A, B), R₂(C, D)
R₁(A, C), R₂(B, D)
R₁(A, B), R₂(A, C, D)
R₁(A, C), R₂(B, C)

solution.concept: For a binary decomposition into R₁ and R₂, the decomposition is lossless exactly when R₁ ∩ R₂ determines every attribute of at least one of the two parts — that is, the intersection is a superkey of R₁ or of R₂.
steps: (A) R₁ ∩ R₂ = ∅, which is never a superkey. Lossy.
(B) R₁ ∩ R₂ = ∅ again. Lossy.
(C) R₁ ∩ R₂ = {A}, and A → B holds, so {A} determines all of R₁(A, B). Lossless.
(D) R₁ ∩ R₂ = {C}. Neither C → A (for R₁(A, C)) nor C → B (for R₂(B, C)) holds. Lossy.
(A) and (B) have empty intersections, so the join reconstructs the full cross product of the parts.
(D) shares C but C determines only D, which is in neither part, so nothing is pinned down.
solution.trap: Assuming any two parts that share an attribute join losslessly. The shared attributes must actually be a key of one of the parts.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. For a binary decomposition into R₁ and R₂, the decomposition is lossless exactly when R₁ ∩ R₂ determines every attribute of at least one of the two parts — that is, the intersection is a superkey of R₁ or of R₂.

Step by step.

  1. (A) R₁ ∩ R₂ = ∅, which is never a superkey. Lossy.
  2. (B) R₁ ∩ R₂ = ∅ again. Lossy.
  3. (C) R₁ ∩ R₂ = {A}, and A → B holds, so {A} determines all of R₁(A, B). Lossless.
  4. (D) R₁ ∩ R₂ = {C}. Neither C → A (for R₁(A, C)) nor C → B (for R₂(B, C)) holds. Lossy.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) and (B) have empty intersections, so the join reconstructs the full cross product of the parts.
  • (D) shares C but C determines only D, which is in neither part, so nothing is pinned down.

Common misconception. Assuming any two parts that share an attribute join losslessly. The shared attributes must actually be a key of one of the parts.

Takeaway. Binary losslessness = "the intersection is a superkey of one side". Test it with the closure of the intersection.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C) satisfies the multivalued dependency A →→ B. Which one of the following multivalued dependencies is guaranteed to hold in R as well?
questions.question_html: Relation R(A, B, C) satisfies the multivalued dependency A →→ B. Which one of the following multivalued dependencies is guaranteed to hold in R as well?
options: A →→ C
A → B
B →→ A
C →→ B
options_html: A →→ C
A → B
B →→ A
C →→ B

solution.concept: Multivalued dependencies come with a complementation rule: if X →→ Y holds in R, then X →→ (R − X − Y) holds too. The two right-hand sides partition what is left of R once X is removed.
steps: Here X = A and Y = B in R(A, B, C).
So A →→ C follows immediately.
Intuitively, "the set of B values under an A is independent of the C values" is exactly the same statement as "the set of C values is independent of the B values".
(B) is the converse of the implication X → Y ⇒ X →→ Y; an MVD does not give a functional dependency.
(C) reverses the left and right sides, which no rule permits.
(D) moves the determinant to C, which nothing licenses.
solution.trap: Treating an MVD as a weaker functional dependency. It is a different statement — about independent sets of values — and the only guaranteed consequences are complementation, augmentation, transitivity and the trivial cases.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Multivalued dependencies come with a complementation rule: if X →→ Y holds in R, then X →→ (R − X − Y) holds too. The two right-hand sides partition what is left of R once X is removed.

Step by step.

  1. Here X = A and Y = B in R(A, B, C).
  2. R − X − Y = {A, B, C} − {A} − {B} = {C}.
  3. So A →→ C follows immediately.
  4. Intuitively, "the set of B values under an A is independent of the C values" is exactly the same statement as "the set of C values is independent of the B values".

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) is the converse of the implication X → Y ⇒ X →→ Y; an MVD does not give a functional dependency.
  • (C) reverses the left and right sides, which no rule permits.
  • (D) moves the determinant to C, which nothing licenses.

Common misconception. Treating an MVD as a weaker functional dependency. It is a different statement — about independent sets of values — and the only guaranteed consequences are complementation, augmentation, transitivity and the trivial cases.

Takeaway. For every X →→ Y there is a matching X →→ (R − X − Y); always check the complement before concluding anything.

solution.concept: A multivalued dependency X →→ Y in R(X, Y, Z) says the Y values and the Z values under an X vary independently. Storing them in separate relations (X, Y) and (X, Z) therefore loses nothing: the cross product on join regenerates exactly the original tuples.
steps: If X →→ Y holds, then for each X value the relation contains every combination of its Y values with its Z values.
Joining R₁(X, Y) with R₂(X, Z) on X regenerates exactly those combinations.
No tuple that was absent can appear, so the join is exactly R — lossless.
This is the standard MVD decomposition used by 4NF.
(B) X → Y is stronger than needed and would also work, but it is not the condition; the MVD is what justifies the split.
(C) Y →→ Z would justify a different split, on Y, not this one.
(D) is false: R₁(X, Y), R₂(Z) is a binary decomposition and is lossy.
solution.trap: Believing losslessness requires a functional dependency. An MVD is enough, and the 4NF decomposition depends on exactly that fact.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A multivalued dependency X →→ Y in R(X, Y, Z) says the Y values and the Z values under an X vary independently. Storing them in separate relations (X, Y) and (X, Z) therefore loses nothing: the cross product on join regenerates exactly the original tuples.

Step by step.

  1. If X →→ Y holds, then for each X value the relation contains every combination of its Y values with its Z values.
  2. Joining R₁(X, Y) with R₂(X, Z) on X regenerates exactly those combinations.
  3. No tuple that was absent can appear, so the join is exactly R — lossless.
  4. This is the standard MVD decomposition used by 4NF.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) X → Y is stronger than needed and would also work, but it is not the condition; the MVD is what justifies the split.
  • (C) Y →→ Z would justify a different split, on Y, not this one.
  • (D) is false: R₁(X, Y), R₂(Z) is a binary decomposition and is lossy.

Common misconception. Believing losslessness requires a functional dependency. An MVD is enough, and the 4NF decomposition depends on exactly that fact.

Takeaway. Lossless binary rule: the intersection is a superkey of one part or an MVD holds across the split.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about fourth normal form are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements about fourth normal form are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Every relation in 4NF is also in BCNF.
Every relation in BCNF is also in 4NF.
Decomposing R on a multivalued dependency X →→ Y into (X ∪ Y) and (X ∪ (R − X − Y)) is lossless.
4NF is defined using functional dependencies alone.
options_html: Every relation in 4NF is also in BCNF.
Every relation in BCNF is also in 4NF.
Decomposing R on a multivalued dependency X →→ Y into (X ∪ Y) and (X ∪ (R − X − Y)) is lossless.
4NF is defined using functional dependencies alone.

solution.concept: 4NF strengthens BCNF: for every non-trivial multivalued dependency X →→ Y, X must be a superkey. Since every functional dependency is also a multivalued dependency, the 4NF condition subsumes the BCNF condition.
steps: (A) True: if every non-trivial MVD has a superkey determinant, then in particular every non-trivial FD does, because X → Y ⇒ X →→ Y. So 4NF implies BCNF.
(B) False: a relation can have a non-trivial MVD with a non-superkey determinant while having no non-trivial FD at all.
(C) True: that split is exactly the MVD decomposition, and joining the two parts on X regenerates R.
(D) False: 4NF is defined in terms of multivalued dependencies; using only FDs would just restate BCNF.
(B) reverses the containment: 4NF ⊂ BCNF, not the other way round.
(D) removes the very concept that distinguishes 4NF from BCNF.
solution.final: Answer: Options (A) and (C) are true; (B) and (D) are false.
solution.trap: Thinking 4NF and BCNF are incomparable. They are nested, and the nesting direction matters: a relation can be in BCNF and fail 4NF, never the reverse.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. 4NF strengthens BCNF: for every non-trivial multivalued dependency X →→ Y, X must be a superkey. Since every functional dependency is also a multivalued dependency, the 4NF condition subsumes the BCNF condition.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True: if every non-trivial MVD has a superkey determinant, then in particular every non-trivial FD does, because X → Y ⇒ X →→ Y. So 4NF implies BCNF.
  2. (B) False: a relation can have a non-trivial MVD with a non-superkey determinant while having no non-trivial FD at all.
  3. (C) True: that split is exactly the MVD decomposition, and joining the two parts on X regenerates R.
  4. (D) False: 4NF is defined in terms of multivalued dependencies; using only FDs would just restate BCNF.

Answer: Options (A) and (C) are true; (B) and (D) are false.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) reverses the containment: 4NF ⊂ BCNF, not the other way round.
  • (D) removes the very concept that distinguishes 4NF from BCNF.

Common misconception. Thinking 4NF and BCNF are incomparable. They are nested, and the nesting direction matters: a relation can be in BCNF and fail 4NF, never the reverse.

Takeaway. Order: 1NF ⊂ 2NF ⊂ 3NF ⊂ BCNF ⊂ 4NF, each defined by a strictly stronger condition.

questions.question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies the multivalued dependencies A →→ B and A →→ C. Applying the 4NF decomposition repeatedly until no non-trivial multivalued dependency with a non-superkey left-hand side remains, how many relations result?(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Relation R(A, B, C, D) satisfies the multivalued dependencies A →→ B and A →→ C. Applying the 4NF decomposition repeatedly until no non-trivial multivalued dependency with a non-superkey left-hand side remains, how many relations result?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: The 4NF decomposition on X →→ Y replaces R with (X ∪ Y) and (X ∪ (R − X − Y)), and the process repeats on each part until every remaining MVD is trivial or has a superkey left-hand side.
steps: A is not a superkey of R(A, B, C, D) and A →→ B is non-trivial, so split on it: (A, B) and (A, C, D).
In (A, B), the restriction of A →→ B is trivial because A ∪ B is the whole part. Done.
In (A, C, D), the restriction of A →→ C is non-trivial and A is not a superkey. Split: (A, C) and (A, D).
Both remaining parts have two attributes, so every MVD in them is trivial. The process stops.
Resulting relations: (A, B), (A, C), (A, D) — three relations.
solution.trap: Answering 2 by splitting only once on A →→ B and stopping. The second MVD survives inside (A, C, D) and must be applied again.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The 4NF decomposition on X →→ Y replaces R with (X ∪ Y) and (X ∪ (R − X − Y)), and the process repeats on each part until every remaining MVD is trivial or has a superkey left-hand side.

Step by step.

  1. A is not a superkey of R(A, B, C, D) and A →→ B is non-trivial, so split on it: (A, B) and (A, C, D).
  2. In (A, B), the restriction of A →→ B is trivial because A ∪ B is the whole part. Done.
  3. In (A, C, D), the restriction of A →→ C is non-trivial and A is not a superkey. Split: (A, C) and (A, D).
  4. Both remaining parts have two attributes, so every MVD in them is trivial. The process stops.
  5. Resulting relations: (A, B), (A, C), (A, D) — three relations.

Answer: 3

Common misconception. Answering 2 by splitting only once on A →→ B and stopping. The second MVD survives inside (A, C, D) and must be applied again.

Takeaway. Keep decomposing until every part is either two attributes wide or has only trivial MVDs — the count comes from the recursion, not from the number of given dependencies.

questions.question: Which one of the following relations is in BCNF but not in 4NF?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following relations is in BCNF but not in 4NF?
options: R(A, B, C) with A →→ B and no non-trivial functional dependency.
R(A, B, C) with A → B and B → C.
R(A, B, C) with AB → C and C → B.
R(A, B, C, D) with A → B and C → D.
options_html: R(A, B, C) with A →→ B and no non-trivial functional dependency.
R(A, B, C) with A → B and B → C.
R(A, B, C) with AB → C and C → B.
R(A, B, C, D) with A → B and C → D.

solution.concept: BCNF constrains functional dependencies; 4NF constrains multivalued dependencies. A relation escapes BCNF only through a non-trivial FD with a non-superkey determinant, and escapes 4NF through a non-trivial MVD with a non-superkey determinant. To be in BCNF but not 4NF, the relation must have no offending FD but at least one offending MVD.
steps: (A) With no non-trivial FD, BCNF is satisfied vacuously. But A →→ B is non-trivial (B ¬⊆ A and A ∪ B ≠ R) and A is not a superkey. So 4NF fails. This is the answer.
(B) B → C has B as a non-superkey determinant, so BCNF already fails.
(C) C → B has C as a non-superkey determinant (the keys are AB and AC), so BCNF fails.
(D) A → B has A as a non-superkey determinant, so BCNF fails.
(B), (C) and (D) each contain a non-trivial FD whose determinant is not a superkey, so none of them is even in BCNF.
solution.trap: Assuming that a relation with no functional dependencies must be fully normalized. With no FDs it is in BCNF automatically, but an MVD alone can still leave it outside 4NF — which is precisely why 4NF exists.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. BCNF constrains functional dependencies; 4NF constrains multivalued dependencies. A relation escapes BCNF only through a non-trivial FD with a non-superkey determinant, and escapes 4NF through a non-trivial MVD with a non-superkey determinant. To be in BCNF but not 4NF, the relation must have no offending FD but at least one offending MVD.

Step by step.

  1. (A) With no non-trivial FD, BCNF is satisfied vacuously. But A →→ B is non-trivial (B ¬⊆ A and A ∪ B ≠ R) and A is not a superkey. So 4NF fails. This is the answer.
  2. (B) B → C has B as a non-superkey determinant, so BCNF already fails.
  3. (C) C → B has C as a non-superkey determinant (the keys are AB and AC), so BCNF fails.
  4. (D) A → B has A as a non-superkey determinant, so BCNF fails.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B), (C) and (D) each contain a non-trivial FD whose determinant is not a superkey, so none of them is even in BCNF.

Common misconception. Assuming that a relation with no functional dependencies must be fully normalized. With no FDs it is in BCNF automatically, but an MVD alone can still leave it outside 4NF — which is precisely why 4NF exists.

Takeaway. BCNF looks only at FDs; 4NF looks at MVDs. A relation with MVDs and no FDs is the classic BCNF-but-not-4NF case.
