questions.question:
Three transactions are shown with the full sequence of lock and unlock operations each performs on data items X and Y, where LS is a shared lock, LX an exclusive lock and U an unlock.
T1: LS(X), U(X), LX(X), U(X)
T2: LX(X), U(X)
T3: LX(X), LX(Y), U(X), U(Y)
How many of the three transactions obey two-phase locking?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Three transactions are shown with the full sequence of lock and unlock operations each performs on data items X and Y, where LS is a shared lock, LX an exclusive lock and U an unlock.
T1: LS(X), U(X), LX(X), U(X)
T2: LX(X), U(X)
T3: LX(X), LX(Y), U(X), U(Y)
How many of the three transactions obey two-phase locking?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: A transaction obeys 2PL when, scanning its operation sequence from left to right, no lock acquisition occurs after the first release. A transaction that locks once and unlocks once, or that locks everything and then releases everything, is in two-phase form.
steps: T1: acquires X, releases X, then acquires X again. A lock is requested after a release, so the growing phase is restarted: violates 2PL.
T2: acquires X and releases it. There is a growing phase (one lock) and a shrinking phase (one unlock) with no re-acquisition: obeys 2PL.
T3: acquires X and Y, then releases X and Y. All acquisitions precede all releases: obeys 2PL.
Two of the three transactions are in two-phase form, so the answer is 2.
solution.trap: Judging T3 by how many locks it holds, or judging T1 by its last operation only. The test is positional: the first release closes the growing phase for good.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A transaction obeys 2PL when, scanning its operation sequence from left to right, no lock acquisition occurs after the first release. A transaction that locks once and unlocks once, or that locks everything and then releases everything, is in two-phase form.

Step by step.

  1. T1: acquires X, releases X, then acquires X again. A lock is requested after a release, so the growing phase is restarted: violates 2PL.
  2. T2: acquires X and releases it. There is a growing phase (one lock) and a shrinking phase (one unlock) with no re-acquisition: obeys 2PL.
  3. T3: acquires X and Y, then releases X and Y. All acquisitions precede all releases: obeys 2PL.
  4. Two of the three transactions are in two-phase form, so the answer is 2.

Answer: 2.

Common misconception. Judging T3 by how many locks it holds, or judging T1 by its last operation only. The test is positional: the first release closes the growing phase for good.

Takeaway. 2PL is checked by the position of the first unlock relative to every later lock request.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: In basic timestamp ordering, the read operation r(X) of a transaction T is rejected when
questions.question_html: In basic timestamp ordering, the read operation r(X) of a transaction T is rejected when
options: TS(T) < RTS(X).
TS(T) > WTS(X).
TS(T) < WTS(X).
T holds no lock on X.
options_html: TS(T) < RTS(X).
TS(T) > WTS(X).
TS(T) < WTS(X).
T holds no lock on X.

solution.concept: Timestamp ordering keeps, for every data item, the largest timestamp of any transaction that has read it (RTS) and of any that has written it (WTS). A read by T must behave as though it happened at time TS(T): if a younger transaction has already written X, the read cannot be placed before that write, so T is aborted and restarted.
steps: For a read r(X), the rule compares TS(T) with WTS(X).
If TS(T) < WTS(X), some younger transaction has already written X, so a read at time TS(T) would have to see that write; the schedule cannot be rearranged to allow it, so T is rejected.
Otherwise the read proceeds and RTS(X) is updated to the maximum of its old value and TS(T).
Hence the rejecting condition is TS(T) < WTS(X).
solution.trap: Mixing up the read rule with the write rule. Read compares against WTS; write compares against both WTS and RTS (and Thomas's rule modifies the write case only).

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Timestamp ordering keeps, for every data item, the largest timestamp of any transaction that has read it (RTS) and of any that has written it (WTS). A read by T must behave as though it happened at time TS(T): if a younger transaction has already written X, the read cannot be placed before that write, so T is aborted and restarted.

Step by step.

  1. For a read r(X), the rule compares TS(T) with WTS(X).
  2. If TS(T) < WTS(X), some younger transaction has already written X, so a read at time TS(T) would have to see that write; the schedule cannot be rearranged to allow it, so T is rejected.
  3. Otherwise the read proceeds and RTS(X) is updated to the maximum of its old value and TS(T).
  4. Hence the rejecting condition is TS(T) < WTS(X).

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) TS(T) < RTS(X) is not a rejection condition: a reader older than the last reader is always allowed.
  • (B) a read older than nothing in particular is irrelevant; the comparison that matters is against the last write.
  • (D) timestamp ordering uses no locks at all; that is precisely why it cannot deadlock.

Common misconception. Mixing up the read rule with the write rule. Read compares against WTS; write compares against both WTS and RTS (and Thomas's rule modifies the write case only).

Takeaway. Read rule: reject if TS(T) < WTS(X). Write rule: reject if TS(T) < WTS(X) or TS(T) < RTS(X), with Thomas's rule replacing the first rejection by ignoring the write.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Under basic timestamp ordering, a write w(X) by T with TS(T) < WTS(X) is rejected. Under Thomas's write rule the same operation is
questions.question_html: Under basic timestamp ordering, a write w(X) by T with TS(T) < WTS(X) is rejected. Under Thomas's write rule the same operation is
options: always rejected.
ignored when RTS(X) ≤ TS(T), because the value it would write is already obsolete.
executed after waiting for the younger writer to commit.
ignored whenever TS(T) < WTS(X), whatever RTS(X) is.
options_html: always rejected.
ignored when RTS(X) ≤ TS(T), because the value it would write is already obsolete.
executed after waiting for the younger writer to commit.
ignored whenever TS(T) < WTS(X), whatever RTS(X) is.

solution.concept: Thomas's write rule observes that a write which is older than the current value of the item and which nobody has read in the meantime can never be observed: the value it produces is overwritten by the younger write before any read can see it. Discarding such a write keeps the schedule view-equivalent to a serial one and avoids an unnecessary abort.
steps: Basic rule: if TS(T) < WTS(X), a younger transaction has already written X, so T is aborted.
Thomas's refinement adds a second condition: if additionally RTS(X) ≤ TS(T), no transaction has read the younger version, so T's write would be invisible anyway.

In that case the write is simply skipped (an obsolete write) and T continues; only when RTS(X) > TS(T) must T be aborted, because a reader has already seen a version that T's write would have to precede.
Hence Thomas's rule ignores the write when RTS(X) ≤ TS(T), which is option (B).
solution.trap: Applying Thomas's rule to reads as well. It refines the write rule only; reads are still rejected whenever TS(T) < WTS(X).

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Thomas's write rule observes that a write which is older than the current value of the item and which nobody has read in the meantime can never be observed: the value it produces is overwritten by the younger write before any read can see it. Discarding such a write keeps the schedule view-equivalent to a serial one and avoids an unnecessary abort.

Step by step.

  1. Basic rule: if TS(T) < WTS(X), a younger transaction has already written X, so T is aborted.
  2. Thomas's refinement adds a second condition: if additionally RTS(X) ≤ TS(T), no transaction has read the younger version, so T's write would be invisible anyway.
  3. In that case the write is simply skipped (an obsolete write) and T continues; only when RTS(X) > TS(T) must T be aborted, because a reader has already seen a version that T's write would have to precede.
  4. Hence Thomas's rule ignores the write when RTS(X) ≤ TS(T), which is option (B).

Answer: Option (B).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the basic rule, which Thomas's rule relaxes.
  • (C) timestamp ordering never waits, so no operation is ever delayed for a commit.
  • (D) drops the RTS condition, which would discard a write that a reader has already observed.

Common misconception. Applying Thomas's rule to reads as well. It refines the write rule only; reads are still rejected whenever TS(T) < WTS(X).

Takeaway. Thomas's write rule = ignore obsolete writes. It makes timestamp ordering tolerate some out-of-order writes without aborting, and it is the reason the resulting schedules are view-serializable rather than conflict-serializable.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which one of the following statements about deadlock detection is TRUE?
questions.question_html: Which one of the following statements about deadlock detection is TRUE?
options: A cycle in the wait-for graph means that a deadlock exists, and the cycle may involve any number of transactions.
A cycle in the wait-for graph is necessary but not sufficient for a deadlock.
Timestamp ordering can deadlock, so it needs a wait-for graph.
Wait-die and wound-wait can deadlock.
options_html: A cycle in the wait-for graph means that a deadlock exists, and the cycle may involve any number of transactions.
A cycle in the wait-for graph is necessary but not sufficient for a deadlock.
Timestamp ordering can deadlock, so it needs a wait-for graph.
Wait-die and wound-wait can deadlock.

solution.concept: The wait-for graph has one node per active transaction and an edge Ti → Tj when Ti is waiting for a lock held by Tj. A cycle is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock, because each transaction in the cycle waits for the next and none can proceed.
steps: A transaction blocked on a lock is waiting for the holder to release it.
If the wait-for edges form a cycle, every member of the cycle waits for another member, so none can ever proceed: deadlock.
If there is no cycle, the waits form a partial order and the transaction at the end of the longest chain will eventually finish.
The cycle may be of length 2 (the common case) or longer; nothing limits it to two transactions.
solution.trap: Thinking only two-transaction deadlocks matter. Cycles of any length occur, and a cycle of length 3 is common with three-way lock orders.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The wait-for graph has one node per active transaction and an edge Ti → Tj when Ti is waiting for a lock held by Tj. A cycle is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock, because each transaction in the cycle waits for the next and none can proceed.

Step by step.

  1. A transaction blocked on a lock is waiting for the holder to release it.
  2. If the wait-for edges form a cycle, every member of the cycle waits for another member, so none can ever proceed: deadlock.
  3. If there is no cycle, the waits form a partial order and the transaction at the end of the longest chain will eventually finish.
  4. The cycle may be of length 2 (the common case) or longer; nothing limits it to two transactions.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) reverses necessity and sufficiency: a cycle is exactly the criterion, not merely a symptom.
  • (C) timestamp ordering never makes a transaction wait, so it cannot deadlock and needs no wait-for graph.
  • (D) wait-die and wound-wait are deadlock-prevention schemes based on timestamps; one of the two transactions is always aborted rather than allowed to wait cyclically.

Common misconception. Thinking only two-transaction deadlocks matter. Cycles of any length occur, and a cycle of length 3 is common with three-way lock orders.

Takeaway. Cycle in wait-for graph ⇔ deadlock. Detection means finding a cycle; resolution means aborting a victim in it.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html: Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Basic timestamp ordering is free of deadlock because no transaction ever waits for another.
Thomas's write rule ignores an obsolete write instead of aborting the writing transaction.
In wait-die, an older transaction waits for a younger one, while a younger transaction that requests an item held by an older one is aborted.
In wound-wait, an older transaction that requests an item held by a younger one is aborted.
options_html: Basic timestamp ordering is free of deadlock because no transaction ever waits for another.
Thomas's write rule ignores an obsolete write instead of aborting the writing transaction.
In wait-die, an older transaction waits for a younger one, while a younger transaction that requests an item held by an older one is aborted.
In wound-wait, an older transaction that requests an item held by a younger one is aborted.

solution.concept: Timestamp-based protocols avoid deadlock by never blocking: a transaction either proceeds, has its operation skipped, or is aborted and restarted. The two prevention schemes, wait-die and wound-wait, decide by age who waits and who dies, always in the same direction, which is what rules out cycles.
steps: (A) True. Timestamp ordering decides every operation immediately against RTS and WTS; a transaction is aborted rather than queued, so no wait-for edge ever exists.
(B) True. That is the definition of Thomas's write rule.
(C) True. Wait-die: the older transaction is allowed to wait for the younger; the younger is aborted (dies) if it asks for an item held by an older one.
(D) False. Wound-wait is the mirror image: the older transaction wounds (aborts) the younger holder, and the younger waits for the older.
solution.trap: Swapping the two schemes. Mnemonic: wait-die is 'old waits, young dies'; wound-wait is 'old wounds, young waits'.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Timestamp-based protocols avoid deadlock by never blocking: a transaction either proceeds, has its operation skipped, or is aborted and restarted. The two prevention schemes, wait-die and wound-wait, decide by age who waits and who dies, always in the same direction, which is what rules out cycles.

Step by step.

  1. (A) True. Timestamp ordering decides every operation immediately against RTS and WTS; a transaction is aborted rather than queued, so no wait-for edge ever exists.
  2. (B) True. That is the definition of Thomas's write rule.
  3. (C) True. Wait-die: the older transaction is allowed to wait for the younger; the younger is aborted (dies) if it asks for an item held by an older one.
  4. (D) False. Wound-wait is the mirror image: the older transaction wounds (aborts) the younger holder, and the younger waits for the older.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (D) reverses wound-wait: in wound-wait the older preempts the younger, so an older requester is never the one aborted.

Common misconception. Swapping the two schemes. Mnemonic: wait-die is 'old waits, young dies'; wound-wait is 'old wounds, young waits'.

Takeaway. Both schemes are deadlock-free because waits always go in one direction of age; both can starve, which restarts with the original timestamp are meant to bound.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question:
Transactions T1, T2 and T3 start with timestamps 10, 20 and 30 respectively. Basic timestamp ordering (not Thomas's write rule) is used, and the operations below are executed in the order shown: 1. r1(X) 2. w3(X) 3. r2(X) 4. w2(Y) 5. r3(Y) 6. w1(Y). How many transactions are aborted during this execution?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Transactions T1, T2 and T3 start with timestamps 10, 20 and 30 respectively. Basic timestamp ordering (not Thomas's write rule) is used, and the operations below are executed in the order shown: 1. r1(X) 2. w3(X) 3. r2(X) 4. w2(Y) 5. r3(Y) 6. w1(Y). How many transactions are aborted during this execution?
(Enter an integer.)

solution.concept: Every operation is checked against the read and write timestamps of its item. A read is rejected when TS(T) < WTS(X); a write is rejected when TS(T) < WTS(X) or TS(T) < RTS(X). A rejected operation aborts its transaction, whose later operations are then not executed.
steps: 1. r1(X): WTS(X) is empty, so the read is granted and RTS(X) = 10.
2. w3(X): TS(T3) = 30 ≥ WTS(X) and TS(T3) = 30 ≥ RTS(X) = 10, so the write is granted and WTS(X) = 30.
3. r2(X): TS(T2) = 20 < WTS(X) = 30, so the read is rejected and T2 is aborted. That is 1 abort.
4. w2(Y): T2 has already been aborted, so this operation is not executed.
5. r3(Y): TS(T3) = 30 ≥ WTS(Y) = 0, so the read is granted and RTS(Y) = 30.
6. w1(Y): TS(T1) = 10 ≥ WTS(Y) = 0 but TS(T1) = 10 < RTS(Y) = 30, so the write is rejected and T1 is aborted. That is 2 aborts.
Total aborts = 2, one at step 3 and one at step 6.
solution.trap: Checking only WTS and forgetting the read timestamp, which is what rejects the write at step 6; or executing step 4 for an already aborted T2.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Every operation is checked against the read and write timestamps of its item. A read is rejected when TS(T) < WTS(X); a write is rejected when TS(T) < WTS(X) or TS(T) < RTS(X). A rejected operation aborts its transaction, whose later operations are then not executed.

Step by step.

  1. 1. r1(X): WTS(X) is empty, so the read is granted and RTS(X) = 10.
  2. 2. w3(X): TS(T3) = 30 ≥ WTS(X) and TS(T3) = 30 ≥ RTS(X) = 10, so the write is granted and WTS(X) = 30.
  3. 3. r2(X): TS(T2) = 20 < WTS(X) = 30, so the read is rejected and T2 is aborted. That is 1 abort.
  4. 4. w2(Y): T2 has already been aborted, so this operation is not executed.
  5. 5. r3(Y): TS(T3) = 30 ≥ WTS(Y) = 0, so the read is granted and RTS(Y) = 30.
  6. 6. w1(Y): TS(T1) = 10 ≥ WTS(Y) = 0 but TS(T1) = 10 < RTS(Y) = 30, so the write is rejected and T1 is aborted. That is 2 aborts.
  7. Total aborts = 2, one at step 3 and one at step 6.

Answer: 2.

Common misconception. Checking only WTS and forgetting the read timestamp, which is what rejects the write at step 6; or executing step 4 for an already aborted T2.

Takeaway. Simulate timestamp ordering with a table of RTS and WTS per item and check every operation against both timestamps; a rejected operation removes the transaction from the rest of the schedule.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: A transaction debits ₹2,000 from account A and credits ₹2,000 to account B. The debit reaches the database, the credit does not, and the system then crashes. Recovery undoes the debit. Which ACID property is the one that demands this undo?
questions.question_html:
Question 1MCQeasyacid-propertiesstandard textbookMarks: 1

A transaction debits ₹2,000 from account A and credits ₹2,000 to account B. The debit reaches the database, the credit does not, and the system then crashes. Recovery undoes the debit. Which ACID property is the one that demands this undo?
options: Consistency: the invariant that the sum of the two balances is preserved.
Atomicity: every update of the transaction is applied, or none of them is.
Isolation: no other transaction observes the intermediate state.
Durability: an update of a committed transaction survives a crash.
options_html: Consistency: the invariant that the sum of the two balances is preserved.
Atomicity: every update of the transaction is applied, or none of them is.
Isolation: no other transaction observes the intermediate state.
Durability: an update of a committed transaction survives a crash.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Atomicity makes a transaction an all-or-nothing unit. A transaction that has applied half of its updates must be rolled back to the state it started from, and the mechanism that does that rollback is what atomicity requires.Step by step.The transaction has two updates that must travel together: debit A, credit B.The debit reached the database and the credit did not, so the transaction is only partly applied.Recovery finds no commit record for the transaction in the log and undoes the debit, restoring the before-image.The requirement that a partly applied transaction be removed completely, rather than left half done, is exactly atomicity.Answer: Option (B) — atomicity demands the undo.Why the other options are wrong.(A) Consistency is about the transaction taking the database from one valid state to another; it is the property the application programmer preserves by writing a correct transaction, not the mechanism that undoes a half-finished one.(C) Isolation is about what concurrent transactions may observe, and no second transaction appears in this example.(D) Durability protects a committed transaction; this one never committed.Common misconception. Answering "consistency" because the sum of the balances changed. The sum changed only because the transaction was left half applied, and the undo that fixes it is atomicity’s job.Takeaway. Half-applied and then removed is atomicity; half-applied and left there would be the failure atomicity exists to prevent.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Atomicity makes a transaction an all-or-nothing unit. A transaction that has applied half of its updates must be rolled back to the state it started from, and the mechanism that does that rollback is what atomicity requires.

Step by step.

  1. The transaction has two updates that must travel together: debit A, credit B.
  2. The debit reached the database and the credit did not, so the transaction is only partly applied.
  3. Recovery finds no commit record for the transaction in the log and undoes the debit, restoring the before-image.
  4. The requirement that a partly applied transaction be removed completely, rather than left half done, is exactly atomicity.

Answer: Option (B) — atomicity demands the undo.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Consistency is about the transaction taking the database from one valid state to another; it is the property the application programmer preserves by writing a correct transaction, not the mechanism that undoes a half-finished one.
  • (C) Isolation is about what concurrent transactions may observe, and no second transaction appears in this example.
  • (D) Durability protects a committed transaction; this one never committed.

Common misconception. Answering "consistency" because the sum of the balances changed. The sum changed only because the transaction was left half applied, and the undo that fixes it is atomicity’s job.

Takeaway. Half-applied and then removed is atomicity; half-applied and left there would be the failure atomicity exists to prevent.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which one of the following is the mechanism through which a DBMS guarantees the durability of a committed transaction?
questions.question_html:
Question 2MCQeasyacid-propertiesstandard textbookMarks: 1

Which one of the following is the mechanism through which a DBMS guarantees the durability of a committed transaction?
options: Forcing the transaction’s log records to stable storage before the commit is acknowledged, so that redo can reapply the updates after a crash.
Keeping the transaction’s updated pages in the buffer pool until the next checkpoint.
Holding every lock of the transaction until the transaction terminates.
Taking a full backup of the database after every commit.
options_html: Forcing the transaction’s log records to stable storage before the commit is acknowledged, so that redo can reapply the updates after a crash.
Keeping the transaction’s updated pages in the buffer pool until the next checkpoint.
Holding every lock of the transaction until the transaction terminates.
Taking a full backup of the database after every commit.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Durability says that once the DBMS acknowledges a commit, the transaction’s effects survive a crash. The acknowledgement is therefore tied to the log reaching stable storage, not to the data pages reaching it: a redo record on disk is enough, because recovery can replay it.Step by step.At commit the DBMS appends a commit record to the log.It forces the log, including that commit record, to stable storage before it answers the client.If a crash follows, the data pages may be stale or missing entirely, but the log holds every after-image of the committed transaction.Recovery replays those after-images during redo, so the commit survives.Answer: Option (A) — force the log at commit, redo the pages later.Why the other options are wrong.(B) Pages in the buffer pool vanish with the buffer pool; buffering is what makes redo necessary.(C) Holding locks is isolation, not durability, and locks are meaningless after a crash.(D) A backup taken after each commit is neither required nor how any real system works.Common misconception. Believing the data page must be on disk at commit. It need not be; the log record must be.Takeaway. Durability is a promise about the log at commit time, not about the data file.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Durability says that once the DBMS acknowledges a commit, the transaction’s effects survive a crash. The acknowledgement is therefore tied to the log reaching stable storage, not to the data pages reaching it: a redo record on disk is enough, because recovery can replay it.

Step by step.

  1. At commit the DBMS appends a commit record to the log.
  2. It forces the log, including that commit record, to stable storage before it answers the client.
  3. If a crash follows, the data pages may be stale or missing entirely, but the log holds every after-image of the committed transaction.
  4. Recovery replays those after-images during redo, so the commit survives.

Answer: Option (A) — force the log at commit, redo the pages later.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) Pages in the buffer pool vanish with the buffer pool; buffering is what makes redo necessary.
  • (C) Holding locks is isolation, not durability, and locks are meaningless after a crash.
  • (D) A backup taken after each commit is neither required nor how any real system works.

Common misconception. Believing the data page must be on disk at commit. It need not be; the log record must be.

Takeaway. Durability is a promise about the log at commit time, not about the data file.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: A buffer manager follows the steal and force policy: an updated page may be written to disk before its transaction commits, and all of a transaction’s pages are forced to disk before its commit is acknowledged. Which one of the following is TRUE about the recovery work this policy can require?
questions.question_html:
Question 3MCQhardacid-propertiesoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

A buffer manager follows the steal and force policy: an updated page may be written to disk before its transaction commits, and all of a transaction’s pages are forced to disk before its commit is acknowledged. Which one of the following is TRUE about the recovery work this policy can require?
options: Recovery may need both undo and redo.
Recovery may need redo, but never undo.
Recovery needs neither undo nor redo.
Recovery may need undo, but never redo.
options_html: Recovery may need both undo and redo.
Recovery may need redo, but never undo.
Recovery needs neither undo nor redo.
Recovery may need undo, but never redo.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. The two buffer-policy questions decide recovery independently. Steal asks whether an uncommitted transaction’s page can reach disk, and if it can, that page must be undone when the transaction aborts. Force asks whether a committed transaction’s pages are on disk at commit, and if they are, nothing has to be redone.Step by step.Steal is allowed, so a page holding an uncommitted update can be on disk when the system crashes.That page must be rolled back to its before-image, so undo is required.Force is required, so every page of a committed transaction was already written before the commit was acknowledged.A committed transaction therefore leaves no work for redo, so redo is never required.Answer: Option (D) — undo yes, redo no.Why the other options are wrong.(A) Redo would be needed only if a committed transaction could leave stale pages on disk, which force rules out.(B) This is the answer for the opposite policy, no-steal plus no-force.(C) Steal alone is enough to demand undo.Common misconception. Treating steal and force as one setting. They are two independent decisions: steal decides undo, force decides redo.Takeaway. steal ⇒ undo needed; no-force ⇒ redo needed. Here steal and force together give undo without redo.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The two buffer-policy questions decide recovery independently. Steal asks whether an uncommitted transaction’s page can reach disk, and if it can, that page must be undone when the transaction aborts. Force asks whether a committed transaction’s pages are on disk at commit, and if they are, nothing has to be redone.

Step by step.

  1. Steal is allowed, so a page holding an uncommitted update can be on disk when the system crashes.
  2. That page must be rolled back to its before-image, so undo is required.
  3. Force is required, so every page of a committed transaction was already written before the commit was acknowledged.
  4. A committed transaction therefore leaves no work for redo, so redo is never required.

Answer: Option (D) — undo yes, redo no.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Redo would be needed only if a committed transaction could leave stale pages on disk, which force rules out.
  • (B) This is the answer for the opposite policy, no-steal plus no-force.
  • (C) Steal alone is enough to demand undo.

Common misconception. Treating steal and force as one setting. They are two independent decisions: steal decides undo, force decides redo.

Takeaway. steal ⇒ undo needed; no-force ⇒ redo needed. Here steal and force together give undo without redo.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the ACID properties and the way a DBMS implements them are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 4MSQmediumacid-propertiesoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about the ACID properties and the way a DBMS implements them are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Write-ahead logging — the log record for an update reaches stable storage before the data page it describes — is what makes undo possible after a crash.
A transaction whose commit record is on stable storage can still be lost after a crash, because its updated pages may have been only in the buffer pool.
Isolation is normally enforced by a concurrency-control protocol such as two-phase locking or timestamp ordering, rather than by running transactions one at a time.
Durability requires the effects of a committed transaction to survive a failure that wipes out the contents of main memory.
options_html: Write-ahead logging — the log record for an update reaches stable storage before the data page it describes — is what makes undo possible after a crash.
A transaction whose commit record is on stable storage can still be lost after a crash, because its updated pages may have been only in the buffer pool.
Isolation is normally enforced by a concurrency-control protocol such as two-phase locking or timestamp ordering, rather than by running transactions one at a time.
Durability requires the effects of a committed transaction to survive a failure that wipes out the contents of main memory.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Each ACID letter maps to a mechanism: atomicity and durability to the log, isolation to a concurrency-control protocol, consistency to the programmer’s invariants.Step by step.(A) is true. Undo restores a before-image, and that before-image is only available if the log record reached stable storage first. That ordering is the write-ahead rule.(B) is false. If the commit record is durable, redo replays the after-images and the transaction survives; the missing data pages are exactly what redo is for.(C) is true. Serial execution is the definition of the ideal, not the implementation; 2PL, timestamp ordering and validation are how real systems approximate it.(D) is true. That is the definition of durability: the loss of volatile memory must not lose a committed transaction.Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).Common misconception. Reading (B) as true because the pages are missing. Missing pages are recoverable from the log; only a missing commit record is fatal.Takeaway. Log first, then pages — and a durable commit record is enough on its own.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each ACID letter maps to a mechanism: atomicity and durability to the log, isolation to a concurrency-control protocol, consistency to the programmer’s invariants.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true. Undo restores a before-image, and that before-image is only available if the log record reached stable storage first. That ordering is the write-ahead rule.
  2. (B) is false. If the commit record is durable, redo replays the after-images and the transaction survives; the missing data pages are exactly what redo is for.
  3. (C) is true. Serial execution is the definition of the ideal, not the implementation; 2PL, timestamp ordering and validation are how real systems approximate it.
  4. (D) is true. That is the definition of durability: the loss of volatile memory must not lose a committed transaction.

Answer: Options (A), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Reading (B) as true because the pages are missing. Missing pages are recoverable from the log; only a missing commit record is fatal.

Takeaway. Log first, then pages — and a durable commit record is enough on its own.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: A system uses the deferred-update technique, so no update reaches the database until its transaction has committed. The log on stable storage reads, in order: ⟨T1 start⟩, ⟨T1 write A⟩, ⟨T1 commit⟩, ⟨T2 start⟩, ⟨T2 write B⟩, ⟨T3 start⟩, ⟨T3 write C⟩, ⟨T3 commit⟩, and then the machine crashes. Under deferred-update (redo-only) recovery, how many transactions are redone?(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Question 5NATmediumacid-propertiesoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

A system uses the deferred-update technique, so no update reaches the database until its transaction has committed. The log on stable storage reads, in order: ⟨T1 start⟩, ⟨T1 write A⟩, ⟨T1 commit⟩, ⟨T2 start⟩, ⟨T2 write B⟩, ⟨T3 start⟩, ⟨T3 write C⟩, ⟨T3 commit⟩, and then the machine crashes. Under deferred-update (redo-only) recovery, how many transactions are redone?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Under deferred update no uncommitted update ever reaches the database, so nothing needs undoing; recovery is redo-only, and only transactions with a commit record in the log are redone.Step by step.Scan the log and list the transactions that carry a commit record: T1 and T3.T2 has a start record and a write record but no commit record, so it never committed and its write never reached the database. It is simply ignored.Redo replays the after-images of T1 and T3.Number of transactions redone = 2.Answer: 2Common misconception. Counting T2 because it appears in the log, or counting data items instead of transactions. The question asks for transactions redone, and an uncommitted transaction contributes none.Takeaway. Redo-only recovery redoes exactly the transactions with a commit record.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Under deferred update no uncommitted update ever reaches the database, so nothing needs undoing; recovery is redo-only, and only transactions with a commit record in the log are redone.

Step by step.

  1. Scan the log and list the transactions that carry a commit record: T1 and T3.
  2. T2 has a start record and a write record but no commit record, so it never committed and its write never reached the database. It is simply ignored.
  3. Redo replays the after-images of T1 and T3.
  4. Number of transactions redone = 2.

Answer: 2

Common misconception. Counting T2 because it appears in the log, or counting data items instead of transactions. The question asks for transactions redone, and an uncommitted transaction contributes none.

Takeaway. Redo-only recovery redoes exactly the transactions with a commit record.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Two operations conflict when they belong to different transactions, access the same data item, and at least one of them is a write. Which one of the following pairs of operations does NOT conflict?
questions.question_html:
Question 6MCQeasyschedules-serializability-conflict-viewstandard textbookMarks: 1

Two operations conflict when they belong to different transactions, access the same data item, and at least one of them is a write. Which one of the following pairs of operations does NOT conflict?
options: r1(X) and w2(X)
w1(X) and w2(X)
r1(X) and r2(X)
w1(X) and r2(X)
options_html: r1(X) and w2(X)
w1(X) and w2(X)
r1(X) and r2(X)
w1(X) and r2(X)
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. A conflict needs three things at once: different transactions, the same data item, and at least one write. Two reads on the same item fail the third condition, because neither operation can change what the other sees.Step by step.(A) r1(X) and w2(X): same item, different transactions, one write. Conflict (read–write).(B) w1(X) and w2(X): two writes on the same item. Conflict (write–write).(C) r1(X) and r2(X): two reads on the same item. Neither changes the value, so their order cannot matter. No conflict.(D) w1(X) and r2(X): one write. Conflict (write–read).Answer: Option (C) — two reads never conflict.Why the other options are wrong. Each of (A), (B) and (D) contains a write on X by a different transaction, so swapping the two operations could change a value that someone reads.Common misconception. Believing that any two operations on the same item conflict. Read–read is the one combination that is always harmless.Takeaway. Conflicts come in three shapes: R–W, W–R and W–W. R–R is not one of them.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A conflict needs three things at once: different transactions, the same data item, and at least one write. Two reads on the same item fail the third condition, because neither operation can change what the other sees.

Step by step.

  1. (A) r1(X) and w2(X): same item, different transactions, one write. Conflict (read–write).
  2. (B) w1(X) and w2(X): two writes on the same item. Conflict (write–write).
  3. (C) r1(X) and r2(X): two reads on the same item. Neither changes the value, so their order cannot matter. No conflict.
  4. (D) w1(X) and r2(X): one write. Conflict (write–read).

Answer: Option (C) — two reads never conflict.

Why the other options are wrong. Each of (A), (B) and (D) contains a write on X by a different transaction, so swapping the two operations could change a value that someone reads.

Common misconception. Believing that any two operations on the same item conflict. Read–read is the one combination that is always harmless.

Takeaway. Conflicts come in three shapes: R–W, W–R and W–W. R–R is not one of them.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Consider the schedule S = r1(X); w2(X); r3(X); w1(Y); w3(Y) of three transactions over data items X and Y. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html:
Question 7MCQmediumschedules-serializability-conflict-vieworiginal synthesisMarks: 1

Consider the schedule S = r1(X); w2(X); r3(X); w1(Y); w3(Y) of three transactions over data items X and Y. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: S is conflict serializable, and it is conflict equivalent to the serial order T1, T2, T3.
S is conflict serializable, and it is conflict equivalent to the serial order T2, T1, T3.
S is not conflict serializable, because the precedence graph contains the cycle T1 → T2 → T1.
S is conflict serializable, and it is conflict equivalent to the serial order T1, T3, T2.
options_html: S is conflict serializable, and it is conflict equivalent to the serial order T1, T2, T3.
S is conflict serializable, and it is conflict equivalent to the serial order T2, T1, T3.
S is not conflict serializable, because the precedence graph contains the cycle T1 → T2 → T1.
S is conflict serializable, and it is conflict equivalent to the serial order T1, T3, T2.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Draw the precedence graph: an edge Ti → Tj for every pair of conflicting operations in which Ti comes first. The schedule is conflict serializable exactly when that graph is acyclic, and any topological order of it is an equivalent serial order.Step by step.r1(X) before w2(X): edge T1 → T2.w2(X) before r3(X): edge T2 → T3.w1(Y) before w3(Y): edge T1 → T3.r1(X) and r3(X) are both reads, so they add no edge; the two writes are on different items, so they add none either.The graph is T1 → T2 → T3 with the shortcut T1 → T3. It is acyclic, and the only topological order is T1, T2, T3.Answer: Option (A) — acyclic, equivalent to T1, T2, T3.Why the other options are wrong.(B) The edge T1 → T2 forbids putting T2 first.(C) There is no edge T2 → T1 anywhere: the only operations T2 and T1 share are on X, and there r1(X) precedes w2(X).(D) The edge T2 → T3 forbids putting T3 before T2.Common misconception. Counting r1(X) and r3(X) as a conflict and inventing an edge T1 → T3 (or T3 → T1) that the schedule does not justify.Takeaway. Read the graph off the conflicting pairs only, then topologically sort it.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Draw the precedence graph: an edge Ti → Tj for every pair of conflicting operations in which Ti comes first. The schedule is conflict serializable exactly when that graph is acyclic, and any topological order of it is an equivalent serial order.

Step by step.

  1. r1(X) before w2(X): edge T1 → T2.
  2. w2(X) before r3(X): edge T2 → T3.
  3. w1(Y) before w3(Y): edge T1 → T3.
  4. r1(X) and r3(X) are both reads, so they add no edge; the two writes are on different items, so they add none either.
  5. The graph is T1 → T2 → T3 with the shortcut T1 → T3. It is acyclic, and the only topological order is T1, T2, T3.

Answer: Option (A) — acyclic, equivalent to T1, T2, T3.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) The edge T1 → T2 forbids putting T2 first.
  • (C) There is no edge T2 → T1 anywhere: the only operations T2 and T1 share are on X, and there r1(X) precedes w2(X).
  • (D) The edge T2 → T3 forbids putting T3 before T2.

Common misconception. Counting r1(X) and r3(X) as a conflict and inventing an edge T1 → T3 (or T3 → T1) that the schedule does not justify.

Takeaway. Read the graph off the conflicting pairs only, then topologically sort it.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which of the following statements about view serializability are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 8MSQmediumschedules-serializability-conflict-vieworiginal synthesisMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about view serializability are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Every view-serializable schedule is conflict serializable.
Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable.
Deciding whether a given schedule is view serializable is NP-complete.
A schedule that contains a blind write can be view serializable without being conflict serializable.
options_html: Every view-serializable schedule is conflict serializable.
Every conflict-serializable schedule is view serializable.
Deciding whether a given schedule is view serializable is NP-complete.
A schedule that contains a blind write can be view serializable without being conflict serializable.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. View equivalence is weaker than conflict equivalence. Two schedules are view equivalent if they have the same reads-from relation and the same final write on every item; they are conflict equivalent only if one can be turned into the other by swapping adjacent non-conflicting operations.Step by step.(A) is false. The inclusion runs the other way: conflict serializability implies view serializability, not the reverse.(B) is true. If a schedule is conflict equivalent to a serial schedule, it reads the same values from the same transactions and has the same final writes, so it is also view equivalent to it.(C) is true. View serializability has no polynomial test; the decision problem is NP-complete, which is why practical schedulers settle for conflict serializability.(D) is true. Blind writes are the extra freedom view equivalence allows: the writer does not read, so its position relative to other writes can matter less than conflict equivalence assumes.Answer: Options (B), (C) and (D).Common misconception. Assuming the two notions coincide because they coincide on schedules without blind writes. That is exactly the case where the difference disappears.Takeaway. Conflict serializable ⊂ view serializable ⊂ serializable, and only the first has an efficient test.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. View equivalence is weaker than conflict equivalence. Two schedules are view equivalent if they have the same reads-from relation and the same final write on every item; they are conflict equivalent only if one can be turned into the other by swapping adjacent non-conflicting operations.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is false. The inclusion runs the other way: conflict serializability implies view serializability, not the reverse.
  2. (B) is true. If a schedule is conflict equivalent to a serial schedule, it reads the same values from the same transactions and has the same final writes, so it is also view equivalent to it.
  3. (C) is true. View serializability has no polynomial test; the decision problem is NP-complete, which is why practical schedulers settle for conflict serializability.
  4. (D) is true. Blind writes are the extra freedom view equivalence allows: the writer does not read, so its position relative to other writes can matter less than conflict equivalence assumes.

Answer: Options (B), (C) and (D).

Common misconception. Assuming the two notions coincide because they coincide on schedules without blind writes. That is exactly the case where the difference disappears.

Takeaway. Conflict serializable ⊂ view serializable ⊂ serializable, and only the first has an efficient test.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Consider the schedule S = r1(X); w2(X); w1(X); w3(X) of three transactions over the single data item X, where every write stores a distinct value. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html:
Question 9MCQhardschedules-serializability-conflict-vieworiginal synthesisMarks: 1

Consider the schedule S = r1(X); w2(X); w1(X); w3(X) of three transactions over the single data item X, where every write stores a distinct value. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: S is conflict serializable but not view serializable.
S is view serializable but not conflict serializable.
S is both conflict serializable and view serializable.
S is neither conflict serializable nor view serializable.
options_html: S is conflict serializable but not view serializable.
S is view serializable but not conflict serializable.
S is both conflict serializable and view serializable.
S is neither conflict serializable nor view serializable.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Test the two notions separately. The precedence graph settles conflict serializability. For view serializability, compare the reads-from relation and the final write with those of a serial schedule.Step by step.Conflicts on X: r1(X) before w2(X) gives T1 → T2.w2(X) before w1(X) gives T2 → T1. The graph already contains the cycle T1 → T2 → T1, so S is not conflict serializable.Now look at what S actually does: T1 reads the initial value of X (no write precedes r1(X)), and the last write is w3(X).The serial schedule T1, T2, T3 gives exactly the same two facts: T1 reads the initial value, and T3 writes last. T2 and T3 are blind writers, so nothing they read can differ.Hence S is view equivalent to the serial order T1, T2, T3, and is view serializable.Answer: Option (B) — view serializable, not conflict serializable.Why the other options are wrong.(A) and (C) fail because the cycle T1 → T2 → T1 is real: two writes to X by different transactions are in the order w2 then w1, which is the reverse of the order r1 then w2.(D) fails because of step 4: the serial order T1, T2, T3 reproduces every read and the final write.Common misconception. Stopping at the precedence graph. A cycle rules out conflict serializability, not serializability itself; a blind write is precisely the case where the extra freedom matters.Takeaway. Blind writes are the reason view serializability is strictly weaker than conflict serializability.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Test the two notions separately. The precedence graph settles conflict serializability. For view serializability, compare the reads-from relation and the final write with those of a serial schedule.

Step by step.

  1. Conflicts on X: r1(X) before w2(X) gives T1 → T2.
  2. w2(X) before w1(X) gives T2 → T1. The graph already contains the cycle T1 → T2 → T1, so S is not conflict serializable.
  3. Now look at what S actually does: T1 reads the initial value of X (no write precedes r1(X)), and the last write is w3(X).
  4. The serial schedule T1, T2, T3 gives exactly the same two facts: T1 reads the initial value, and T3 writes last. T2 and T3 are blind writers, so nothing they read can differ.
  5. Hence S is view equivalent to the serial order T1, T2, T3, and is view serializable.

Answer: Option (B) — view serializable, not conflict serializable.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) and (C) fail because the cycle T1 → T2 → T1 is real: two writes to X by different transactions are in the order w2 then w1, which is the reverse of the order r1 then w2.
  • (D) fails because of step 4: the serial order T1, T2, T3 reproduces every read and the final write.

Common misconception. Stopping at the precedence graph. A cycle rules out conflict serializability, not serializability itself; a blind write is precisely the case where the extra freedom matters.

Takeaway. Blind writes are the reason view serializability is strictly weaker than conflict serializability.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. The precedence graph has one edge Ti → Tj for each pair of conflicting operations in which Ti executes first. Several conflicting pairs between the same two transactions still give a single edge.

Step by step.

  1. On X: r1(X) precedes w2(X), so edge T1 → T2.
  2. On Y: r2(Y) precedes w3(Y), so edge T2 → T3.
  3. On Y: r2(Y) precedes w1(Y), so edge T2 → T1.
  4. On Y: w3(Y) precedes w1(Y), so edge T3 → T1.
  5. Distinct edges: T1 → T2, T2 → T3, T2 → T1 and T3 → T1, that is 4.

Answer: 4

Common misconception. Counting conflicting operation pairs instead of distinct edges, which double-counts the T2 → T1 pair, or forgetting the write–write pair w3(Y), w1(Y).

Takeaway. List the conflicting pairs, then collapse them into distinct transaction edges. (The graph has the cycle T1 → T2 → T1, so S is not conflict serializable — but the edge count is what was asked.)

questions.question_html:
Question 11MCQeasyrecoverability-cascadelessstandard textbookMarks: 1

A schedule is NOT recoverable when there are transactions Ti and Tj such that Tj reads a data item written by Ti, and
options: Ti commits before Tj commits.
Tj aborts after Ti has committed.
both transactions read the item before either of them writes it.

Tj aborts after Ti has committed.
both transactions read the item before either of them writes it.
Tj commits before Ti commits.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Recoverability is about being able to undo a transaction that others have read from. If the reader commits first and the writer then aborts, the reader’s commit rests on a value that never existed, and there is no way to take it back.Step by step.Tj reads a value written by Ti, so Tj depends on Ti.A recoverable schedule must delay Tj’s commit until Ti has committed.If Tj commits first and Ti then aborts, Tj has already published a value derived from a transaction that was rolled back.That is exactly the definition of a non-recoverable schedule.Answer: Option (D) — the reader commits before the writer.Why the other options are wrong.(A) is the recoverable case: the writer finishes first, so a rollback can still cascade to the reader.(B) is harmless: an aborted reader leaves nothing behind.(C) describes a read–read pair, which is not a dependency at all.Common misconception. Confusing recoverability with "no dirty reads". A schedule can have dirty reads and still be recoverable, as long as the readers wait for the writer to finish.Takeaway. Reader commits first, writer aborts later ⇒ non-recoverable.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Recoverability is about being able to undo a transaction that others have read from. If the reader commits first and the writer then aborts, the reader’s commit rests on a value that never existed, and there is no way to take it back.

Step by step.

  1. Tj reads a value written by Ti, so Tj depends on Ti.
  2. A recoverable schedule must delay Tj’s commit until Ti has committed.
  3. If Tj commits first and Ti then aborts, Tj has already published a value derived from a transaction that was rolled back.
  4. That is exactly the definition of a non-recoverable schedule.

Answer: Option (D) — the reader commits before the writer.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) is the recoverable case: the writer finishes first, so a rollback can still cascade to the reader.
  • (B) is harmless: an aborted reader leaves nothing behind.
  • (C) describes a read–read pair, which is not a dependency at all.

Common misconception. Confusing recoverability with "no dirty reads". A schedule can have dirty reads and still be recoverable, as long as the readers wait for the writer to finish.

Takeaway. Reader commits first, writer aborts later ⇒ non-recoverable.

questions.question: Which one of the following statements about a strict schedule is TRUE?
questions.question_html:
Question 12MCQeasyrecoverability-cascadelessoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

Which one of the following statements about a strict schedule is TRUE?
options: Every strict schedule is cascadeless, and therefore recoverable as well.
A strict schedule can still be non-recoverable when two transactions interleave their writes.
Strictness is a property of the locking protocol alone; no schedule can be strict unless locks are used.
A strict schedule can never contain a blind write.
options_html: Every strict schedule is cascadeless, and therefore recoverable as well.
A strict schedule can still be non-recoverable when two transactions interleave their writes.
Strictness is a property of the locking protocol alone; no schedule can be strict unless locks are used.
A strict schedule can never contain a blind write.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. A strict schedule forbids a transaction from reading or writing an item until the last transaction that wrote it has committed or aborted. Cascadelessness forbids only the read part. So strict is the stronger condition, and the implications run one way.Step by step.Strict forbids both dirty reads and dirty writes.Cascadeless forbids only dirty reads, so every strict schedule is cascadeless.Cascadeless forbids every dependency on an uncommitted value, so the commit of a reader can never precede the commit of its writer; every cascadeless schedule is recoverable.Chaining the two gives: strict ⇒ cascadeless ⇒ recoverable.Answer: Option (A).Why the other options are wrong.(B) Strictness is defined on the schedule, and it already rules out the dependency that non-recoverability needs.(C) Locks are one way to enforce strictness, not the definition of it; the definition talks only about when reads and writes may occur.(D) A blind write is a write without a read; it is perfectly compatible with strictness, which constrains the order of writes, not their presence.Common misconception. Treating strict and cascadeless as synonyms, or believing the implication runs both ways.Takeaway. strict ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ recoverable ⊂ all schedules.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A strict schedule forbids a transaction from reading or writing an item until the last transaction that wrote it has committed or aborted. Cascadelessness forbids only the read part. So strict is the stronger condition, and the implications run one way.

Step by step.

  1. Strict forbids both dirty reads and dirty writes.
  2. Cascadeless forbids only dirty reads, so every strict schedule is cascadeless.
  3. Cascadeless forbids every dependency on an uncommitted value, so the commit of a reader can never precede the commit of its writer; every cascadeless schedule is recoverable.
  4. Chaining the two gives: strict ⇒ cascadeless ⇒ recoverable.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) Strictness is defined on the schedule, and it already rules out the dependency that non-recoverability needs.
  • (C) Locks are one way to enforce strictness, not the definition of it; the definition talks only about when reads and writes may occur.
  • (D) A blind write is a write without a read; it is perfectly compatible with strictness, which constrains the order of writes, not their presence.

Common misconception. Treating strict and cascadeless as synonyms, or believing the implication runs both ways.

Takeaway. strict ⊂ cascadeless ⊂ recoverable ⊂ all schedules.

questions.question: Consider the schedule S = r1(X); w1(X); r2(X); w2(Y); c2; a1, in which T1 finally aborts. Which one of the following is TRUE?
questions.question_html:
Question 13MCQhardrecoverability-cascadelessoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

Consider the schedule S = r1(X); w1(X); r2(X); w2(Y); c2; a1, in which T1 finally aborts. Which one of the following is TRUE?
options: S is recoverable, because rolling back T1 leaves T2’s commit valid.
S is cascadeless, because T2 wrote only Y, which T1 never touched.
S is not recoverable, because T2 read X from T1 and committed before T1 terminated.
S is strict, because T1’s abort has no effect on the value of Y.
options_html: S is recoverable, because rolling back T1 leaves T2’s commit valid.
S is cascadeless, because T2 wrote only Y, which T1 never touched.
S is not recoverable, because T2 read X from T1 and committed before T1 terminated.
S is strict, because T1’s abort has no effect on the value of Y.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Check the dependency first, then the commit order. T2 read a value written by T1, so T2 must not commit until T1 has committed. A schedule that breaks that rule cannot be repaired by any later action.Step by step.r2(X) follows w1(X), so T2 reads from T1 — a dirty read, since T1 has not committed.c2 comes before a1, so T2 commits while T1 is still unresolved.T1 then aborts, so the value of X that T2 used is rolled back.T2’s committed effect, which was derived from that value, can no longer be undone. The schedule is not recoverable.Answer: Option (C).Why the other options are wrong.(A) Recoverability is decided by the commit order of reader and writer, and here it is the wrong way round.(B) Cascadelessness forbids exactly the dirty read in step 1, regardless of which item was written later.(D) Strictness requires that no other transaction read or write X before T1 finished; r2(X) breaks that.Common misconception. Thinking the writer’s abort is enough to fix things. Once the reader has committed, a cascading rollback is impossible.Takeaway. A dirty read plus a reader that commits first is the textbook non-recoverable pattern.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Check the dependency first, then the commit order. T2 read a value written by T1, so T2 must not commit until T1 has committed. A schedule that breaks that rule cannot be repaired by any later action.

Step by step.

  1. r2(X) follows w1(X), so T2 reads from T1 — a dirty read, since T1 has not committed.
  2. c2 comes before a1, so T2 commits while T1 is still unresolved.
  3. T1 then aborts, so the value of X that T2 used is rolled back.
  4. T2’s committed effect, which was derived from that value, can no longer be undone. The schedule is not recoverable.

Answer: Option (C).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) Recoverability is decided by the commit order of reader and writer, and here it is the wrong way round.
  • (B) Cascadelessness forbids exactly the dirty read in step 1, regardless of which item was written later.
  • (D) Strictness requires that no other transaction read or write X before T1 finished; r2(X) breaks that.

Common misconception. Thinking the writer’s abort is enough to fix things. Once the reader has committed, a cascading rollback is impossible.

Takeaway. A dirty read plus a reader that commits first is the textbook non-recoverable pattern.

Which of the following statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Every strict schedule is cascadeless.
Every cascadeless schedule is recoverable.
Every recoverable schedule is cascadeless.
A schedule in which no transaction reads uncommitted data is necessarily conflict serializable.
options_html: Every strict schedule is cascadeless.
Every cascadeless schedule is recoverable.
Every recoverable schedule is cascadeless.
A schedule in which no transaction reads uncommitted data is necessarily conflict serializable.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Three nested classes: strict schedules inside cascadeless schedules inside recoverable schedules. Serializability is a different axis altogether — it is about the order of conflicting operations, not about when commits happen.Step by step.(A) is true. Strict forbids dirty reads and dirty writes; cascadeless forbids dirty reads. The stronger condition implies the weaker.(B) is true. With no dirty read there is no dependency on an uncommitted value, so every reader commits after its writer and the schedule is recoverable.(C) is false. A recoverable schedule may still contain a dirty read, provided the reader commits only after the writer. It then needs cascading rollback but stays recoverable.(D) is false. questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Three nested classes: strict schedules inside cascadeless schedules inside recoverable schedules. Serializability is a different axis altogether — it is about the order of conflicting operations, not about when commits happen.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true. Strict forbids dirty reads and dirty writes; cascadeless forbids dirty reads. The stronger condition implies the weaker.
  2. (B) is true. With no dirty read there is no dependency on an uncommitted value, so every reader commits after its writer and the schedule is recoverable.
  3. (C) is false. A recoverable schedule may still contain a dirty read, provided the reader commits only after the writer. It then needs cascading rollback but stays recoverable.
  4. (D) is false. Cascadelessness says nothing about the order of conflicting operations between transactions that never share uncommitted data, so a cascadeless schedule can still be non-serializable.

Answer: Options (A) and (B).

Common misconception. Merging the recoverability family with the serializability family. A schedule can be serializable but non-recoverable, and recoverable but non-serializable.

Takeaway. Recoverability and serializability answer different questions and neither implies the other.

questions.question: Consider the schedule S = r1(X); w1(X); r2(X); r1(Y); w2(Y), and suppose T1 aborts. Under cascading rollback, what is the total number of transactions that are rolled back, counting T1 itself?(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Question 15NATeasyrecoverability-cascadelessoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

Consider the schedule S = r1(X); w1(X); r2(X); r1(Y); w2(Y), and suppose T1 aborts. Under cascading rollback, what is the total number of transactions that are rolled back, counting T1 itself?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Cascading rollback propagates along dirty reads: if Tj read an item from Ti and Ti rolls back, Tj must roll back too, and so on transitively.Step by step.T1 aborts: rollback count = 1.r2(X) read X after w1(X), so T2 depends on T1.T2 must therefore roll back as well: rollback count = 2.T2 wrote only Y and no third transaction read it, so the cascade stops.Answer: 2Common misconception. Counting only T1, or adding T1 twice because it both writes and aborts.Takeaway. Follow the reads-from edges out of the aborted transaction; each reachable transaction rolls back once.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Cascading rollback propagates along dirty reads: if Tj read an item from Ti and Ti rolls back, Tj must roll back too, and so on transitively.

Step by step.

  1. T1 aborts: rollback count = 1.
  2. r2(X) read X after w1(X), so T2 depends on T1.
  3. T2 must therefore roll back as well: rollback count = 2.
  4. T2 wrote only Y and no third transaction read it, so the cascade stops.

Answer: 2

Common misconception. Counting only T1, or adding T1 twice because it both writes and aborts.

Takeaway. Follow the reads-from edges out of the aborted transaction; each reachable transaction rolls back once.

questions.question: Under strict two-phase locking, when may a transaction release an exclusive lock that it holds?
questions.question_html:
Question 16MCQeasytwo-phase-locking-2pl-strict-rigorousstandard textbookMarks: 1

Under strict two-phase locking, when may a transaction release an exclusive lock that it holds?
options: As soon as it has finished using the item, even if it has not yet committed.
Only when it commits or aborts.
At the end of its growing phase, provided that all its other locks are already held.
Whenever the lock manager decides to grant a conflicting request.
options_html: As soon as it has finished using the item, even if it has not yet committed.
Only when it commits or aborts.
At the end of its growing phase, provided that all its other locks are already held.
Whenever the lock manager decides to grant a conflicting request.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Strict 2PL keeps every exclusive lock until the end of the transaction, which is what stops anyone from reading or overwriting an uncommitted value. That is also why strict 2PL removes cascading rollback.Step by step.2PL allows a growing phase, in which locks are acquired, followed by a shrinking phase, in which they are released.Strict 2PL adds one restriction: no exclusive lock may be released before the transaction commits or aborts.The shrinking phase of a strict transaction therefore coincides with its termination.Releasing earlier would let another transaction read or overwrite a value that might still be rolled back.Answer: Option (B) — at commit or abort only.Why the other options are wrong.(A) That is plain lock-based execution, which permits dirty reads.(C) Releasing at the end of the growing phase is basic 2PL, not strict 2PL.(D) Locks are released by their holder, never by the lock manager on someone else’s behalf.Common misconception. Thinking the shrinking phase must start before commit. In strict 2PL it does not start at all until the transaction ends.Takeaway. Strict 2PL = 2PL + hold exclusive locks to the end.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Strict 2PL keeps every exclusive lock until the end of the transaction, which is what stops anyone from reading or overwriting an uncommitted value. That is also why strict 2PL removes cascading rollback.

Step by step.

  1. 2PL allows a growing phase, in which locks are acquired, followed by a shrinking phase, in which they are released.
  2. Strict 2PL adds one restriction: no exclusive lock may be released before the transaction commits or aborts.
  3. The shrinking phase of a strict transaction therefore coincides with its termination.
  4. Releasing earlier would let another transaction read or overwrite a value that might still be rolled back.

Answer: Option (B) — at commit or abort only.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) That is plain lock-based execution, which permits dirty reads.
  • (C) Releasing at the end of the growing phase is basic 2PL, not strict 2PL.
  • (D) Locks are released by their holder, never by the lock manager on someone else’s behalf.

Common misconception. Thinking the shrinking phase must start before commit. In strict 2PL it does not start at all until the transaction ends.

Takeaway. Strict 2PL = 2PL + hold exclusive locks to the end.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which one of the following protocols guarantees both conflict serializability and freedom from cascading rollback?
questions.question_html:
Question 17MCQeasytwo-phase-locking-2pl-strict-rigorousoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

Which one of the following protocols guarantees both conflict serializability and freedom from cascading rollback?
options: Basic two-phase locking.
Conservative two-phase locking.
Two-phase locking with lock upgrades but without the strictness rule.
Strict two-phase locking.
options_html: Basic two-phase locking.
Conservative two-phase locking.
Two-phase locking with lock upgrades but without the strictness rule.
Strict two-phase locking.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Serializability and recoverability are separate guarantees. 2PL in any form gives conflict serializability; only the strict form also keeps exclusive locks to the end and so prevents dirty reads.Step by step.Basic 2PL: conflict serializable, but locks may be released before commit, so cascading rollback is possible.Conservative 2PL: deadlock-free and conflict serializable, but it says nothing about when locks are released.Strict 2PL: 2PL plus hold-exclusive-locks-to-the-end, so no transaction can read an uncommitted value.No dirty read means no cascading rollback; 2PL means conflict serializable. Both guarantees together belong to strict 2PL.Answer: Option (D).Why the other options are wrong. (A) and (C) permit early release, and (B) is silent about release timing; all three can therefore allow cascading rollback.Common misconception. Believing 2PL alone is enough. Serializability does not stop a reader from reading uncommitted data.Takeaway. Conflict serializability ← 2PL; no cascading rollback ← strictness. Strict 2PL supplies both.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Serializability and recoverability are separate guarantees. 2PL in any form gives conflict serializability; only the strict form also keeps exclusive locks to the end and so prevents dirty reads.

Step by step.

  1. Basic 2PL: conflict serializable, but locks may be released before commit, so cascading rollback is possible.
  2. Conservative 2PL: deadlock-free and conflict serializable, but it says nothing about when locks are released.
  3. Strict 2PL: 2PL plus hold-exclusive-locks-to-the-end, so no transaction can read an uncommitted value.
  4. No dirty read means no cascading rollback; 2PL means conflict serializable. Both guarantees together belong to strict 2PL.

Answer: Option (D).

Why the other options are wrong. (A) and (C) permit early release, and (B) is silent about release timing; all three can therefore allow cascading rollback.

Common misconception. Believing 2PL alone is enough. Serializability does not stop a reader from reading uncommitted data.

Takeaway. Conflict serializability ← 2PL; no cascading rollback ← strictness. Strict 2PL supplies both.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which of the following statements about two-phase locking and its variants are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 18MSQhardtwo-phase-locking-2pl-strict-rigorousoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about two-phase locking and its variants are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Rigorous two-phase locking holds every lock, shared as well as exclusive, until the transaction commits or aborts, so it is a special case of strict two-phase locking.
Conservative two-phase locking acquires all of a transaction’s locks before it starts, which removes deadlock at the cost of less concurrency.
Basic two-phase locking guarantees freedom from deadlock.
Strict two-phase locking guarantees conflict-serializable schedules.
options_html: Rigorous two-phase locking holds every lock, shared as well as exclusive, until the transaction commits or aborts, so it is a special case of strict two-phase locking.
Conservative two-phase locking acquires all of a transaction’s locks before it starts, which removes deadlock at the cost of less concurrency.
Basic two-phase locking guarantees freedom from deadlock.
Strict two-phase locking guarantees conflict-serializable schedules.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Keep the guarantees apart: 2PL buys conflict serializability, strictness buys recoverability without cascades, and only the conservative variant buys deadlock freedom — by paying for it with concurrency.Step by step.(A) is true. Rigorous 2PL releases all locks together at commit; since it also holds exclusive locks to the end, it satisfies the strict rule and is the stronger special case.(B) is true. If every lock is obtained up front, a transaction never waits while holding a lock, so a cycle cannot form. The price is that locks are held while they are still unused.(C) is false. Basic 2PL is deadlock-prone: T1 can hold X and wait for Y while T2 holds Y and waits for X.(D) is true. That is the theorem behind 2PL: any schedule produced by a 2PL-compliant set of transactions is conflict serializable.Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).Common misconception. Assuming the growing and shrinking phases make deadlock impossible. They only fix the order of acquisition and release; two transactions can still each hold what the other wants.Takeaway. 2PL ⇒ serializable; strict ⇒ no cascades; conservative ⇒ no deadlock.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Keep the guarantees apart: 2PL buys conflict serializability, strictness buys recoverability without cascades, and only the conservative variant buys deadlock freedom — by paying for it with concurrency.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true. Rigorous 2PL releases all locks together at commit; since it also holds exclusive locks to the end, it satisfies the strict rule and is the stronger special case.
  2. (B) is true. If every lock is obtained up front, a transaction never waits while holding a lock, so a cycle cannot form. The price is that locks are held while they are still unused.
  3. (C) is false. Basic 2PL is deadlock-prone: T1 can hold X and wait for Y while T2 holds Y and waits for X.
  4. (D) is true. That is the theorem behind 2PL: any schedule produced by a 2PL-compliant set of transactions is conflict serializable.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (D).

Common misconception. Assuming the growing and shrinking phases make deadlock impossible. They only fix the order of acquisition and release; two transactions can still each hold what the other wants.

Takeaway. 2PL ⇒ serializable; strict ⇒ no cascades; conservative ⇒ no deadlock.

questions.question: Under two-phase locking, which one of the following is TRUE about changing the mode of a lock that the transaction already holds?
questions.question_html:
Question 19MCQmediumtwo-phase-locking-2pl-strict-rigorousstandard textbookMarks: 1

Under two-phase locking, which one of the following is TRUE about changing the mode of a lock that the transaction already holds?
options: An upgrade from shared to exclusive must happen in the growing phase, and a downgrade from exclusive to shared may only happen in the shrinking phase.
An upgrade and a downgrade may both happen in either phase.
An upgrade must happen in the shrinking phase and a downgrade in the growing phase.
Lock conversions are not permitted in two-phase locking at all.
options_html: An upgrade from shared to exclusive must happen in the growing phase, and a downgrade from exclusive to shared may only happen in the shrinking phase.
An upgrade and a downgrade may both happen in either phase.
An upgrade must happen in the shrinking phase and a downgrade in the growing phase.
Lock conversions are not permitted in two-phase locking at all.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. An upgrade asks for more privilege, which is an acquisition, so it belongs to the growing phase. A downgrade gives privilege back, which is a release, so it belongs to the shrinking phase.

Step by step.

  1. The growing phase may only add locks or strengthen them.
  2. An upgrade S(X) → X(X) strengthens a lock, so it must occur while the transaction is still growing.
  3. The shrinking phase may only drop locks or weaken them.
  4. A downgrade X(X) → S(X) weakens a lock, so it can occur only after the growing phase has ended.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong. (B) would let a transaction strengthen a lock after it had begun releasing others, which is exactly what 2PL forbids. (C) inverts the two phases. (D) is false: upgrades are standard practice and are what let a transaction read an item and then write it.

Common misconception. Treating an upgrade as "not a new lock request". It is one, and it must respect the phase rule — and it can also deadlock two transactions that hold shared locks and both try to upgrade.

Takeaway. Strengthen while growing, weaken while shrinking.

questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. A deadlock is a cycle in the wait-for graph, and aborting one transaction on a cycle breaks that cycle. Disjoint cycles need one victim each, because no single transaction lies on both.

Step by step.

  1. The graph has two cycles and they are disjoint, so they share no transaction.
  2. One abort on the 3-cycle removes all three of its edges and leaves the 2-cycle untouched.
  3. The 2-cycle still needs its own victim.
  4. Two aborts therefore suffice, and one cannot: a single victim lies on at most one of the two cycles.

Answer: 2

Common misconception. Taking the length of a cycle as the number of victims, or the total edge count. Only the number of disjoint cycles matters.

Takeaway. Minimum victims = number of disjoint cycles in the wait-for graph.
