questions.question: In timestamp-based concurrency control, the timestamp of a transaction is normally assigned
questions.question_html:
Question 21MCQeasytimestamp-ordering-and-deadlocksstandard textbookMarks: 1

In timestamp-based concurrency control, the timestamp of a transaction is normally assigned
options: when the transaction issues its first write.
when the transaction commits.
when the transaction starts.
by the order in which its operations happen to reach the scheduler.
options_html: when the transaction issues its first write.
when the transaction commits.
when the transaction starts.
by the order in which its operations happen to reach the scheduler.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Timestamp ordering enforces the serial order in which transactions started. The timestamp must therefore be fixed at start time and must never change, or the protocol would have no fixed serial order to enforce.Step by step.The scheduler assigns TS(T) when T begins, typically from a counter or the system clock.Every data item carries the largest timestamp of any transaction that has read it (RTS(X)) and written it (WTS(X)).Each operation is checked against those values, and a transaction whose timestamp is too old is rejected.Because the timestamp is fixed at start, the accepted operations always reproduce the serial order of the start times.Answer: Option (C) — at start.Why the other options are wrong.(A) The first write may come long after the transaction began and would not define a consistent order.(B) A commit-time timestamp would order transactions by completion, which is not known in advance and cannot be enforced online.(D) Arrival order at the scheduler is what timestamp ordering replaces, because arrival order can differ from the order in which operations were logically issued.Common misconception. Confusing the timestamp with a lock request time. It is the start time of the transaction, assigned once.Takeaway. One timestamp per transaction, fixed at start.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Timestamp ordering enforces the serial order in which transactions started. The timestamp must therefore be fixed at start time and must never change, or the protocol would have no fixed serial order to enforce.

Step by step.

  1. The scheduler assigns TS(T) when T begins, typically from a counter or the system clock.
  2. Every data item carries the largest timestamp of any transaction that has read it (RTS(X)) and written it (WTS(X)).
  3. Each operation is checked against those values, and a transaction whose timestamp is too old is rejected.
  4. Because the timestamp is fixed at start, the accepted operations always reproduce the serial order of the start times.

Answer: Option (C) — at start.

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (A) The first write may come long after the transaction began and would not define a consistent order.
  • (B) A commit-time timestamp would order transactions by completion, which is not known in advance and cannot be enforced online.
  • (D) Arrival order at the scheduler is what timestamp ordering replaces, because arrival order can differ from the order in which operations were logically issued.

Common misconception. Confusing the timestamp with a lock request time. It is the start time of the transaction, assigned once.

Takeaway. One timestamp per transaction, fixed at start.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which one of the following concurrency-control schemes is free from deadlock?
questions.question_html:
Question 22MCQeasytimestamp-ordering-and-deadlocksoriginal synthesisMarks: 1

Which one of the following concurrency-control schemes is free from deadlock?
options: Basic two-phase locking.
Basic timestamp ordering.
Strict two-phase locking.
Two-phase locking with lock upgrades.
options_html: Basic two-phase locking.
Basic timestamp ordering.
Strict two-phase locking.
Two-phase locking with lock upgrades.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Deadlock needs a cycle of transactions each waiting for something another holds. A protocol in which no transaction ever waits cannot form such a cycle.Step by step.Timestamp ordering never blocks a request: it either executes the operation or rejects the transaction.With no waiting there is no wait-for graph to contain a cycle, so no deadlock.All three 2PL variants in the options do block: a transaction waits for a lock held by another.Lock upgrades make the waiting worse, since two transactions holding shared locks can each wait for the other to release.Answer: Option (B) — basic timestamp ordering.Why the other options are wrong. (A), (C) and (D) all allow a transaction to wait while holding locks, which is the raw material of deadlock; strictness and upgrades change the details, not the possibility.Common misconception. Believing strictness or conservativeness of the strict kind removes deadlock. Only the conservative (pre-claiming) variant does that, and it is not among the options.Takeaway. No waiting, no deadlock — the trade is that timestamp ordering aborts instead.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Deadlock needs a cycle of transactions each waiting for something another holds. A protocol in which no transaction ever waits cannot form such a cycle.

Step by step.

  1. Timestamp ordering never blocks a request: it either executes the operation or rejects the transaction.
  2. With no waiting there is no wait-for graph to contain a cycle, so no deadlock.
  3. All three 2PL variants in the options do block: a transaction waits for a lock held by another.
  4. Lock upgrades make the waiting worse, since two transactions holding shared locks can each wait for the other to release.

Answer: Option (B) — basic timestamp ordering.

Why the other options are wrong. (A), (C) and (D) all allow a transaction to wait while holding locks, which is the raw material of deadlock; strictness and upgrades change the details, not the possibility.

Common misconception. Believing strictness or conservativeness of the strict kind removes deadlock. Only the conservative (pre-claiming) variant does that, and it is not among the options.

Takeaway. No waiting, no deadlock — the trade is that timestamp ordering aborts instead.

questions.question: Under the wait–die scheme, transaction Ti requests a lock held by transaction Tj, and TS(Ti) < TS(Tj), so Ti is the older of the two. What does the scheme do?
questions.question_html:
Question 23MCQmediumtimestamp-ordering-and-deadlocksstandard textbookMarks: 1

Under the wait–die scheme, transaction Ti requests a lock held by transaction Tj, and TS(Ti) < TS(Tj), so Ti is the older of the two. What does the scheme do?
options: Ti waits for Tj to release the lock; a younger requester facing an older holder is rolled back instead.
Ti is rolled back at once, and Tj waits for Ti to restart.
Both transactions are rolled back, so that the deadlock cannot form.
Ti waits, and Tj is rolled back the next time it requests a lock held by Ti.
options_html: Ti waits for Tj to release the lock; a younger requester facing an older holder is rolled back instead.
Ti is rolled back at once, and Tj waits for Ti to restart.
Both transactions are rolled back, so that the deadlock cannot form.
Ti waits, and Tj is rolled back the next time it requests a lock held by Ti.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Wait–die removes deadlock by never letting a younger transaction wait for an older one. The older transaction waits; the younger one dies (rolls back) and restarts with its original timestamp.Step by step.TS(Ti) < TS(Tj) means Ti is older.An older requester is allowed to wait, so Ti blocks until Tj releases.Had the requester been younger (TS(Ti) > TS(Tj)), it would have been rolled back immediately rather than allowed to wait.Since waits always run from older to younger, a cycle of waits is impossible, so the scheme is deadlock-free.Answer: Option (A).Why the other options are wrong.(B) describes wound–wait, where the older transaction wounds the younger holder.(C) is not part of either scheme; only one transaction is ever a victim.(D) mixes the two schemes and would reintroduce cycles.Common misconception. Swapping wait–die with wound–wait. In wait–die the older waits and the younger dies; in wound–wait the older wounds (rolls back) the younger.Takeaway. Older waits, younger dies — and a restarted transaction keeps its old timestamp, which is why it eventually wins.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Wait–die removes deadlock by never letting a younger transaction wait for an older one. The older transaction waits; the younger one dies (rolls back) and restarts with its original timestamp.

Step by step.

  1. TS(Ti) < TS(Tj) means Ti is older.
  2. An older requester is allowed to wait, so Ti blocks until Tj releases.
  3. Had the requester been younger (TS(Ti) > TS(Tj)), it would have been rolled back immediately rather than allowed to wait.
  4. Since waits always run from older to younger, a cycle of waits is impossible, so the scheme is deadlock-free.

Answer: Option (A).

Why the other options are wrong.

  • (B) describes wound–wait, where the older transaction wounds the younger holder.
  • (C) is not part of either scheme; only one transaction is ever a victim.
  • (D) mixes the two schemes and would reintroduce cycles.

Common misconception. Swapping wait–die with wound–wait. In wait–die the older waits and the younger dies; in wound–wait the older wounds (rolls back) the younger.

Takeaway. Older waits, younger dies — and a restarted transaction keeps its old timestamp, which is why it eventually wins.

questions.subject: databases
questions.question: Which of the following statements about timestamp ordering are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
questions.question_html:
Question 24MSQmediumtimestamp-ordering-and-deadlocksoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

Which of the following statements about timestamp ordering are TRUE? (Select all that apply.)
options: Basic timestamp ordering is deadlock-free because a transaction never waits for a lock; a conflicting operation is rejected instead.
Basic timestamp ordering can roll a transaction back even when the schedule it would have produced was serializable.
Thomas’s write rule ignores an obsolete write instead of rejecting it, and so admits some schedules that basic timestamp ordering rejects.
Basic timestamp ordering on its own guarantees that every schedule it produces is recoverable.
options_html: Basic timestamp ordering is deadlock-free because a transaction never waits for a lock; a conflicting operation is rejected instead.
Basic timestamp ordering can roll a transaction back even when the schedule it would have produced was serializable.
Thomas’s write rule ignores an obsolete write instead of rejecting it, and so admits some schedules that basic timestamp ordering rejects.
Basic timestamp ordering on its own guarantees that every schedule it produces is recoverable.
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Timestamp ordering buys deadlock freedom by rejecting operations instead of waiting. The price is unnecessary aborts, which Thomas’s write rule partly recovers, and the protocol says nothing about commit order, so recoverability needs a separate rule.Step by step.(A) is true. Requests are checked against RTS and WTS and either executed or refused; nothing blocks, so no cycle can form.(B) is true. The checks are local to one data item, so a transaction can be aborted even though the schedule as a whole would have been serializable.(C) is true. If w(X) arrives with TS(T) < WTS(X), its value would be overwritten at once and can be ignored rather than causing a rollback, which admits more schedules.(D) is false. Basic timestamp ordering allows a transaction to read a value written by an uncommitted transaction, so a schedule it accepts can be non-recoverable unless the reads are additionally deferred.Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).Common misconception. Assuming a serializable protocol is automatically recoverable. Serializability orders operations; recoverability orders commits, and the two are independent.Takeaway. Timestamp ordering: no deadlock, extra aborts, no built-in recoverability.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Timestamp ordering buys deadlock freedom by rejecting operations instead of waiting. The price is unnecessary aborts, which Thomas’s write rule partly recovers, and the protocol says nothing about commit order, so recoverability needs a separate rule.

Step by step.

  1. (A) is true. Requests are checked against RTS and WTS and either executed or refused; nothing blocks, so no cycle can form.
  2. (B) is true. The checks are local to one data item, so a transaction can be aborted even though the schedule as a whole would have been serializable.
  3. (C) is true. If w(X) arrives with TS(T) < WTS(X), its value would be overwritten at once and can be ignored rather than causing a rollback, which admits more schedules.
  4. (D) is false. Basic timestamp ordering allows a transaction to read a value written by an uncommitted transaction, so a schedule it accepts can be non-recoverable unless the reads are additionally deferred.

Answer: Options (A), (B) and (C).

Common misconception. Assuming a serializable protocol is automatically recoverable. Serializability orders operations; recoverability orders commits, and the two are independent.

Takeaway. Timestamp ordering: no deadlock, extra aborts, no built-in recoverability.

questions.question: The read and write timestamps of both X and Y are 0, and TS(T1) = 10, TS(T2) = 20, TS(T3) = 30. The schedule is r1(X); w3(X); r2(X); w2(Y); r1(Y); w3(Y). Using basic timestamp ordering, how many of the six operations are rejected?(Enter an integer.)
questions.question_html:
Question 25NAThardtimestamp-ordering-and-deadlocksoriginal synthesisMarks: 2

The read and write timestamps of both X and Y are 0, and TS(T1) = 10, TS(T2) = 20, TS(T3) = 30. The schedule is r1(X); w3(X); r2(X); w2(Y); r1(Y); w3(Y). Using basic timestamp ordering, how many of the six operations are rejected?
(Enter an integer.)
questions.solution: Detailed solutionConcept. Each operation is checked against the item’s timestamps: a read is rejected if TS(T) < WTS(X), and a write is rejected if TS(T) < RTS(X) or TS(T) < WTS(X). A rejected operation aborts its transaction; the checks for the other operations still follow the same rule.Step by step.r1(X): 10 ≥ WTS(X) = 0, accepted. Now RTS(X) = 10.w3(X): 30 ≥ RTS(X) = 10 and 30 ≥ WTS(X) = 0, accepted. Now WTS(X) = 30.r2(X): 20 < WTS(X) = 30, so T2 would read a value written by a younger transaction. Rejected (1).w2(Y): 20 ≥ RTS(Y) = 0 and 20 ≥ WTS(Y) = 0, accepted. Now WTS(Y) = 20.r1(Y): 10 < WTS(Y) = 20, rejected (2).w3(Y): 30 ≥ RTS(Y) = 0 and 30 ≥ WTS(Y) = 20, accepted. Now WTS(Y) = 30.Answer: 2Common misconception. Checking a read only against WTS but forgetting to update RTS, or checking a write against WTS only. Both timestamps must be maintained on every accepted operation.Takeaway. Older operations that arrive late are the ones rejected: here two reads by older transactions, both of them too late.
questions.solution_html:
Detailed solution

Concept. Each operation is checked against the item’s timestamps: a read is rejected if TS(T) < WTS(X), and a write is rejected if TS(T) < RTS(X) or TS(T) < WTS(X). A rejected operation aborts its transaction; the checks for the other operations still follow the same rule.

Step by step.

  1. r1(X): 10 ≥ WTS(X) = 0, accepted. Now RTS(X) = 10.
  2. w3(X): 30 ≥ RTS(X) = 10 and 30 ≥ WTS(X) = 0, accepted. Now WTS(X) = 30.
  3. r2(X): 20 < WTS(X) = 30, so T2 would read a value written by a younger transaction. Rejected (1).
  4. w2(Y): 20 ≥ RTS(Y) = 0 and 20 ≥ WTS(Y) = 0, accepted. Now WTS(Y) = 20.
  5. r1(Y): 10 < WTS(Y) = 20, rejected (2).
  6. w3(Y): 30 ≥ RTS(Y) = 0 and 30 ≥ WTS(Y) = 20, accepted. Now WTS(Y) = 30.

Answer: 2

Common misconception. Checking a read only against WTS but forgetting to update RTS, or checking a write against WTS only. Both timestamps must be maintained on every accepted operation.

Takeaway. Older operations that arrive late are the ones rejected: here two reads by older transactions, both of them too late.
